A.q: A 3-year-old boy is brought for a routine visit. His father had a heart attack at 40 and was found to have very high cholesterol. What is the most appropriate step regarding the boy's lipids?
opts: Screen only after puberty
His father's premature heart attack and high cholesterol make screening appropriate from age 2, well before puberty.
Start a statin without testing
A statin follows a diagnosis of familial hypercholesterolemia; he has not yet been tested.
Wait until age 9 to 11
Routine screening is at 9 to 11, but his father's premature disease and high cholesterol justify elective screening now.
Elective lipid screening now
Correct. Elective screening is appropriate for patients as young as 2 years old with a family history of heart disease or high cholesterol.

A.q: A 55-year-old man needs two agents. Which pairing is appropriate?
opts: A beta blocker with verapamil
Both slow the sinus and atrioventricular nodes, so combining them risks severe bradycardia and heart block.
An angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor with an angiotensin receptor blocker
This combination must NEVER be used: dual blockade raises hyperkalemia and acute kidney injury risk without additional benefit.
An angiotensin receptor blocker with a dihydropyridine
Correct. The preferred combinations pair a renin-angiotensin blocker with either a dihydropyridine or a thiazide-type diuretic, because the classes act by complementary mechanisms.
Two thiazide-type diuretics together
Duplicating a class adds adverse effects without the complementary mechanism the preferred pairings provide.

A.io: Aortic stenosis
A.q: A 72-year-old woman reports six months of breathlessness when she walks her dog and one episode of fainting while gardening. She has never had cardiac imaging. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Electrocardiogram alone
An electrocardiogram may show left ventricular hypertrophy in severe disease, but with low sensitivity and questionable specificity. It cannot exclude the lesion; echocardiography is needed.
Transthoracic echocardiogram

Correct. Any patient with symptoms suggestive of aortic stenosis (exertional chest pressure, shortness of breath or syncope) should get an echocardiogram. Transthoracic imaging shows thickened, calcified leaflets with reduced opening.
Transesophageal echocardiogram
Transesophageal imaging is useful for congenital aortic stenosis. In an older adult with likely degenerative disease, the transthoracic echocardiogram is the study to order.
Left heart catheterization
Left heart catheterization gives the definitive findings, but it is not where the workup starts. Suggestive symptoms are first answered with a transthoracic echocardiogram.

A.q: When should primary aldosteronism be screened for?
opts: Every newly diagnosed hypertensive patient
Screening is targeted at the listed clues rather than applied universally, since primary hypertension accounts for the vast majority of cases.
Resistant pressure with unexplained hypokalemia

Correct. Each is a departure from the ordinary pattern, and together they define a group in which a single morning blood test can change the whole direction of management. An adrenal incidentaloma and early or familial hypertension are the other triggers.
Only after three drugs have failed and sleep apnea is excluded
Resistance is one trigger for screening, but the others -- hypokalemia, an adrenal mass, early or familial disease -- do not require that sequence first.
Only in patients with a known adrenal tumor
An adrenal incidentaloma is one trigger among several rather than a prerequisite for screening.

A.io: Tricuspid regurgitation
A.q: A 63-year-old man has a holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border that increases with inspiration. Which test confirms the lesion?
opts: Chest radiograph
A chest radiograph cannot show regurgitant flow across the tricuspid valve. The leak is confirmed with Doppler echocardiography.
Doppler echocardiogram
Correct. Tricuspid regurgitation is diagnosed with Doppler echocardiography, which shows the regurgitation and may show prolapsed, scarred or displaced leaflets.
Heart catheterization
Catheterization is not how tricuspid regurgitation is diagnosed. Doppler echocardiography shows the regurgitation and the leaflets.
Electrocardiogram
An electrocardiogram does not show a leaking valve. Tricuspid regurgitation is confirmed by Doppler echocardiography showing the regurgitant flow.

A.q: A 45-year-old man has two days of breathlessness after a viral illness. His N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide is 90. How should the result be read?
opts: Heart failure is likely
Younger than 75, heart failure becomes likely above 125. A level of 90 rules out acute failure.
The result is indeterminate
At 90 the result is clearly below the rule-out level of 300. Acute heart failure is ruled out.
Acute heart failure is ruled out
Correct. An N-terminal fragment below 300 rules out acute heart failure with a negative predictive value above 90%, and 90 is also below the under-75 heart failure threshold of 125.
Acute heart failure is likely
Nothing near this level suggests acute failure. Below 300 the N-terminal fragment rules it out.

A.q: A 52-year-old woman has a fasting low-density lipoprotein of 215 mg/dL on repeat testing. Her thyroid function, kidney function and urinalysis are normal, and she has no atherosclerotic disease. What is the most appropriate treatment?
opts: High-intensity statin
Correct. Low-density lipoprotein of 190 mg/dL or more is severe primary hypercholesterolemia: begin a high-intensity statin without calculating 10-year risk.
Coronary artery calcium scoring
Calcium scoring is reserved for uncertain intermediate-risk decisions, not severe hypercholesterolemia.
Moderate-intensity statin after risk calculation
Risk calculation and moderate intensity belong to low-density lipoprotein of 70 to 189; at 190 or more no calculation is needed.
Lifestyle alone for six months
Lifestyle continues, but at this level a high-intensity statin is indicated now rather than after a delay.

A.q: A 44-year-old man describes episodes of pounding headache, drenching sweats, palpitations and pallor, each lasting about twenty minutes. Between episodes he feels well. His blood pressure is 176/104 during an episode. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Primary aldosteronism
Aldosteronism raises pressure steadily with hypokalemia rather than producing discrete symptomatic paroxysms.
Hyperthyroidism
Thyroid excess raises cardiac output with predominantly systolic elevation and persistent symptoms rather than episodic pallor and sweating.
Pheochromocytoma
Correct. The five Ps are pressure, perspiration, palpitations, pallor and tremor, and the paroxysmal pattern with well intervals is what distinguishes it from sustained hypertension.
Obstructive sleep apnea
Sleep apnea drives sustained sympathetic activation through nocturnal hypoxemia, presenting with snoring and daytime sleepiness rather than daytime paroxysms.

A.q: A 63-year-old woman has right-sided heart failure confirmed by echocardiogram. Her team now wants to know how hemodynamically severe it is. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Right heart catheterization
Correct. Once right-sided failure is established, right heart catheterization measures its hemodynamic severity. The echocardiogram has already made the diagnosis.
Chest radiograph series
A radiograph shows effusions and heart size but not hemodynamics. Severity is measured by right heart catheterization.
Repeat echocardiogram
The echocardiogram made the diagnosis by ejection fraction. Hemodynamic severity is measured by right heart catheterization.
Troponin trend over a day
Troponin addresses infarction or ischemic cardiomyopathy. Severity is measured by right heart catheterization.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
A.q: A 74-year-old man with Parkinson disease reports lightheadedness and dimming vision within minutes of standing and fainted once in his kitchen. He is well hydrated. Supine he is 138/80 with a heart rate of 68; standing he is 106/70 with a heart rate of 70. What is the most likely cause of his syncope?
opts: A vasovagal reflex on standing
A vasovagal reflex follows emotional or physical triggers and is transient, rather than a reproducible fall each time he stands.
Volume depletion from poor intake
Volume depletion drives a significant compensatory heart rate rise and is usually visible on examination; he is well hydrated with a flat heart rate.
A ventricular arrhythmia
An arrhythmia causes abrupt collapse, often with palpitations and a fast rhythm, rather than symptoms that build after standing.
Autonomic failure from Parkinson disease
Correct. Parkinson disease is an example cause of neurogenic orthostatic hypotension, and a large pressure fall with almost no heart rate rise marks autonomic failure.

A.io: Mitral regurgitation
A.q: A 60-year-old man has palpitations and fatigue. There is a holosystolic blowing murmur at the apex that radiates to the axilla and is loudest in the left lateral decubitus position (lying on the left side). Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Mitral regurgitation
Correct. Blowing means regurgitation and holosystolic narrows it to the mitral or tricuspid valve; the apex, the radiation to the axilla and the left lateral position mark mitral regurgitation.
Aortic stenosis
Aortic stenosis is a harsh crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur at the second right intercostal space radiating to the carotids. This murmur is blowing and holosystolic.
Tricuspid regurgitation
Tricuspid regurgitation is holosystolic too, but it sits at the left mid or lower sternal border near the epigastrium and grows louder with inspiration. It does not radiate to the axilla.
Mitral valve prolapse
Mitral valve prolapse gives a mid-systolic click at the apex and is usually asymptomatic. A holosystolic blowing murmur to the axilla is established mitral regurgitation.

A.io: Angina pectoris
A.q: A 55-year-old man who received a heart transplant has exertional shortness of breath and fatigue but no chest pain. His daughter asks how he could have heart disease without pain. Which explanation is accurate?
opts: His shortness of breath rules out the heart
Shortness of breath is one of the presenting symptoms of silent ischemia, alongside cough, nausea, diaphoresis, dizziness and fatigue. It points toward the heart, not away.
Transplanted hearts cannot become ischemic
A transplanted heart can become ischemic; it simply may not signal pain. A transplanted heart is listed among the causes of silent ischemia.
Transplanted hearts can have silent ischemia

Correct. A transplanted heart is one of the settings for silent ischemia, along with diabetes and peripheral neuropathy: chest discomfort may be absent, and shortness of breath or fatigue may be the only signs.
Chest pain appears only with a full infarct
Angina is chest discomfort from transient ischemia short of infarction, so pain does not wait for an infarct. In a transplanted heart the ischemia may be silent.

A.q: A 70-year-old woman with non-neurogenic orthostatic hypotension from volume loss is lightheaded on standing in the clinic but alert, with a standing pressure of 100/62. Which treatment is inappropriate in this setting?
opts: Reviewing her medications
Medication is a listed non-neurogenic cause, so reviewing and reducing an offending drug is appropriate.
A norepinephrine infusion
Correct. Epinephrine, norepinephrine, dopamine, phenylephrine and vasopressin are listed for the emergency department and intensive care only.
Correcting the volume loss
Treating the underlying cause, here volume loss, is exactly the listed principle for orthostasis.
Slow position changes
Slow positional changes are first-line treatment for orthostatic syncope and suit an alert outpatient.

A.q: A 60-year-old man with hypertension has never had cardiac symptoms. An echocardiogram shows left ventricular hypertrophy with preserved function. Which heart failure stage is he in?
opts: Stage B
Correct. Asymptomatic structural heart disease, including left ventricular hypertrophy, is stage B, pre-heart failure. Stage A requires a structurally normal heart.
Stage A
Stage A is risk factors with a normal heart. Hypertrophy is structural disease, which puts him in stage B even without symptoms.
Stage D
Stage D is advanced heart failure. Asymptomatic hypertrophy is stage B, pre-heart failure.
Stage C
Stage C requires past or current symptoms. He has never had any, so his hypertrophy places him in stage B.

A.q: A 69-year-old man has breathlessness and orthopnea (breathlessness lying flat). His chest radiograph shows blunted costophrenic angles, cephalization (prominent upper-lobe vessels) and an enlarged cardiac silhouette. Which study best measures his ejection fraction?
opts: Multigated acquisition scan

Correct. The radiograph supports heart failure with effusion, cephalization and an increased cardiothoracic ratio, but cannot measure function. The multigated acquisition scan is the most accurate for ejection fraction.
Right heart catheterization
Catheterization grades hemodynamic severity. The multigated acquisition scan is the most accurate for ejection fraction.
Twelve-lead electrocardiogram
The electrocardiogram shows ischemia, hypertrophy or strain but not ejection fraction. The multigated acquisition scan is the most accurate.
A repeat chest radiograph
A radiograph shows effusion, vessels and heart size but no ejection fraction. The multigated acquisition scan measures it most accurately.

A.q: A 57-year-old woman with a hypertensive emergency has her pressure reduced from 240/130 to 125/75 within thirty minutes. She then develops a new hemiparesis. What happened?
opts: Hyperkalemia precipitated the event
Potassium disturbance relates to renin-angiotensin blockade rather than to the rate of pressure reduction.
She developed rebound hypertension
Rebound on abrupt withdrawal is a limitation of central alpha-2 agonists and does not explain a deficit after an over-rapid reduction.
The reduction was appropriate and the deficit is unrelated
Reducing to a chronic goal within the first hour is specifically capable of causing ischemic stroke, myocardial injury or renal failure.
Autoregulation had adapted to the higher pressure

Correct. Her organs had reset the range over which they protect their own perfusion, so a value that would be safe in anyone else left her brain underperfused. Reducing it that fast left her brain underperfused.

A.io: Pulmonic regurgitation
A.q: A 62-year-old woman with pulmonary hypertension has pulmonic regurgitation. She has no symptoms of right heart failure. Which is the most appropriate management?
opts: Treat the underlying condition

Correct. Management of pulmonic regurgitation is to treat the underlying condition -- here the pulmonary hypertension, the high-pressure cause -- with referral when it is seen on echo or right heart failure develops.
Pulmonic balloon valvuloplasty
Balloon valvuloplasty opens severe symptomatic pulmonic stenosis, and valvuloplasty is itself the most common cause of pulmonic regurgitation. Treat the underlying condition.
Transcatheter valve replacement
Transcatheter replacement is used for severe aortic stenosis. Pulmonic regurgitation is managed by treating what drives it, such as pulmonary hypertension.
Lifelong warfarin therapy
Warfarin is for mechanical valves. Pulmonic regurgitation is managed by treating the underlying condition, here pulmonary hypertension.

A.q: In the natural history staging of heart failure, what is stage D called?
opts: Symptomatic heart failure
Symptomatic heart failure, with past or current symptoms, is stage C. Stage D is advanced heart failure.
Advanced heart failure

Correct. Stage D is advanced heart failure, alongside stage A at risk, stage B pre-heart failure and stage C symptomatic heart failure. Stages C and D share the treatment columns sorted by ejection fraction.
Pre-heart failure
Pre-heart failure is stage B, asymptomatic structural disease. Stage D is advanced heart failure.
At risk for heart failure
At risk is stage A, risk factors with a normal heart. Stage D is advanced heart failure.

A.q: A 64-year-old man with reduced ejection fraction (fraction 30%) on sacubitril-valsartan, a beta blocker, spironolactone and empagliflozin develops atrial fibrillation, and rate control is being planned. Which medication should be avoided?
opts: Spironolactone
Spironolactone is a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist, a strong recommendation in reduced ejection fraction. The drug to avoid is diltiazem.
Empagliflozin
Empagliflozin is a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor, part of core therapy in reduced ejection fraction. The drug to avoid is diltiazem.
Diltiazem
Correct. Diltiazem is a calcium channel blocker, and calcium channel blockers are avoided in heart failure. His existing beta blocker belongs to core therapy.
Sacubitril-valsartan
Sacubitril-valsartan is recommended in reduced ejection fraction for class II to III. The drug to avoid is diltiazem.

A.io: Acute myocardial infraction
A.q: Why does left ventricular involvement matter in coronary occlusion?
opts: It rarely leads to heart failure
The reverse is closer: cardiogenic shock is more common in left-sided infarctions. Left ventricular involvement carries a higher mortality rate.
It spares the conduction system
Sparing conduction is not the point, and the right coronary artery is the one tied to the atrioventricular node. Left ventricular involvement matters because it carries higher mortality.
It causes only silent ischemia
Silent ischemia depends on the patient (diabetes, neuropathy, a transplanted heart), not the territory. Left ventricular involvement matters because of its higher mortality.
It carries higher mortality
Correct. The left ventricle is supplied by the anterior interventricular, circumflex, left marginal and diagonal arteries, and left ventricular involvement carries a higher mortality rate.

A.q: How many criteria establish metabolic syndrome?
opts: Any two of five
Two criteria are not enough; metabolic syndrome needs any three of the five defining levels.
Any three of five
Correct. Any 3 of abdominal obesity by waist circumference, triglyceride above 150, low high-density lipoprotein, blood pressure above 130/85 and fasting glucose above 110 establish it.
All five together
All five are not required; any three of the five defining levels are enough to establish the syndrome.
Any four of six
There are five criteria, not six, and any three of them are enough to establish metabolic syndrome.

A.io: Compare and contrast precipitating factors, clinical manifestations, diagnosis (including role of B-type natriuretic peptide, BNP), and treatment of acute decompensated heart failure.
A.q: A 58-year-old woman has a week of fatigue and mild breathlessness. Her B-type natriuretic peptide is 250. How should this result be interpreted?
opts: Acute heart failure is likely
Acute heart failure becomes likely only above 900. At 250 the result sits in the indeterminate range.
Indeterminate for heart failure
Correct. Between 100 and 400 the peptide has no useful sensitivity or specificity for heart failure, so the clinical picture and imaging have to settle the question.
Heart failure is likely
Heart failure becomes likely only above 400. At 250 the result sits in the indeterminate range.
Acute heart failure is ruled out
Rule-out applies only below 100. At 250 the level sits in the indeterminate range of 100 to 400.

A.topic: ST-elevation infarction and right ventricular infarct
A.io: ST segment elevation
A.q: Nitroglycerin is withheld in a right ventricular infarct because the injured right ventricle depends on what?
opts: A slow heart rate
Bradycardia is the reason a beta blocker is withheld in an infarction, not a need of the right ventricle. Nitroglycerin is withheld because it removes the preload the right ventricle depends on.
Extra oxygen
Oxygen is given in an infarction only when the oxygen saturation is below 91%, and nitroglycerin does not take it away. Nitroglycerin lowers the preload the right ventricle depends on.
Relief of spasm
Coronary spasm drives vasospastic angina, and nitroglycerin relieves it. A right ventricular infarct comes from right coronary artery occlusion, and its failing ventricle depends on preload.
Adequate preload

Correct. The infarcted right ventricle is preload dependent: nitroglycerin decreases preload, which reduces the Frank-Starling effect on its myocardium, so it fails into right-sided heart failure, output drops and shock follows.

A.q: A 55-year-old man remains above goal despite the described sequence: adherence confirmed, diuretic optimized, three agents titrated, spironolactone added and tolerated. What now?
opts: Add a second mineralocorticoid antagonist
Duplicating the mineralocorticoid antagonist class is not among the described escalation steps.
Refer to a hypertension specialist
Correct. Referral is reserved for truly difficult cases after the full sequence has been worked through rather than being an early substitute for it.
Accept the current pressure as his individual goal
A defined numeric goal of below 130/80 applies, and specialist options remain beyond this sequence.
Stop spironolactone and restart from a single agent
The approach builds on the regimen already in place rather than discarding it and beginning again.

A.io: Compare and contrast anticoagulation therapy for prosthetic heart valves.
A.q: A 58-year-old woman with a mechanical mitral valve asks whether she could take daily aspirin instead of her current anticoagulant. Which long-term therapy is recommended for her?
opts: Aspirin in place of it
Antiplatelet agents are specifically ranked below vitamin K antagonist therapy for a mechanical valve. Aspirin cannot replace her anticoagulant.
Heparin every day
Heparin bridges gaps in warfarin around surgery; it is not the long-term therapy. The recommendation is a vitamin K antagonist.
A vitamin K antagonist
Correct. With a mechanical heart valve, vitamin K antagonist therapy is recommended over no vitamin K antagonist and over antiplatelet agents. Warfarin is the one most commonly used.
No drug after one year
A mechanical valve requires lifelong anticoagulation; it is biological valves that stop after the postoperative period. She stays on a vitamin K antagonist.

A.io: Acute coronary syndrome
A.q: A 46-year-old man with six hours of atypical chest discomfort has a normal electrocardiogram and two high-sensitivity troponin I values of 4 ng/L. Which disposition is most appropriate?
opts: Start thrombolytic therapy
Thrombolytics treat ST-elevation infarction when catheterization is far away. His normal electrocardiogram and high-sensitivity troponin I of 4 ng/L show no infarct.
Admit to intensive care

Intensive care is for high-risk acute coronary syndrome, such as a TIMI (Thrombolysis in Myocardial Infarction) score of 3 or higher. Two not-abnormal high-sensitivity troponin I values allow safe discharge.
Discharge with follow-up
Correct. Troponin is a tool that says who can safely go home. Two high-sensitivity troponin I values of 4 ng/L, far below the men's 20 ng/L, with a normal electrocardiogram rule out an infarct.
Urgent cardiac catheterization
Catheterization is for a patient with an infarct or high risk. Two high-sensitivity troponin I values of 4 ng/L and a normal electrocardiogram rule out a heart attack.

A.io: Develop a differential diagnosis for a patient presenting with hypotension based on history, physical examination, and diagnostic findings.
A.q: Which two broad mechanisms lower pressure enough to cause cerebral hypoperfusion?
opts: Raised brain pressure or a seizure focus
Seizure is a non-hypotensive cause of loss of consciousness. Hypotensive syncope comes from reduced resistance or reduced cardiac output.
Low glucose or low oxygen delivery
Hypoglycemia and hypoxia are non-hypotensive causes of syncope, listed separately from the hypotensive mechanisms of low resistance or low output.
Low peripheral resistance or low output
Correct. Reflex and autonomic causes lower peripheral resistance, while volume depletion, venous pooling and cardiac causes lower cardiac output; either leaves the brain underperfused.
High peripheral resistance or high output
Both would raise rather than lower pressure. Syncope follows a fall in pressure from reduced resistance or reduced cardiac output.

Hypertriglyceridemia 2. Hypercholesterolemia 3. HDL cholesterol 4. LDL and VLDL cholesterol
A.q: A 42-year-old woman has low-density lipoprotein of 290 mg/dL with a normal triglyceride. She has firm nodules along both Achilles tendons (tendon xanthomas), and her father had a heart attack at 48. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Mixed dyslipidemia
Mixed dyslipidemia raises triglyceride above 150 as well as low-density lipoprotein; her triglyceride is normal.
Homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia
The homozygous form presents in childhood with total cholesterol of about 400 to above 1000 mg/dL and atherosclerosis before puberty.
Heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia

Correct. Low-density lipoprotein of 200 to 400 mg/dL, normal triglyceride, Achilles tendon xanthomas (present in about 75%) and premature coronary disease in a first-degree relative fit one mutant allele.
Severe hypertriglyceridemia
Severe hypertriglyceridemia means triglyceride above 500 mg/dL, usually without raised low-density lipoprotein, the reverse of her panel.

A.q: A 47-year-old woman starting home monitoring calls alarmed because one reading was 168/102, although her seven-day average is 128/80. What should she be told?
opts: Reassure her that the average matters, not one reading
Correct. Overreacting to an outlier generates anxiety and unnecessary changes in therapy, which is why the schedule is built around averaging fourteen readings.
Increase her medication on the basis of the highest reading
Acting on a single outlier is precisely what the averaging schedule exists to prevent.
Tell her home readings are unreliable and to stop monitoring
Home monitoring with a validated upper-arm device is a standard part of assessment.
Send her to the emergency department
An isolated raised reading without symptoms of acute organ injury is not an emergency.

A.topic: Post-infarction care and sudden cardiac death
A.io: Acute myocardial infraction
A.q: A 70-year-old man is admitted with a large myocardial infarction and develops hypotension, cool extremities and falling urine output from cardiogenic shock. Which infarct feature makes this complication more common?
opts: A small subendocardial infarct
A subendocardial infarct involves only the inner wall and shows ST depression. Cardiogenic shock follows loss of pump function and is more common with left-sided infarcts.
A right-sided infarct
Right ventricular infarction can tip into shock if nitroglycerin drops the preload it depends on, but as an infarct complication, cardiogenic shock is more common after left-sided infarcts.
Reperfusion inside 90 minutes
A door-to-balloon time under 90 minutes is the goal because time is muscle; prompt reperfusion limits damage. Shock is more common with a left-sided infarct, not with timely care.
A left-sided infarct

Correct. Cardiogenic shock is more common in left-sided myocardial infarctions, and left ventricular involvement carries a higher mortality. The left ventricle supplies the systemic output that shock takes away.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, prevention, and prognosis for heart failure.
A.q: A 45-year-old woman with a family history of heart failure smokes, drinks heavily and is obese. Her heart is structurally normal. Which counseling point best lowers her heart failure risk?
opts: Start a loop diuretic as prevention
Diuretics treat congestion and do not prevent heart failure. Counseling targets tobacco, alcohol and obesity.
Family history cannot be offset at all
Family history is fixed, but her modifiable risk factors (tobacco, alcohol, obesity) can still be changed to lower her risk.
Wait for symptoms before changing
Waiting forfeits prevention. Tobacco, excess alcohol and obesity are modifiable now.
Quit tobacco, cut alcohol, lose weight
Correct. Tobacco, excessive alcohol and obesity are modifiable risk factors for heart failure. Her family history is a risk factor she cannot change, so counseling targets the ones she can.

Hypertriglyceridemia 2. Hypercholesterolemia 3. HDL cholesterol 4. LDL and VLDL cholesterol
A.q: What is the treatment for a patient with familial hypercholesterolemia refractory to drug therapy?
opts: A very low-fat diet alone
The very low-fat diet is for triglyceride above 500 mg/dL; this disorder is a low-density lipoprotein receptor defect.
Evolocumab or alirocumab

Correct. Patients refractory to drug therapy may be treated with a proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 inhibitor such as evolocumab or alirocumab, after high-intensity statins with ezetimibe and nicotinic acid. It is not a first step.
Low-intensity statin instead
Lowering statin intensity moves the wrong way; high-intensity statins are the common regimen before escalation.
Switch the statin to a fibrate
Triglyceride is normal in familial hypercholesterolemia; stopping the statin removes the core low-density lipoprotein therapy.

A.io: Vasospastic (Prinzmetal variant)
A.q: A 38-year-old woman who smokes has recurrent chest pain at rest between 3 and 5 a.m., each episode lasting about 10 minutes. An electrocardiogram during one episode shows transient ST-segment elevation that resolves, and coronary angiography shows no significant stenosis. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: ST-elevation myocardial infarction
ST-elevation infarction shows ST elevation not quickly reversed and ends in necrosis from an occlusion. Her elevation is transient and resolves, and her arteries are free of high-grade stenosis.
Unstable angina

Unstable angina is a change in stable angina from an atherosclerotic plaque, with normal troponin. A young smoker with clean arteries and transient ST elevation in early-morning episodes has vasospasm.
Stable angina
Stable angina is precipitated by activity and relieved by rest and nitroglycerin, with atherosclerotic narrowing. Her pain comes at rest in the early morning with normal arteries, which is vasospasm.
Vasospastic angina

Correct. Vasospastic (Prinzmetal) angina occurs at rest, most often between midnight and early morning, in younger patients who smoke, with transient ST-segment elevation during an episode and no high-grade stenosis.

A.q: A 43-year-old man has a fasting triglyceride of 620 mg/dL. He drinks heavily most nights. Before any drug is started, which additional conditions should be evaluated?
opts: Diabetes, kidney disease, hypothyroidism
Correct. With triglyceride of 500 or more rule out diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease, alcoholism, pregnancy and hypothyroidism; his alcohol history is important too.
Lipoprotein(a) and coronary calcium
These are risk-enhancing tools for primary prevention, not the secondary causes of very high triglyceride.
Tendon xanthomas and corneal arcus
These are physical signs of high-cholesterol genetic states, not secondary causes to exclude for high triglyceride.
Anorexia nervosa and biliary cirrhosis
Anorexia nervosa and primary biliary cirrhosis are rule-outs for elevated low-density lipoprotein, not very high triglyceride.

A.q: What characterizes primary, or essential, hypertension?
opts: Blood pressure that responds to no medication
Failure to respond to three complementary agents describes resistant hypertension, which may be primary or secondary in origin.
No single identifiable underlying cause

Correct. It is a diagnosis of pattern rather than of mechanism, which is why the clinical work is about recognizing when the pattern does NOT fit and a secondary cause should be sought. It accounts for the vast majority of adult cases.
Onset before the age of thirty in most patients
Early onset is one of the clues that should prompt a search for a secondary cause rather than a feature of primary hypertension.
An identifiable underlying condition in most cases
An identifiable cause defines secondary hypertension, which accounts for the minority of adult cases rather than the majority.

A.topic: Chest pain workup and risk scores
A.io: Acute coronary syndrome
A.q: A 54-year-old man arrives at the emergency department with 30 minutes of chest pressure. Which pair of studies does every patient with chest pain receive?
opts: Calcium score and a lipid panel
A calcium score is for risk stratification, not acute chest pain, and lipids can come later. The universal first pair is a stat electrocardiogram and a chest radiograph.
Electrocardiogram and chest radiograph
Correct. All chest pain patients get a chest radiograph and a stat electrocardiogram. Blood work (complete blood count, metabolic panel, coagulation studies, troponin) follows.
Treadmill stress test and D-dimer
A D-dimer is only a maybe in the chest pain workup, and a stress test is not done on arrival with active pain. Every patient gets a stat electrocardiogram and a chest radiograph.
Coronary angiography and echocardiogram
Coronary angiography is the gold standard for coronary disease but not the universal first study. Every chest pain patient starts with a stat electrocardiogram and a chest radiograph.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
A.q: A 70-year-old man has had diarrhea and poor oral intake for 3 days and fainted when he stood up quickly this morning. His oral mucous membranes are dry. Supine he is 134/76 with a heart rate of 66; standing he is 104/62 with a heart rate of 94. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Non-neurogenic orthostatic hypotension
Correct. A 30 mmHg systolic fall with a heart rate rise from 66 to 94 shows an intact sympathetic reflex, and diarrhea with poor intake explains the volume depletion.
Neurogenic orthostatic hypotension
Neurogenic orthostatic hypotension shows only a minimal heart rate rise and usually no volume depletion, the opposite of his findings.
Postural orthostatic tachycardia
That syndrome is a heart rate rise on standing without the pressure fall that meets orthostatic criteria; he has a clear 30 mmHg fall.
Situational reflex syncope
Situational syncope follows a bodily function such as nighttime urination, with a transient reflex rather than a sustained fall on standing.

A.io: Aortic regurgitation
A.q: A 58-year-old man with a known aortic dissection develops sudden aortic regurgitation with cardiogenic shock and pulmonary edema. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
opts: Repeat echocardiogram in six months
Surveillance suits mild chronic disease, not a patient in cardiogenic shock. Acute severe aortic regurgitation needs emergency valve replacement or repair.
Emergency valve replacement or repair

Correct. Acute severe aortic regurgitation is treated with emergency aortic valve replacement or repair, ideally within 24 hours. Acute causes include myocardial infarction, endocarditis, aortic dissection and trauma.
Percutaneous balloon valve dilation
Balloon procedures open stenotic valves; they do not stop a valve from leaking. Acute severe aortic regurgitation is treated with emergency valve replacement or repair.
Outpatient afterload reduction therapy
Afterload reduction is medical management for chronic aortic regurgitation with preserved ejection fraction or no symptoms. Acute severe regurgitation in shock needs emergency surgery.

A.io: Compare and contrast risk factors, management, and complications of arteriosclerosis and atherosclerosis.
A.q: A 45-year-old woman without diabetes has low-density lipoprotein of 120 mg/dL and a 10-year atherosclerotic risk of 3%. She has no risk-enhancing factors. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Ezetimibe alone
Ezetimibe is an adjunct to a maximal statin in higher-risk patients, not therapy for low-risk primary prevention.
Moderate-intensity statin
A moderate-intensity statin is started at intermediate risk when the discussion favors it; at 3% lifestyle is emphasized.
High-intensity statin
High intensity is for clinical disease, severe hypercholesterolemia or high 10-year risk, not a 3% estimate.
Emphasize lifestyle
Correct. Low risk (under 5%) calls for a risk discussion that emphasizes lifestyle to reduce risk factors, rather than a statin.

A.io: Define the following diagnostic and therapeutic groups of HF patients, and the treatment implications/recommendations for each group: a. HF with reduced EF (HFrEF) b. HF with mildly reduced EF (HFmrEF) c. HF with preserved EF (HFpEF)
A.q: A 74-year-old woman with long-standing hypertension has leg edema, crackles and breathlessness climbing stairs. Echocardiogram shows an ejection fraction of 62% and B-type natriuretic peptide is 640. Which therapy carries the strongest recommendation now?
opts: An inotrope such as dobutamine
Inotropes are for intensive care use only. With preserved fraction and congestion, the strong recommendation is a diuretic as needed.
Hydralazine with isosorbide dinitrate
That pairing is for African American patients with reduced ejection fraction in functional class III or IV. With preserved fraction and congestion, the strong recommendation is a diuretic.
A diuretic as needed for congestion

Correct. With preserved ejection fraction and congestion, diuretics as needed carry the strong recommendation. A sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor is next at moderate strength; the neprilysin combination, antagonist and receptor blocker are weak.
A beta blocker titrated to heart rate
A beta blocker is core therapy in reduced ejection fraction, not the strongest recommendation with a preserved fraction. Her congestion is treated with a diuretic as needed.

A.io: Identify medical care strategies for atherosclerosis and lipid disorders in the lecture topic list for the following populations. 6. infant 7. child 8. adolescent 9. adult 10. elderly
A.q: A 7-year-old boy with homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia and under 2% of normal receptor activity asks, through his parents, why he needs frequent sessions attached to a machine. Which explanation is most appropriate?
opts: It replaces his missing liver cells
Replacing receptors is what liver transplantation may do; apheresis removes low-density particles from the blood.
It filters the bad cholesterol out
Correct. Apheresis is like dialysis: the elective removal of low-density particles from the circulation, and it is the treatment of choice for the homozygous disorder.
It cures the disorder in weeks
Apheresis removes particles repeatedly; the inherited receptor defect remains, so treatment continues.
It lowers his triglyceride level
His triglyceride is normal; the machine removes low-density lipoprotein particles.

A.q: A 61-year-old with abrupt severe interscapular pain has symmetric, normal-volume pulses in all four limbs. What follows?
opts: An aortic regurgitation murmur would be required to proceed
A murmur is one supporting finding among several, not a prerequisite for imaging.
Dissection is excluded and another cause should be sought
Symmetric pulses do not exclude it; the clinical suspicion still drives imaging.
A normal chest radiograph would then exclude it
A normal chest radiograph does not exclude dissection either, so neither finding can close the question.
Normal pulses do not exclude dissection
Correct. Absent pulse findings specifically do not exclude the diagnosis, which is why a normal pulse examination must not close the question. Imaging is still driven by the clinical suspicion.

A.q: A 49-year-old man with hypertriglyceridemia has a total cholesterol of 250 mg/dL, high-density lipoprotein of 40 mg/dL and triglyceride of 300 mg/dL. What is his non-high-density cholesterol?
opts: 190 mg/dL
The formula does not involve triglyceride; subtracting the high-density value of 40 from 250 gives 210.
210 mg/dL
Correct. Non-high-density cholesterol is total cholesterol minus high-density cholesterol: 250 minus 40 is 210 mg/dL.
290 mg/dL
Adding high-density cholesterol to the total gives 290, but the formula subtracts it: 250 minus 40.
50 mg/dL
Subtracting triglyceride from total cholesterol gives an unrelated number; the formula is total minus high-density cholesterol.

A.io: Compare and contrast precipitating factors, clinical manifestations, diagnosis (including role of B-type natriuretic peptide, BNP), and treatment of acute decompensated heart failure.
A.q: A 59-year-old man is recovering from acute heart failure after an infarction with an ejection fraction of 29%. He wears a defibrillator vest while his guideline-directed therapy is being optimized. Which referral should accompany this phase?
opts: Valve surgery review
Nothing points to valve disease. The referral that accompanies optimized therapy after acute failure is cardiac rehabilitation.
Transplant evaluation
Transplant is for failure that progresses despite management. The referral that accompanies this phase is cardiac rehabilitation.
Cardiac rehabilitation

Correct. After acute heart failure with an ejection fraction below 35%, the pathway pairs optimized guideline-directed therapy with cardiac rehabilitation while he wears the vest, before the echocardiogram is repeated.
Hospice enrollment
Hospice does not fit a recovery pathway that ends in a repeat echocardiogram. The referral that accompanies this phase is cardiac rehabilitation.

A.io: ST segment elevation
A.q: A 58-year-old woman has chest pain with ST elevation in V1 through V4. Which pattern of ischemia does ST elevation reflect?
opts: Transmural ischemia
Correct. Transmural ischemia, involving the full thickness of the wall, produces ST elevation in the leads over that region. Subendocardial ischemia of the inner wall produces ST depression instead.
Microvascular dysfunction
Microvascular angina gives angina with ST changes but normal coronary arteries on angiography. ST elevation in V1-V4 reflects transmural ischemia of the anterior wall.
Reversible demand ischemia
Demand ischemia in stable angina produces stress-induced changes, usually T-wave inversion. Persistent ST elevation reflects transmural ischemia.
Subendocardial ischemia
Subendocardial ischemia, confined to the inner wall, produces ST depression over the ischemic region. ST elevation reflects full-thickness, transmural ischemia.

A.io: Tricuspid stenosis
A.q: Which description fits the tricuspid stenosis murmur?
opts: Holosystolic murmur near the epigastrium, louder on inspiration
A holosystolic murmur near the epigastrium that grows on inspiration is tricuspid regurgitation. Stenosis is a mid-diastolic rumble.
Diastolic rumble at the apex, best on the left side
A diastolic rumble at the apex, heard with the patient on the left side, is mitral stenosis. The tricuspid rumble is near the xiphoid and grows on inspiration.
Harsh mid-systolic murmur at the left upper sternal border
A harsh mid-systolic ejection murmur at the left upper sternal border is pulmonic stenosis. Tricuspid stenosis is a diastolic rumble near the xiphoid.
Mid-diastolic rumble near the xiphoid, louder on inspiration
Correct. Tricuspid stenosis gives a soft opening snap and a mid-diastolic rumble at the left lower sternal border near the xiphoid process, increasing with inspiration, with jugular vein distension.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
A.q: A 69-year-old man reports lightheadedness and dimming vision within a minute or two of standing, which settles when he sits. His examination at rest is normal. Which test should be performed first?
opts: Orthostatic vital signs
Correct. Pressure and heart rate taken supine and again within 3 minutes of standing show whether orthostatic criteria are met and which type the heart rate response suggests.
A tilt-table test
The tilt-table test is the listed test for postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome, and its sensitivity of about 40% makes a negative result weak.
An echocardiogram
Echocardiography evaluates structural cardiogenic syncope; symptoms that follow standing call first for a postural pressure measurement.
A stress test
A stress test belongs to the arrhythmia work-up of cardiogenic syncope, not the first test for a postural pattern of symptoms.

A.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education, and prognosis
A.q: A 49-year-old newly diagnosed hypertensive patient has fundoscopy showing generalized arteriolar narrowing and arteriovenous nicking, with no hemorrhages or exudates. What does this tell you?
opts: They reflect current and previous pressure
Correct. Generalized narrowing and nicking record the accumulated burden, whereas focal narrowing, hemorrhages and exudates relate to CURRENT pressure only.
These changes reflect current blood pressure only
Focal narrowing, hemorrhages and exudates are the findings tied to current pressure; these two relate to current and previous.
These findings carry no prognostic weight
Hypertensive retinopathy predicts long-term stroke risk independently of the blood pressure level.
These findings indicate a hypertensive emergency
Optic disc edema marks acute hypertensive injury; chronic arteriolar changes do not.

A.io: Differentiate between systolic dysfunction and diastolic dysfunction..
A.q: A 64-year-old man with a myocardial infarction three years ago has breathlessness on exertion and orthopnea (breathlessness lying flat). Blood pressure is 104/68. There is a third heart sound (an extra sound in early diastole just after the second heart sound) and bibasilar crackles. B-type natriuretic peptide is 820. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Diastolic failure from hypertrophic disease
The diastolic chain runs with hypertension, a fourth heart sound and edema that starts peripherally. His low pressure, third sound and prior infarction point to systolic failure.
Isolated right-sided failure from the lungs
Right-sided failure shows peripheral edema, distended neck veins and portal overload. Crackles, orthopnea and a third sound point to left-sided systolic failure.
Systolic failure from ischemic cardiomyopathy

Correct. Every link of the systolic chain is here: ischemic cardiomyopathy after infarction, a low-normal blood pressure, a third heart sound from rapid filling of a dilated ventricle, and pulmonary edema, confirmed by an elevated natriuretic peptide.
High-output failure from increased demand
High-output failure comes from anemia, hyperthyroidism or an arteriovenous fistula, with no infarction behind it. This is systolic failure from ischemic cardiomyopathy.

A.io: Compare and contrast precipitating factors, clinical manifestations, diagnosis (including role of B-type natriuretic peptide, BNP), and treatment of acute decompensated heart failure.
A.q: A 73-year-old woman has grade II diastolic dysfunction with an ejection fraction of 46%. She has fatigue and breathlessness with exertion but has never had pulmonary or peripheral edema and has never needed a diuretic. Does she meet a clinical diagnosis of congestive heart failure?
opts: No, because congestion is required

Correct. A clinical diagnosis of congestive heart failure requires congestion, meaning pulmonary or peripheral edema. She has symptoms and a mildly reduced ejection fraction, but without edema the congestive label does not apply.
Yes, because she has symptoms
Symptoms make heart failure clinical, but calling it congestive requires congestion, meaning edema, which she has never had.
Yes, because she is older than 65
Age does not define the diagnosis. A clinical diagnosis of congestive heart failure requires congestion, meaning edema.
Yes, because her fraction is 46%
Her fraction places her in the mildly reduced group; it does not make the heart failure congestive. Congestion, meaning edema, is required.

A.io: Identify medical care strategies for hypotension in the lecture topic list for the following populations. a. infant b. child c. adolescent d. adult e. elderly
A.q: What heart rate rise defines postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome in adolescents?
opts: An increase of 20 beats per minute
Twenty is the systolic pressure fall used for orthostatic hypotension, not a heart rate threshold for the syndrome.
An increase of 30 beats per minute
More than 30 beats per minute is the adult threshold. Adolescents need a larger rise of 40 to meet the definition.
An increase of 10 beats per minute
Ten is the diastolic pressure fall used for orthostatic hypotension. The adolescent heart rate threshold is 40.
An increase of 40 beats per minute
Correct. In adolescents the threshold is an increase of 40 beats per minute, higher than the adult rise of more than 30, and adolescence is when the syndrome is often first considered.

A.io: Mitral stenosis
A.q: A 48-year-old woman with rheumatic mitral stenosis has an echocardiogram showing a markedly enlarged left atrium. Which complication is she at greatest risk of developing?
opts: Left ventricular dilation
Eccentric left ventricular dilation is the volume response of aortic and mitral regurgitation. Mitral stenosis loads the left atrium, predisposing to atrial fibrillation.
Concentric hypertrophy
Concentric left ventricular hypertrophy is the pressure response to aortic stenosis. Mitral stenosis enlarges the left atrium instead, and that leads to atrial fibrillation.
Aortic root dilation
Aortic root dilation is a cause of aortic regurgitation, found on echo. Mitral stenosis enlarges the left atrium, which predisposes to atrial fibrillation.
Atrial fibrillation

Correct. In mitral stenosis the left atrium enlarges under raised pressure, and left atrial enlargement predisposes to an abnormal rhythm such as atrial fibrillation, which is common in severe disease.

A.io: Pulmonic stenosis
A.q: What treatment does mild to moderate pulmonic stenosis need?
opts: None
Correct. Mild to moderate pulmonic stenosis needs no treatment and carries a 94% 20-year survival. Severe symptomatic disease is treated with diuretics and pulmonic balloon valvuloplasty.
A loop diuretic
Diuretics are for symptomatic right heart failure in severe pulmonic stenosis. Mild to moderate disease needs no treatment.
Balloon valvuloplasty
Pulmonic balloon valvuloplasty is for severe pulmonic stenosis with symptoms. Mild to moderate disease needs none.
Valve replacement
Replacement may be needed for severe congenital disease. Mild to moderate pulmonic stenosis needs no treatment.

A.io: Define the following diagnostic and therapeutic groups of HF patients, and the treatment implications/recommendations for each group: a. HF with reduced EF (HFrEF) b. HF with mildly reduced EF (HFmrEF) c. HF with preserved EF (HFpEF)
A.q: A 66-year-old African American man with reduced ejection fraction (fraction 25%) remains short of breath with slight exertion despite optimized sacubitril-valsartan, a beta blocker, spironolactone and dapagliflozin. Which addition is recommended?
opts: Hydralazine with isosorbide dinitrate

Correct. For African American patients with reduced ejection fraction in functional class III or IV, hydralazine with nitrates carries a strong recommendation on top of the core classes. Slight-exertion symptoms put him in functional class III.
Dobutamine continued at home
Dobutamine is an inotrope for intensive care use only. The recommended outpatient addition is hydralazine with isosorbide dinitrate.
Verapamil for additional rate control
Verapamil is a calcium channel blocker, which is avoided in heart failure. His class III disease qualifies for hydralazine with isosorbide dinitrate.
Isosorbide mononitrate on its own
The recommendation pairs hydralazine with isosorbide dinitrate. A nitrate alone is not the recommended addition for class III or IV.

A.io: Develop a differential diagnosis for a patient presenting with hypotension based on history, physical examination, and diagnostic findings.
A.q: A 76-year-old man is seen in the emergency department after fainting while voiding at night. His examination is normal. Which test excludes hypoglycemia as the cause?
opts: Orthostatic vital signs
Orthostatic readings test for a postural pressure fall; hypoglycemia is excluded by measuring glucose.
A tilt-table test
Tilt-table testing is for postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome and says nothing about blood sugar.
A blood glucose level
Correct. A normal blood glucose rules out hypoglycemia, a non-hypotensive cause, as blood counts and a metabolic panel address infection and metabolic causes.
An echocardiogram
Echocardiography evaluates structural heart disease, not the glucose level at the time of a faint.

A.io: Develop a differential diagnosis for a patient presenting with hypotension based on history, physical examination, and diagnostic findings.
A.q: A 35-year-old woman standing at an outdoor event in the heat develops tunnel vision, lightheadedness and dizziness but is still conscious. If her pressure keeps falling, what is likely to follow?
opts: A generalized seizure
Seizure is a separate, non-hypotensive cause of loss of consciousness and does not follow near-syncope from low pressure.
Supine hypertension
Supine hypertension is high pressure while lying flat, a comorbidity rather than a consequence of near-syncope.
A prolonged coma
Syncope is transient and self-limited, so a prolonged coma is not the expected outcome of falling pressure here.
A brief faint
Correct. Her symptoms are near-syncope, which precedes syncope: a transient, self-limited loss of consciousness followed by spontaneous recovery.

A.io: Define hypotension
A.q: A 58-year-old man's pressure is 100/64, which is normal for many adults but far below his usual 150/90, and he now feels lightheaded. How should this reading be interpreted?
opts: As proof of autonomic failure
Autonomic failure is shown by a postural fall with a minimal heart rate rise, not by one resting reading.
As a measurement artifact
A reading consistent with his symptoms should not be dismissed; each reading is a snapshot to interpret, not to discard.
As relative hypotension for him
Correct. Hypotension is a fall below normal, and normal is judged against the patient's age, comorbidities and own baseline, so a relative fall can be significant.
As normal, since it is above 90
No single fixed number defines hypotension; relative hypotension must be considered against the patient's usual pressure.

A.io: Non-ST segment elevation
A.q: A 64-year-old man is diagnosed with a non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction. His oxygen saturation (SpO2) is 97% on room air and his heart rate is 88. Which is part of his initial treatment?
opts: Supplemental oxygen
Oxygen is given only if the oxygen saturation is below 91%. At 97% on room air, supplemental oxygen is withheld because it causes peripheral vasoconstriction.
A calcium channel blocker
A beta blocker, not a calcium channel blocker, is used to reduce myocardial oxygen demand in the initial treatment. Calcium channel blockers do not improve prognosis after infarction overall.
Chewable aspirin

Correct. Unstable angina and non-ST-elevation infarction are a medical emergency treated alike: chewable aspirin, a beta blocker and intravenous nitrates if appropriate, and dual antiplatelet therapy with or without anticoagulation.
A thrombolytic agent
Thrombolytics are reserved for an ST-elevation infarction when percutaneous intervention is two or more hours away. A non-ST-elevation infarction is treated like unstable angina.

A.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, prevention, and prognosis for heart failure.
A.q: Which drug class is recommended to prevent heart failure in patients with diabetes who have no structural heart disease?
opts: Angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor
This combination belongs to symptomatic reduced ejection fraction in functional class II or III. Stage A prevention in diabetes uses a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor.
Hydralazine with isosorbide dinitrate
This pairing is reserved for African American patients with reduced ejection fraction in functional class III or IV. Stage A prevention uses a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor.
Beta blocker started at diagnosis
A beta blocker is not part of stage A prevention; it is a stage B therapy once structural disease appears. Prevention in diabetes uses a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor.
Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor

Correct. Prevention in stage A, risk factors with a normal heart, carries one strong drug recommendation: a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor for patients with diabetes, ahead of any beta blocker, which is a stage B therapy.

A.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education, and prognosis
A.q: A 58-year-old woman with fatigue, cold intolerance and constipation is found to have blood pressure of 146/96 with a predominantly diastolic elevation. Which mechanism fits?
opts: Autonomous aldosterone secretion
Aldosteronism produces resistant hypertension with hypokalemia rather than cold intolerance and constipation.
Hypothyroidism raising vascular resistance
Correct. Hypothyroidism raises systemic vascular resistance, which lifts the diastolic pressure, whereas hyperthyroidism raises cardiac output and lifts the systolic.
Hyperthyroidism raising cardiac output
That produces a predominantly SYSTOLIC elevation with tachycardia, and her symptoms point the other way.
Catecholamine excess from an adrenal tumor
Pheochromocytoma causes paroxysmal symptoms rather than the sustained hypothyroid picture described.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atherosclerosis and lipid disorders: 1. Hypertriglyceridemia 2. Hypercholesterolemia 3. HDL cholesterol 4. LDL and VLDL cholesterol
B.q: A 38-year-old man has yellow deposits in the creases of his palms (palmar xanthomas). His triglyceride is 410 mg/dL and total cholesterol 390 mg/dL. Genetic testing shows homozygosity for apolipoprotein E2. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia
The heterozygous cholesterol disorder has normal triglyceride and tendon xanthomas, not palmar ones.
Familial chylomicronemia syndrome
Chylomicronemia raises triglyceride usually above 1000 with eruptive papules and pancreatitis, not matched elevations with palmar xanthomas.
Familial dysbetalipoproteinemia

Correct. An apolipoprotein E mutation with apolipoprotein E2 homozygosity lets chylomicron and very-low-density remnants accumulate, raising triglyceride and total cholesterol both to 250 to 500, with distinctive palmar xanthomas.
Metabolic syndrome
Metabolic syndrome is diagnosed from three of five clinical criteria and has no palmar xanthomas or apolipoprotein E2 link.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atherosclerosis and lipid disorders: 1. Hypertriglyceridemia 2. Hypercholesterolemia 3. HDL cholesterol 4. LDL and VLDL cholesterol
B.q: Which laboratory monitoring is listed for statin therapy?
opts: Lipids, kidney function and potassium
Potassium and kidney function are not statin monitoring parameters; liver function and creatine kinase are monitored alongside lipids.
Lipids, glucose and uric acid
Glucose and uric acid are not on the list; monitoring is lipid levels, liver function and creatine kinase.
Lipids, liver function and creatine kinase
Correct. The statin monitoring parameters are lipid levels, liver function and creatine kinase (also called creatine phosphokinase), checked alongside the repeat lipid panel.
Lipids, thyroid function and blood count
Thyroid function is checked before starting, to rule out hypothyroidism as a cause of high low-density lipoprotein, but the monitoring list is lipids, liver function and creatine kinase.

B.io: Mitral stenosis
B.q: A 36-year-old woman has mitral stenosis found on an echocardiogram done before pregnancy. She has no symptoms and is in sinus rhythm. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Cardiology consultation

Correct. All patients with evidence of mitral stenosis on echocardiogram should have a cardiology consult to evaluate them and set the frequency of follow-up. Asymptomatic disease in sinus rhythm needs no therapy yet.
Start a loop diuretic
Loop diuretics treat dyspnea and orthopnea in mitral stenosis. With no symptoms and sinus rhythm she needs no therapy, but the echo finding still warrants a cardiology consult.
Balloon valvotomy now
Balloon valvotomy is for severe mitral stenosis with symptoms or pulmonary hypertension. An asymptomatic patient in sinus rhythm is referred to cardiology for evaluation.
No follow-up needed
Mitral stenosis on echocardiogram is not dismissed; it should have a cardiology consult to set follow-up. Only therapy, not referral, is withheld when she is asymptomatic.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, prevention, and prognosis for heart failure.
B.q: Which diuretics are potassium-wasting?
opts: Dapagliflozin and empagliflozin
These are sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors, not the potassium-wasting diuretics. Those are loops and thiazide-like agents such as furosemide and hydrochlorothiazide.
Lisinopril and irbesartan
These block the renin-angiotensin system and are not diuretics. The potassium-wasting diuretics are loops and thiazide-like agents such as furosemide and hydrochlorothiazide.
Furosemide and hydrochlorothiazide

Correct. Loop diuretics such as furosemide and bumetanide, and thiazide-like diuretics such as hydrochlorothiazide and metolazone, waste potassium. The mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists are potassium-sparing.
Spironolactone and eplerenone
These mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists are potassium-sparing diuretics. The potassium-wasting ones are loops and thiazide-like diuretics such as furosemide and hydrochlorothiazide.

B.io: Non-ST segment elevation
B.q: A 68-year-old woman has an hour of substernal pressure. Her electrocardiogram shows ST-segment depression of 2 mm in V5 and V6 without ST elevation, and her standard troponin I is 0.62 ng/mL. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Unstable angina
Unstable angina has the same kind of electrocardiogram changes but a troponin I that is not abnormal. Her troponin I of 0.62 ng/mL is elevated, which makes it an infarction.
Infarction with ST elevation
An ST-elevation infarction needs ST elevation above 1 mm in two or more leads. Her tracing shows ST depression with no elevation, so the infarct is non-ST-elevation.
Vasospastic angina
Vasospastic angina causes transient ST changes during an episode of rest pain that resolve, with normal coronaries at angiography. It does not explain an hour of pain with an elevated troponin I.
Infarction without ST elevation

Correct. ST-segment depression above 1 mm and/or T-wave inversion in two or more consecutive leads, with symptoms and an elevated troponin I (standard troponin I above 0.04 ng/mL), is a non-ST-elevation infarction.

B.q: A 45-year-old woman has new swelling of both legs, heavy protein in her urine and low-density lipoprotein of 220 mg/dL. Before a statin is started, which condition should be ruled out?
opts: Familial chylomicronemia
Chylomicronemia is a triglyceride disorder with pancreatitis and eruptive xanthomas, not edema and proteinuria.
Heterozygous familial form
A genetic cause is sought only after secondary causes are ruled out, and her edema and proteinuria point to the kidney.
Nephrotic syndrome
Correct. Elevated low-density lipoprotein calls for ruling out nephrotic syndrome, which drives excess very-low-density production and raises triglyceride and low-density lipoprotein.
Metabolic syndrome
Metabolic syndrome is diagnosed from waist, triglyceride, high-density lipoprotein, blood pressure and glucose, not proteinuria.

B.io: Define the following diagnostic and therapeutic groups of HF patients, and the treatment implications/recommendations for each group: a. HF with reduced EF (HFrEF) b. HF with mildly reduced EF (HFmrEF) c. HF with preserved EF (HFpEF)
B.q: A 66-year-old woman with reduced ejection fraction (fraction 30%) has gained weight with leg edema and crackles. She takes a beta blocker, sacubitril-valsartan, spironolactone and dapagliflozin. Which drug relieves her fluid overload now?
opts: A loop diuretic such as furosemide
Correct. Diuretics are used as needed for congestion in every ejection fraction group; loops such as furosemide and bumetanide are the potassium-wasting diuretics that clear fluid.
Dobutamine given at home
Dobutamine is an inotrope for intensive care use only. Her congestion needs a loop diuretic.
Hydralazine given on its own
Hydralazine is paired with isosorbide dinitrate for selected patients in functional class III or IV; it does not clear fluid. Her congestion needs a loop diuretic.
Diltiazem to slow the heart rate
Diltiazem is a calcium channel blocker, which is avoided in heart failure. Her congestion needs a loop diuretic.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
B.q: A 67-year-old woman with diabetic autonomic neuropathy has recently begun fainting on standing. She has no supine hypertension (high pressure while lying flat), heart disease or kidney disease. Which is the most appropriate initial management?
opts: A vasopressor infusion in clinic
Vasopressor infusions are for the emergency department and intensive care only, not initial outpatient management.
Strict fluid restriction each day
Restricting fluid lowers volume and makes postural falls worse, so it is not part of management.
Fludrocortisone before anything else
Fludrocortisone is best with the tachycardia syndrome; for neurogenic syncope, midodrine is the best listed drug if one is needed.
Slow position changes, treat the cause
Correct. Slow positional changes and treatment of the underlying condition are first-line for orthostatic syncope; drugs come in when these are not enough.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
B.q: A 60-year-old woman has vomited for 2 days, has dry mucous membranes, and fainted on standing; her heart rate rises from 70 to 98 as her pressure falls 30 mmHg. Which is the most appropriate next step in management?
opts: Treat the underlying volume loss
Correct. Her intact heart rate response and dryness point to volume depletion, and orthostasis is managed by treating the underlying condition.
Order a tilt-table test first
Tilt-table testing belongs to the tachycardia syndrome; her diagnosis is already clear from orthostatic readings.
Start midodrine for autonomic failure
Midodrine is best with neurogenic syncope; a brisk heart rate rise shows her autonomic reflex is intact.
Refer her for an echocardiogram
Echocardiography evaluates structural cardiogenic syncope, which nothing in her history suggests.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atherosclerosis and lipid disorders: 1. B.q: Which lipoprotein consists mostly of cholesterol and supplies cholesterol for cellular needs?
opts: High-density lipoprotein
High-density lipoprotein carries excess cholesterol away from the periphery to the liver, the reverse direction.
Chylomicrons
Chylomicrons carry dietary triglyceride after a fatty meal and are the least dense class.
Low-density lipoprotein

Correct. Low-density lipoprotein consists mostly of cholesterol, is used to provide cholesterol for cellular needs, and its increased levels put patients at risk for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease.
Very-low-density lipoprotein
Very-low-density lipoprotein consists mainly of triglyceride with some cholesterol and transfers triglycerides to the cells.

B.io: Acute coronary syndrome
B.q: A 34-year-old man has chest tightness the morning after a long-distance run that left his leg muscles sore. The team wants a blood marker specific to heart muscle. Which marker should be measured?
opts: Any troponin type
Troponins occur in both cardiac and skeletal muscle, so the type matters after a long run. Troponin I is the heart-specific troponin.
Smooth-muscle troponin
Smooth muscle cells contain no troponin at all; troponins belong to cardiac and skeletal muscle. The heart-specific marker is troponin I.
Troponin C
Troponin C is one of the three troponin types but is not the heart-specific one. Troponin I is specific to the heart, which matters after skeletal muscle strain.
Troponin I

Correct. Troponins are proteins of cardiac and skeletal muscle, and there are three types (I, T and C), but troponin I is the one specific to the heart, so skeletal muscle injury from his run does not confound it.

B.io: Tricuspid regurgitation
B.q: A 72-year-old man with worsening tricuspid regurgitation from pulmonary hypertension is being followed. Which symptoms mark that his regurgitation has become severe?
opts: Hoarseness and dysphagia
Hoarseness and dysphagia come from an enlarged left atrium in mitral stenosis. Severe tricuspid regurgitation causes pedal edema and ascites.
Pedal edema and ascites
Correct. Mild to moderate tricuspid regurgitation is usually asymptomatic; severe disease causes pedal edema and ascites from right-sided congestion.
Exertional angina and syncope
Exertional angina and syncope are cardinal symptoms of aortic stenosis. Severe tricuspid regurgitation shows pedal edema and ascites.
Hemoptysis and orthopnea
Hemoptysis and orthopnea reflect high left atrial pressure in mitral stenosis. Severe tricuspid regurgitation causes pedal edema and ascites.

B.q: A 58-year-old woman has a blood pressure of 224/126 with no headache, no visual change, no chest pain, a normal neurological examination and a normal creatinine. How should this be classified?
opts: Hypertensive encephalopathy
Encephalopathy would require confusion, seizures or a neurological deficit, and her examination is normal.
A hypertensive emergency, because the systolic exceeds 220
No absolute numeric cutoff defines an emergency; acute hypertension-mediated organ injury is what does.
Severe asymptomatic hypertension

Correct. An emergency is defined by acute hypertension-mediated ORGAN INJURY, not by crossing a numeric threshold. A very high pressure with no acute organ involvement is not an emergency, and that distinction decides how fast the pressure is brought down. It is not a hypertensive emergency.
Resistant hypertension
Resistance means pressure above goal despite three complementary drugs at maximally tolerated doses, which is not what is described.

B.io: Identify medical care strategies for coronary artery disease in the lecture topic list for the following populations.
B.q: A 24-year-old man has chest pain at rest with transient ST-segment elevation during the episode that resolves, and his coronary arteries show no high-grade stenosis. He smokes cigarettes and uses a recreational drug on weekends. Which substance should he be counseled to avoid because it can precipitate this condition?
opts: Diltiazem
Diltiazem is a calcium channel blocker, the first-line therapy for vasospastic angina, not a trigger. Cocaine is among the drugs that precipitate spasm.
Cocaine
Correct. Drugs that may precipitate vasospastic angina include cocaine, ephedrine, marijuana, alcohol, amphetamine and triptans. It is relatively uncommon and often strikes those under 50.
Nitroglycerin
Nitroglycerin relieves vasospastic episodes, and response to it is part of the diagnosis. The substance to avoid is cocaine, a known precipitant of spasm.
Amlodipine
Amlodipine is a first-line calcium channel blocker that prevents vasospastic episodes. Cocaine, along with amphetamine and ephedrine, precipitates them.

B.io: Stable
B.q: A 58-year-old man with exertional chest pain says he "had a heart cath" last week. The report shows dye was injected and the coronary arteries were imaged, revealing a stenosis, but nothing was done to the vessel. Which term names what was performed?
opts: Plain old balloon angioplasty
Plain old balloon angioplasty opens a narrowed artery with a balloon and no stent. This report describes imaging only, with nothing done to the stenosis.
Coronary angiography

Correct. Coronary angiography is the injection of dye to identify a lesion or blockage, and it is the gold standard for diagnosing coronary artery disease. Nothing was done to the vessel, so no intervention took place.
Coronary artery bypass graft
A coronary artery bypass graft anastomoses a mammary or radial artery, or a vein, to the coronary artery beyond the obstruction. It is open surgery, not dye imaging through a catheter.
Percutaneous coronary intervention
Percutaneous coronary intervention is the placement of a stent to keep the artery open. No stent or balloon was used here; the vessel was only imaged with dye.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atherosclerosis and lipid disorders: 1. B.q: A 51-year-old man with obesity and type 2 diabetes has a triglyceride of 720 mg/dL, elevated total cholesterol, reduced high-density lipoprotein and a normal low-density lipoprotein. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Severe hypertriglyceridemia

Correct. Triglyceride above 500 with elevated total cholesterol and reduced high-density lipoprotein, usually without raised low-density lipoprotein, defines it, typically on a polygenic background with obesity or insulin resistance.
Familial dysbetalipoproteinemia
Dysbetalipoproteinemia raises triglyceride and total cholesterol together to 250 to 500 with palmar xanthomas.
Mixed dyslipidemia
Mixed dyslipidemia raises low-density lipoprotein above 130 as well as triglyceride; his low-density lipoprotein is normal.
Heterozygous familial form
Familial hypercholesterolemia raises low-density lipoprotein with normal triglyceride, the reverse of his panel.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
B.q: What causes neurogenic orthostatic syncope?
opts: Autonomic nervous system dysfunction
Correct. It is a sustained drop in pressure on standing or sitting upright caused by underlying damage or dysfunction in the autonomic nervous system.
Volume loss from diarrhea or bleeding
Volume loss produces non-neurogenic orthostatic syncope, in which the autonomic system is intact and the heart rate rises significantly.
Emotional triggers raising vagal tone
Emotional triggers cause vasovagal reflex syncope, a transient reflex event, rather than a sustained postural drop from autonomic damage.
An arrhythmia lowering cardiac output
An arrhythmia causes cardiogenic syncope, investigated with an electrocardiogram and monitoring, rather than orthostatic syncope.
