B.q: A 71-year-old woman with resistant hypertension is started on lisinopril. Her creatinine rises markedly within a week. What does this suggest?
opts: Acute interstitial nephritis from the medication
Interstitial nephritis is not the mechanism described for this pattern; the abrupt rise on renin-angiotensin blockade points to renal artery stenosis.
Progression of underlying diabetic nephropathy
Diabetic nephropathy declines over months to years rather than jumping within a week of starting a renin-angiotensin blocker.
Expected drug effect requiring no change in approach
A small early creatinine rise can be acceptable, but a MARKED rise specifically points toward renovascular disease rather than being dismissed.
Bilateral renal artery stenosis

Correct. Where perfusion depends on angiotensin-mediated efferent arteriolar tone, blocking it drops the filtration pressure sharply. This is one of the recognized clues to renovascular disease, and it is why the agent is contraindicated in bilateral stenosis. A hemodynamically significant unilateral stenosis does the same.

B.io: Tricuspid stenosis
B.q: A 50-year-old woman has severe symptomatic tricuspid stenosis with leg swelling and jugular venous distension. Before any procedure, which medical regimen is appropriate?
opts: Warfarin with a heparin bridge
Warfarin with heparin bridging is anticoagulation for mechanical valves. Tricuspid stenosis is managed with low salt, a diuretic and an aldosterone antagonist.
Low salt, diuretic, aldosterone antagonist
Correct. Severe symptomatic tricuspid stenosis is managed with a low-salt diet, diuretics and an aldosterone antagonist, with bioprosthetic valve replacement preferred when the valve is replaced.
Nitrates, beta blocker, calcium blocker
Nitrates, beta blockers and calcium channel blockers are the avoid list for aortic stenosis. Tricuspid stenosis is managed with salt restriction, diuretics and an aldosterone antagonist.
Afterload reduction with hydralazine
Afterload reduction is medical management for chronic aortic regurgitation. Tricuspid stenosis uses low salt, a diuretic and an aldosterone antagonist.

B.io: Compare and contrast anticoagulation therapy for prosthetic heart valves.
B.q: A 60-year-old man with a mechanical aortic valve on warfarin is scheduled for a colectomy that requires stopping it. Which plan should be avoided?
opts: Bridging with heparin
Heparin bridging is exactly what is required when surgery interrupts warfarin in a patient with a mechanical valve. The plan to avoid is stopping warfarin with no cover.
Resuming a vitamin K antagonist
A mechanical valve needs lifelong vitamin K antagonist therapy, so resuming warfarin after surgery is required. The error is stopping it without a heparin bridge.
Rechecking his ratio after surgery
Warfarin is bridged until the international normalized ratio is therapeutic again, so rechecking it is part of the plan. What must be avoided is an unbridged gap.
Stopping warfarin with no bridge

Correct. If surgery requires interrupting warfarin, it must be bridged with heparin until the international normalized ratio is therapeutic; leaving a mechanical valve uncovered is the thing to avoid.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, prevention, and prognosis for heart failure.
B.q: A 34-year-old woman has progressive leg edema and jugular venous distension (distended neck veins). At the apex there is a low-pitched diastolic rumble with an opening snap. Which is the most likely cause of her right-sided heart failure?
opts: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy leads the diastolic chain with a fourth heart sound. An apical diastolic rumble with a snap is mitral stenosis.
Aortic valve stenosis
Aortic stenosis is the most common valvular cause of heart failure overall but does not give an apical diastolic rumble with a snap. This is mitral stenosis.
Tricuspid regurgitation
Tricuspid regurgitation gives a holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border, louder on inspiration. An apical diastolic rumble with a snap is mitral stenosis.
Mitral valve stenosis

Correct. A rumbling diastolic murmur at the apex with an opening snap is mitral stenosis, one of the three causes of right-sided failure with chronic left-sided failure and pulmonary arterial hypertension.

B.io: Identify medical care strategies for atherosclerosis and lipid disorders in the lecture topic list for the following populations. 6. infant 7. child 8. adolescent 9. adult 10. elderly
B.q: A 14-year-old girl with homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia remains severely elevated despite a high-intensity statin, ezetimibe and regular apheresis. Which adjunct is approved at her age?
opts: Gemfibrozil
Gemfibrozil is a fibrate for triglyceride, which is normal in familial hypercholesterolemia.
Evinacumab
Correct. Evinacumab, an intravenous monoclonal antibody that lowers low-density lipoprotein and triglyceride, is adjunct therapy for patients 12 years and older with the homozygous disorder.
Fish oil
Fish oil is associated with lower coronary death in general, but it is not an adjunct for the homozygous disorder.
Colesevelam
Colesevelam is a bile acid sequestrant for extra low-density lowering, not the adjunct approved for homozygous disease from age 12.

B.topic: ST-elevation infarction and right ventricular infarct
B.io: ST segment elevation
B.q: Why can nitroglycerin cause shock in a right ventricular infarct?
opts: It provokes coronary spasm
Nitroglycerin relieves coronary spasm rather than causing it. The problem in a right ventricular infarct is the fall in preload and output.
It triggers major bleeding
Bleeding is the danger of thrombolytics, not nitroglycerin. Nitroglycerin causes shock here by lowering the preload the right ventricle depends on.
It blocks the atrioventricular node
Nitroglycerin does not block conduction. In a right ventricular infarct it drops the preload the failing right ventricle needs, and output falls.
Lost preload drops output
Correct. The infarcted right ventricle is preload dependent; decreasing preload reduces the Frank-Starling effect, the ventricle fails into right-sided heart failure, output falls and shock follows.

B.io: Develop a differential diagnosis for a patient presenting with hypotension based on history, physical examination, and diagnostic findings.
B.q: A 74-year-old man with a prior heart attack and reduced ejection fraction collapsed abruptly while walking, with no warning except a brief racing heartbeat. He is pale, his pressure is 86/52 and his heart rate is 150 and regular. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Cardiogenic syncope from an arrhythmia

Correct. Abrupt collapse with minimal prodrome after palpitations, in a patient with coronary disease and reduced ejection fraction, with a rapid regular rhythm, points to an arrhythmic cardiac cause.
Situational reflex syncope
Situational syncope follows a bodily function such as urination, with a reflex prodrome and quick recovery.
Non-neurogenic orthostatic hypotension
Non-neurogenic orthostatic hypotension follows standing, often with volume loss; he collapsed abruptly mid-walk after palpitations.
Vasovagal reflex syncope
Vasovagal syncope follows triggers such as fear or heat with a warm, nauseated prodrome and a slow rather than fast heart rate.

B.io: Mitral regurgitation
B.q: A 66-year-old man with chronic mitral regurgitation has an echocardiogram showing a regurgitant fraction of 64%. Which severity does this indicate?
opts: Moderate regurgitation
Moderate mitral regurgitation is a regurgitant fraction of 30 to 49%. At 64%, more than half of each beat leaks back, which is severe.
Ungradeable by echocardiogram
Echocardiography grades mitral regurgitation by regurgitant fraction; left heart catheterization is not required. A fraction of 64% is severe.
Mild regurgitation
Mild mitral regurgitation is a regurgitant fraction below 30%. A fraction of 64% is severe.
Severe regurgitation
Correct. Mitral regurgitation is severe when the regurgitant fraction is 50% or more, meaning over half of the blood ejected goes backward. A fraction of 30 to 49% is moderate and below 30% is mild.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, prevention, and prognosis for heart failure.
B.q: A 64-year-old man has combined right and left heart failure with symptoms at rest despite optimized guideline-directed therapy. Which course is most appropriate to discuss?
opts: Stopping all medicines and observing
Abandoning symptom control is not the plan. Combined failure beyond optimized therapy points to transplant evaluation or comfort care.
Continuing dobutamine at home
Inotropes are for intensive care use only. Combined failure beyond optimized therapy points to transplant evaluation or comfort care.
Transplant evaluation or comfort care
Correct. Combined right and left failure is managed with symptom control, comfort care and heart transplant. When optimized therapy no longer controls symptoms, those are the options to raise.
Adding a calcium channel blocker
Calcium channel blockers are avoided in heart failure. Combined failure beyond optimized therapy points to transplant evaluation or comfort care.

B.io: Distinguish between acute and chronic hypotension
B.q: A 79-year-old woman with cardiomyopathy has had pressures around 92/58 for many months. She has intermittent lightheadedness that comes and goes. How is her hypotension best classified?
opts: Chronic cardiogenic hypotension
Correct. Cardiogenic causes such as cardiomyopathy and reduced ejection fraction heart failure produce chronic hypotension, which waxes and wanes and is intermittently symptomatic.
Acute toxic hypotension
Toxic or medication-mediated overdose causes acute hypotension of sudden onset with a specific trigger.
Long-lasting acute infectious hypotension
Infection from bacteremia to septic shock causes long-lasting acute hypotension, not months of waxing symptoms.
Acute reflex hypotension
Reflex hypotension is triggered and transient, not a pressure that runs low for months.

B.io: Differentiate each stage of the American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association (ACC/AHA), natural history classification of heart failure, and associated treatment recommendations of each stage.
B.q: A 57-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes has asymptomatic left ventricular hypertrophy on echocardiogram. She already takes an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor. Which drug class should be added for her diabetes-related risk?
opts: Calcium channel blocker such as amlodipine
Calcium channel blockers are avoided in heart failure. In stage B with diabetes the added class is the sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor.
Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor
Correct. She is stage B, and stage B carries a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor for patients with diabetes as well as the converting enzyme inhibitor and a beta blocker.
Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist
The antagonist belongs to symptomatic heart failure. In stage B with diabetes the added class is the sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor.
Angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor
The neprilysin combination belongs to symptomatic reduced ejection fraction in functional class II or III. Stage B with diabetes adds a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor.

B.q: A 24-year-old woman with hypertension has weak delayed femoral pulses and a leg pressure lower than her arm pressure. Which study establishes the diagnosis?
opts: A morning aldosterone to renin ratio
That screens for primary aldosteronism, which does not produce an arm-to-leg pressure gradient.
Polysomnography
Sleep study investigates obstructive sleep apnea, suggested by snoring and witnessed apneas.
Echocardiography
Correct, and the referral that follows is to a vascular surgeon or a structural cardiologist. The bedside findings raise the question; the echocardiogram answers it.
Renal duplex ultrasound
Renal duplex investigates renovascular disease, which is suggested by an abdominal bruit and asymmetric kidneys rather than by femoral pulse delay.

B.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis
B.q: Which are the earliest measurable markers of hypertensive kidney damage?
opts: Hematuria and casts on urinalysis
Blood and casts on urinalysis point toward alternative renal causes requiring evaluation rather than serving as the earliest markers of hypertensive damage.
Rising albuminuria and falling filtration rate
Correct, and both are watched as trends rather than single values, because it is the direction of travel over time that identifies progression early enough to act on.
A rising serum potassium concentration
Potassium is measured to screen for aldosteronism and before starting therapy rather than as an early marker of hypertensive renal injury.
A further rise in the blood pressure itself
The pressure is the cause under investigation; albuminuria and falling filtration are what measure the damage it has done.

B.io: Identify medical care strategies for atherosclerosis and lipid disorders in the lecture topic list for the following populations. 6. infant 7. child 8. adolescent 9. adult 10. elderly
B.q: An 81-year-old woman with no history of atherosclerotic disease asks whether she should start a statin for prevention. Her low-density lipoprotein is 145 mg/dL. What is the most appropriate approach?
opts: Calculate the Pooled Cohort risk
The Pooled Cohort Equation estimates risk for ages 40 to 79, so an 81-year-old falls outside its range.
Automatic high-intensity statin
High intensity is not automatic above 75 in primary prevention; the decision follows assessment and discussion.
Clinical assessment and risk discussion
Correct. Above 75 in primary prevention the approach is clinical assessment and a risk discussion rather than an automatic prescription.
Refuse any statin due to age
Age alone does not rule out a statin; the approach is individual assessment and discussion.

B.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education, and prognosis
B.q: A 44-year-old newly diagnosed hypertensive patient asks why treatment matters if she feels well. What is the strongest answer?
opts: Feeling well means her risk is already low
How a patient feels is not a guide to the pressure or to the damage it is doing.
It causes cumulative organ damage with no reliable symptoms
Correct. The heart, brain, kidneys, aorta, arteries and retina are all injured over years, and most patients have no reliable blood pressure-related symptoms to warn them.
She will begin to feel symptoms within a few months if untreated
Most patients with mild to moderate hypertension have no reliable symptoms at any point.
Treatment is optional until organ damage is demonstrated
Waiting for demonstrable damage forfeits the period in which it could have been prevented.

B.io: Pulmonic regurgitation
B.q: A 28-year-old man had a surgical valvuloplasty as a child to relieve right ventricular outflow obstruction. He now has a brief, high-pitched decrescendo early diastolic murmur at the second left intercostal space that radiates toward the mid right sternal border with full inspiration. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Pulmonic stenosis
Pulmonic stenosis is at the left upper sternal border too, but it is a harsh mid-systolic ejection murmur. This murmur is early diastolic, which is regurgitation.
Tricuspid stenosis
Tricuspid stenosis is a mid-diastolic rumble with an opening snap at the left lower sternal border near the xiphoid. This murmur is a brief early diastolic decrescendo.
Pulmonic regurgitation

Correct. A brief, high-pitched early diastolic murmur at the second left intercostal space with inspiratory radiation (the Graham Steell murmur) is pulmonic regurgitation, and surgery on the right ventricular outflow tract is its most common cause.
Aortic regurgitation
Aortic regurgitation is a blowing diastolic murmur at the third intercostal space radiating to the apex, a left-sided murmur louder on expiration, with bounding pulses.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atherosclerosis and lipid disorders: 1. Hypertriglyceridemia 2. Hypercholesterolemia 3. HDL cholesterol 4. LDL and VLDL cholesterol
B.q: A 58-year-old man whose brother had a heart attack at 50 has lipoprotein(a) measured at 85 mg/dL. His low-density lipoprotein is 140 mg/dL. What does the lipoprotein(a) result mean for his management?
opts: He needs aggressive low-density lowering
Correct. Elevated lipoprotein(a) is a causal and independent risk factor for atherosclerotic disease, and a patient with it needs aggressive therapy to decrease low-density lipoprotein.
It changes nothing in his plan
At 50 mg/dL or more it is a risk-enhancing factor and calls for aggressive low-density lowering.
He needs a fibrate for the value
Fibrates are the triglyceride drugs; the response to high lipoprotein(a) is aggressive low-density lowering.
It is protective and lowers his risk
Lipoprotein(a) is a causal factor for atherosclerotic disease and an independent risk factor, not protective.

B.io: Define the following diagnostic and therapeutic groups of HF patients, and the treatment implications/recommendations for each group: a. HF with reduced EF (HFrEF) b. HF with mildly reduced EF (HFmrEF) c. HF with preserved EF (HFpEF)
B.q: A 66-year-old woman with reduced ejection fraction is started on spironolactone alongside her loop diuretic. Which counseling point is most accurate?
opts: It replaces the need for her beta blocker
The antagonist adds to the beta blocker rather than replacing it; both are core classes. It spares potassium, so levels are checked.
It spares potassium, so levels are checked
Correct. Spironolactone is a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist, a potassium-sparing diuretic, which is why her potassium and renal function will be followed alongside the potassium-wasting loop.
It wastes potassium like her loop diuretic
Loops and thiazide-like diuretics waste potassium; spironolactone spares it. That is why her potassium is monitored.
It is only a short course for congestion
Spironolactone is a strong, ongoing recommendation in reduced ejection fraction, not a short diuretic course. It spares potassium, so levels are checked.

B.io: Differentiate between systolic dysfunction and diastolic dysfunction..
B.q: Which heart sound belongs to diastolic heart failure?
opts: A pericardial rub
A rub is not part of the heart failure chain. Diastolic failure gives a fourth heart sound from atrial contraction against a stiff ventricle.
An opening snap
An opening snap belongs to mitral stenosis, a cause of right-sided failure. Diastolic failure gives a fourth heart sound.
Fourth heart sound
Correct. A fourth heart sound is strong left atrial contraction against a stiff, hypertrophied left ventricle, and it sits in the diastolic chain with hypertension and edema that starts peripherally.
Third heart sound
A third heart sound is rapid filling of a dilated left ventricle, which belongs to the systolic chain. Diastolic failure gives a fourth heart sound.

B.io: Compare and contrast precipitating factors, clinical manifestations, diagnosis (including role of B-type natriuretic peptide, BNP), and treatment of acute decompensated heart failure.
B.q: A 62-year-old woman is three days out from a myocardial infarction complicated by acute heart failure, with an ejection fraction of 30%. A colleague proposes an implantable defibrillator before discharge. Which step is premature at this point?
opts: Optimizing her guideline therapy
Optimizing therapy is part of the pathway now. What is premature is the implantable device.
Implanting a defibrillator now

Correct. After acute heart failure from infarction, the pathway is a wearable defibrillator, optimized therapy and cardiac rehabilitation, then a repeat echocardiogram; the implantable device follows only if there is no improvement.
Starting a wearable defibrillator
The wearable defibrillator is exactly the first step for her. What is premature is the implantable device.
Referring to cardiac rehabilitation
Cardiac rehabilitation is part of the pathway now. What is premature is the implantable device.

B.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education, and prognosis
B.q: A 58-year-old hypertensive man has abrupt severe tearing chest pain radiating to his back, maximal at onset. His right arm pressure is 176/92 and his left is 138/78. A chest radiograph is reported as normal. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Delay imaging until the blood pressure is controlled
Imaging is immediate, because the diagnosis determines both the pressure target and the operation.
Reassure him, since the chest radiograph is normal
The radiograph may show a widened mediastinum but cannot rule the diagnosis out.
Obtain an echocardiogram to establish the diagnosis
Echocardiography establishes coarctation; immediate cross-sectional vascular imaging is what is required here.
Obtain immediate cross-sectional vascular imaging

Correct. A normal chest radiograph does NOT exclude dissection, so a normal film must not end the workup. The pain that is maximal at onset and the asymmetric arm pressures both point to it, and surgical involvement is urgent.

B.io: Angina pectoris
B.q: A 55-year-old woman has microvascular angina confirmed after angiography showed normal coronary arteries. Which treatment is appropriate?
opts: Thrombolytic therapy
Thrombolytics are for ST-elevation infarction when a percutaneous unit is 2 or more hours away. Microvascular angina is treated medically, for example with a calcium channel blocker.
Calcium channel blocker

Correct. Treatment of microvascular angina is very similar to coronary artery disease: lifestyle modification and risk-factor reduction, a calcium channel blocker, beta blocker, angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor and statin.
Reassurance alone
Microvascular angina is not left untreated; its treatment is very similar to coronary artery disease, with risk-factor reduction, a calcium channel blocker, beta blocker, statin and more.
Coronary stent placement
A stent holds open a narrowed coronary artery, and her arteries are normal on angiography. Microvascular angina is treated much like coronary artery disease, including a calcium channel blocker.

B.io: Define the following diagnostic and therapeutic groups of HF patients, and the treatment implications/recommendations for each group: a. HF with reduced EF (HFrEF) b. HF with mildly reduced EF (HFmrEF) c. HF with preserved EF (HFpEF)
B.q: A 63-year-old man with mildly reduced ejection fraction (fraction 44%) has ankle edema and breathlessness. Which therapy carries the strongest recommendation?
opts: A diuretic as needed

Correct. In mildly reduced ejection fraction, diuretics as needed carry the one strong recommendation. The sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor is moderate; the beta blocker, antagonist and renin-angiotensin drugs are weak.
A neprilysin combination drug
The angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor is weak in mildly reduced ejection fraction. A diuretic as needed carries the strongest recommendation.
An evidence-based beta blocker
In mildly reduced ejection fraction the beta blocker is a weak recommendation. The strongest is a diuretic as needed for his congestion.
A mineralocorticoid antagonist
The antagonist is a weak recommendation in mildly reduced ejection fraction. A diuretic as needed carries the strongest one.

B.io: Aortic regurgitation
B.q: A 34-year-old man with Marfan syndrome has a high-pitched blowing diastolic murmur at the third intercostal space at the left upper sternal border that radiates to the apex. He has bounding pulses and a wide pulse pressure. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Pulmonic regurgitation
Pulmonic regurgitation is a brief early diastolic murmur at the second left intercostal space that radiates toward the right sternal border. It does not produce bounding pulses.
Mitral stenosis
Mitral stenosis is diastolic too, but it is a low-pitched rumble at the apex that starts with an opening snap. Rumble means stenosis; this murmur is blowing.
Mitral regurgitation
Mitral regurgitation is blowing but holosystolic, at the apex, radiating to the axilla. This murmur is diastolic, which points to the aortic valve.
Aortic regurgitation

Correct. Blowing means regurgitation and diastolic narrows it to the aortic or pulmonic valve; the third intercostal space with radiation to the apex, bounding pulses and a wide pulse pressure mark aortic regurgitation. Marfan syndrome is a root-disease cause.

B.io: Distinguish between acute and chronic hypotension
B.q: A 66-year-old woman in a clinic has hypotension from a suspected overwhelming infection and is awaiting transfer. Which therapy should not be started in the clinic?
opts: Reviewing her medications
Reviewing medications is appropriate, since medication-mediated hypotension is treated by reducing the offending drug.
Arranging urgent transfer
Arranging transfer is appropriate, because the drugs her hypotension may need are used only in the emergency department and intensive care.
A norepinephrine infusion
Correct. Epinephrine, norepinephrine, dopamine, phenylephrine and vasopressin are listed for the emergency department and intensive care only.
Repeating her vital signs
Repeated readings are appropriate, since each reading is only a snapshot in time.

B.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education, and prognosis
B.q: A 59-year-old hypertensive man is breathless with bibasal crackles and raised jugular venous pressure. Is chest radiography appropriate?
opts: Yes, because findings suggest pulmonary edema
Correct. Radiography is appropriate when dyspnea or findings suggest pulmonary edema, when cardiomegaly is suspected, or when a widened mediastinum is a concern.
No, because a normal film would exclude dissection
A normal chest radiograph does not exclude dissection, so that is not a reason either way.
No, because chest radiography is never indicated in hypertension
It is not indicated ROUTINELY for uncomplicated hypertension, which is different from never being indicated.
Yes, as a routine part of every hypertensive workup
Routine chest radiography is specifically not indicated for uncomplicated hypertension.

B.io: Identify medical care strategies for coronary artery disease in the lecture topic list for the following populations.
B.q: A 40-year-old woman's mother had a myocardial infarction at 70 and her brother had one at 50. She asks which relative's heart attack raises her own coronary risk. Which answer is accurate?
opts: Both relatives'
Only one qualifies. The cut-offs are under 55 for a male first-degree relative and under 65 for a female one, so her brother at 50 counts but her mother at 70 does not.
Only her brother's

Correct. Family history counts when a male first-degree relative had sudden death or myocardial infarction before 55, or a female first-degree relative before 65. Her brother at 50 qualifies; her mother at 70 does not.
Neither relative's
Her brother qualifies: a male first-degree relative with a myocardial infarction before 55 is a nonmodifiable genetic risk factor. Only her mother, at 70, falls outside the cut-off.
Only her mother's
A female first-degree relative counts only if the event came before 65. Her mother was 70, so she does not qualify; her brother, a male relative under 55, does.

B.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis
B.q: What is the commonest cause to exclude before labeling hypertension as resistant?
opts: Undiagnosed primary aldosteronism
Secondary hypertension is among the things to rule out, but nonadherence is identified as the commonest cause of apparent resistance.
Incorrect cuff size
Measurement error is on the list to exclude, but nonadherence is specifically named as the commonest cause.
Excess alcohol intake
High sodium or alcohol intake appears on the list, but nonadherence is the commonest single explanation.
Medication nonadherence
Correct, and it heads a list that also includes measurement error, white coat effect, high sodium or alcohol intake, interfering drugs, and undiagnosed sleep apnea or secondary hypertension.

B.io: Mitral valve prolapse
B.q: Which auscultatory finding is typical of mitral valve prolapse?
opts: An opening snap after the second sound
An opening snap after the second heart sound introduces the diastolic rumble of mitral stenosis. Prolapse gives a mid-systolic click.
A blowing diastolic murmur to the apex
A blowing diastolic murmur radiating to the apex is aortic regurgitation. Mitral valve prolapse is a mid-systolic click at the apex.
A mid-systolic click at the apex
Correct. Mitral valve prolapse gives a mid-systolic click at the apex. It is usually benign and asymptomatic, but it may develop the symptoms and signs of mitral regurgitation.
A diastolic rumble near the xiphoid
A mid-diastolic rumble near the xiphoid is tricuspid stenosis. Mitral valve prolapse gives a mid-systolic click at the apex.

B.io: Aortic stenosis
B.q: Which maneuver makes the aortic stenosis murmur louder?
opts: Squatting

Correct. Squatting, like sitting forward, raises preload and left ventricular volume, so more blood crosses the aortic valve and the murmur grows louder; sitting forward also brings the valve closer to the chest wall.
Handgrip
Handgrip raises afterload, which cuts forward flow through the stenotic aortic valve and softens its murmur. It is a maneuver that increases regurgitant murmurs instead.
Standing
Standing lowers venous return and volume, reducing flow through the aortic valve, so the murmur gets softer rather than louder.
Valsalva
Valsalva reduces venous return and cardiac output, so less blood crosses the narrowed valve and the aortic stenosis murmur gets softer.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, prevention, and prognosis for heart failure.
B.q: A 76-year-old man with heart failure has cool extremities, a narrow pulse pressure and increasing confusion. His urine output has fallen and creatinine has doubled. Which complication has developed?
opts: Acute kidney injury from low perfusion
Correct. Cool extremities, narrow pulse pressure and obtundation are signs of low perfusion, and renal dysfunction with acute kidney injury and falling urine output is part of the same picture.
Urinary retention from prostatic disease
Nothing points to an obstructed outlet, and the perfusion signs explain the kidneys. This is acute kidney injury from low perfusion.
Nephrotic syndrome from proteinuria
Nephrotic syndrome is a primary kidney disorder. His low perfusion signs explain acute kidney injury with falling urine output.
Hypertensive kidney damage from years
Chronic hypertensive damage does not appear over days with cool extremities. This is acute kidney injury from low perfusion.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
B.q: A 20-year-old woman has a classic history of palpitations and lightheadedness on standing that improve lying down, but her tilt-table test is negative. How should the negative result be interpreted?
opts: It does not exclude the syndrome
Correct. With a sensitivity of about 40%, many patients with the syndrome test negative, so a negative result tells almost nothing; a positive result, with specificity above 80%, carries more weight.
It points to a cardiac cause
A negative tilt-table test says nothing about the heart; cardiac causes are pursued with an electrocardiogram or echocardiography.
It points to autonomic failure
Autonomic failure is shown by a pressure fall with a minimal heart rate rise, not by a negative tilt-table test.
It rules the syndrome out
Ruling out requires high sensitivity. At about 40%, a negative tilt-table test leaves the diagnosis open.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, prevention, and prognosis for heart failure.
B.q: A 38-year-old woman with very heavy menstrual bleeding has fatigue, palpitations, ankle edema and a raised B-type natriuretic peptide. Echocardiogram is being arranged. Which additional test is most likely to identify the driver of her heart failure?
opts: Complete blood count
Correct. Anemia is one of the causes of high-output failure, and the complete blood count is part of the high-output workup with the echocardiogram, metabolic panel and natriuretic peptide.
Chest radiograph
A radiograph can show congestion but not its cause. The complete blood count identifies anemia, the likely driver of high-output failure.
Cardiac troponin level
Troponin looks for infarction or ischemic cardiomyopathy, which nothing here suggests. The complete blood count looks for the anemia that heavy bleeding causes.
Right heart catheterization
Catheterization grades hemodynamic severity in right-sided failure. The complete blood count identifies anemia, the likely driver here.

B.topic: Post-infarction care and sudden cardiac death
B.io: Acute myocardial infraction
B.q: A 63-year-old man is recovering from an ST-elevation myocardial infarction. Several weeks later he develops pleuritic chest pain and a pericardial friction rub. Which complication of the infarction does this represent?
opts: Myocardial rupture
Myocardial rupture is a catastrophic mechanical complication with sudden collapse. Pleuritic pain and a friction rub weeks later describe pericarditis (Dressler syndrome).
Thromboembolism
Thromboembolism causes stroke or limb ischemia from a clot leaving the heart. Pleuritic chest pain with a pericardial friction rub is pericarditis (Dressler syndrome).
Pericarditis

Correct. Pericarditis (Dressler syndrome) is listed among the mechanical complications of myocardial infarction. Pleuritic pain with a friction rub weeks after the infarct points to the pericardium rather than the ventricle.
Ventricular aneurysm
A ventricular aneurysm is a mechanical complication of the infarcted wall itself. It does not produce pleuritic pain with a pericardial friction rub; that is pericarditis (Dressler syndrome).

B.io: Compare and contrast precipitating factors, clinical manifestations, diagnosis (including role of B-type natriuretic peptide, BNP), and treatment of acute decompensated heart failure.
B.q: A 66-year-old man has breathlessness, leg edema and a B-type natriuretic peptide of 280. Which study should come next to define his cardiac structure and ejection fraction?
opts: Cardiac troponin level
Troponin looks for infarction or ischemic cardiomyopathy. The study that defines structure and ejection fraction is the echocardiogram.
Echocardiogram
Correct. An indeterminate peptide leaves the question open, and the echocardiogram shows structure most accurately and classifies heart failure by ejection fraction.
Repeat the peptide in a year
Waiting a year leaves a symptomatic patient undiagnosed. The echocardiogram defines structure and ejection fraction now.
Right heart catheterization
Catheterization grades hemodynamic severity once right-sided failure is established. The first study for structure and ejection fraction is the echocardiogram.

B.io: Define hypotension
B.q: Which description defines syncope?
opts: Collapse with confusion lasting an hour
Prolonged confusion afterward points away from syncope, whose recovery is spontaneous and complete, and toward causes such as seizure.
Dizziness and tunnel vision without collapse
Warning symptoms such as dizziness, lightheadedness and tunnel vision without losing consciousness define near-syncope, also called presyncope.
Prolonged unconsciousness needing support
Syncope is transient and self-limited, and recovery is spontaneous. Prolonged unconsciousness needing support falls outside the definition.
Brief loss of consciousness, then full recovery
Correct. Syncope is a transient, self-limited loss of consciousness with inability to maintain postural tone, followed by spontaneous recovery.

B.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education, and prognosis
B.q: A 64-year-old man with hypertension has heart failure with a reduced ejection fraction and a myocardial infarction six months ago. Which class is preferred for him?
opts: Clonidine
Central alpha-2 agonists are limited by sedation and rebound hypertension and have no preferred indication here.
A beta blocker

Correct. Beta blockers are not first-line for uncomplicated hypertension, but reduced ejection fraction heart failure, recent infarction and ischemic disease are exactly the comorbidities that select them.
Hydralazine as monotherapy
Hydralazine requires combination therapy because of reflex tachycardia and fluid retention.
A non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker
Verapamil and diltiazem are avoided where the ejection fraction is already reduced, as it is here.

B.io: Define the following diagnostic and therapeutic groups of HF patients, and the treatment implications/recommendations for each group: a. HF with reduced EF (HFrEF) b. HF with mildly reduced EF (HFmrEF) c. HF with preserved EF (HFpEF)
B.q: A 68-year-old woman has fatigue and breathlessness with exertion. Echocardiogram shows an ejection fraction of 45%, and her fraction has never been lower. Which heart failure group describes her?
opts: Preserved ejection fraction
Preserved ejection fraction starts at 50%. At 45% she falls in the mildly reduced band.
Reduced ejection fraction
Reduced ejection fraction is 40% or less. At 45% she falls in the mildly reduced band.
Improved ejection fraction
Improved ejection fraction needs an earlier value of 40% or less. Hers has never been lower, so she is mildly reduced.
Mildly reduced ejection fraction
Correct. 45% falls in the 41 to 49% band, and with no earlier value of 40% or less there is nothing to make it improved ejection fraction. Her treatment then resembles preserved ejection fraction.

B.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education, and prognosis
B.q: A 48-year-old Black man develops lip and tongue swelling three months after starting an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor. What should be known about this?
opts: An angiotensin receptor blocker carries no risk whatsoever
Angioedema with an angiotensin receptor blocker remains possible, although substitution is usually appropriate.
It is a dose-related effect that resolves on dose reduction
It is a class effect rather than a dose phenomenon, and the agent is stopped rather than reduced.
A beta blocker is the appropriate substitution
The usual substitution is an angiotensin receptor blocker, and beta blockers are not first-line for uncomplicated hypertension.
It is two to four times more common in this group

Correct. It is a bradykinin-mediated class effect of angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibition. Angiotensin receptor blockers can usually be used instead, though angioedema with them remains possible. An angiotensin receptor blocker is usually substituted.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, prevention, and prognosis for heart failure.
B.q: A 62-year-old woman with long-standing hypertension has exertional breathlessness. Her electrocardiogram shows tall R waves in V5 and V6 and deep S waves in V1 and V2. What does this pattern show?
opts: Right heart strain
Right heart strain shows right axis deviation, right bundle branch block and T-wave inversions in V1 to V3. Her pattern is left ventricular hypertrophy.
Left ventricular hypertrophy
Correct. Tall R waves in V5 and V6 with deep S waves in V1 and V2 indicate left ventricular hypertrophy, the structural change behind hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and the diastolic chain.
Acute inferior injury
Acute injury shows ischemic changes such as elevation in the inferior leads. Her voltage pattern is left ventricular hypertrophy.
A normal tracing
Tall lateral R waves with deep right precordial S waves are abnormal; they indicate left ventricular hypertrophy.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atherosclerosis and lipid disorders: 1. Hypertriglyceridemia 2. Hypercholesterolemia 3. HDL cholesterol 4. LDL and VLDL cholesterol
B.q: A 47-year-old man with borderline-high low-density lipoprotein asks which foods can help lower his cholesterol. Which dietary advice is most appropriate?
opts: Add soluble fiber and plant sterols

Correct. Therapeutic lifestyle changes include less saturated fat, more soluble fiber and plant stanols or sterols, cholesterol-lowering substances found in grains, vegetables, fruits, nuts and seeds.
Eat more refined carbohydrate
Excess carbohydrate increases hepatic very-low-density triglyceride secretion, worsening the lipid profile.
Cut out all vegetables
Vegetables are among the natural sources of plant stanols and sterols, which lower cholesterol.
Add more saturated and trans fat
Saturated and trans fat down-regulate hepatic low-density lipoprotein receptors and raise low-density lipoprotein, the opposite of the goal.

B.io: Angina pectoris
B.q: Which description fits typical cardiac chest pain?
opts: Sharp pain that shifts with position
Angina is not affected by position. Typical cardiac pain is substernal pressure that worsens with exertion and is relieved by nitroglycerin.
Burning pain relieved by exertion
Exertion worsens angina because it raises oxygen demand. Typical pain is substernal pressure brought on by exertion and relieved by nitroglycerin.
Pain reproduced by pressing the chest
Pain reproduced by pressure points away from the heart. Typical cardiac pain is substernal pressure, worse with exertion, radiating to the neck or shoulder.
Substernal pressure with exertion
Correct. Typical cardiac chest pain is substernal chest pressure, worse with exertion, radiating to the neck or shoulder, with shortness of breath and diaphoresis, relieved by nitroglycerin.

B.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
B.q: A 35-year-old man has fainted twice, each time with warmth and nausea beforehand and quick recovery. Which part of his evaluation is most useful in establishing the diagnosis?
opts: A tilt-table test
Tilt-table testing is listed for postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome and has a sensitivity of only about 40%.
A stress test
A stress test belongs to the arrhythmia work-up of cardiogenic syncope, not the diagnosis of reflex syncope.
The history
Correct. History is the most important portion of diagnosing reflex syncope, summed up as history, history, history, supported by a log of episodes.
An echocardiogram
Echocardiography is for structural cardiogenic syncope; a reflex faint with a prodrome is diagnosed from the history.

C.io: Pulmonic stenosis
C.q: A 25-year-old woman has severe congenital pulmonic stenosis with exertional dyspnea and syncope. Which procedure is the most appropriate treatment?
opts: Mitral balloon valvotomy
Percutaneous balloon valvotomy of the mitral valve treats severe symptomatic mitral stenosis. Her obstruction is at the pulmonic valve.
Aortic valve replacement
Aortic valve replacement treats severe aortic stenosis. Severe symptomatic pulmonic stenosis is opened with pulmonic balloon valvuloplasty.
Pulmonic balloon valvuloplasty

Correct. Severe pulmonic stenosis with symptoms is treated with pulmonic balloon valvuloplasty, with diuretics for right heart failure symptoms; severe congenital disease may require valve replacement.
Tricuspid annuloplasty
Annuloplasty treats tricuspid regurgitation caused by annular dilation. Severe symptomatic pulmonic stenosis is treated with balloon valvuloplasty.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atherosclerosis and lipid disorders: 1. Hypertriglyceridemia 2. Hypercholesterolemia 3. HDL cholesterol 4. LDL and VLDL cholesterol
C.q: A 30-year-old woman has soft yellow plaques on both upper eyelids near the inner canthi (xanthelasmas). Her low-density lipoprotein is 205 mg/dL. Which counseling point is most appropriate?
opts: They are harmless and need no work-up
In a young woman with high low-density lipoprotein they usually indicate an underlying genetic condition and warrant evaluation.
They suggest an inherited lipid disorder
Correct. Xanthelasmas usually indicate an underlying genetic condition, and ruling out primary causes matters because they influence her own risk and the management of her family members.
They are caused by her eye makeup
Xanthelasmas are lipid deposits that usually indicate a genetic condition, not a reaction to cosmetics.
They show her triglyceride is very high
Very high triglyceride produces eruptive xanthomas (small papules on the back and limbs), not eyelid plaques.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, prevention, and prognosis for heart failure.
C.q: A 68-year-old man hospitalized with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction asks why a defibrillator is being discussed. Which cause accounts for about half of cardiac arrests in hospitalized patients like him?
opts: Acute pulmonary embolism
Pulmonary embolism is not the leading cause of these arrests. About half of these cardiac arrests are due to ventricular arrhythmias.
Low potassium alone
Electrolytes matter on diuretics, but about half of these cardiac arrests are due to ventricular arrhythmias.
Complete heart block
Complete heart block is not the leading cause of these arrests. About half of these cardiac arrests are due to ventricular arrhythmias.
Ventricular arrhythmias

Correct. About 52% of cardiac arrests in hospitalized patients with reduced ejection fraction are due to ventricular arrhythmias, which is the reason for defibrillator protection in those who meet the criteria.

C.io: Compare and contrast precipitating factors, clinical manifestations, diagnosis (including role of B-type natriuretic peptide, BNP), and treatment of acute decompensated heart failure.
C.q: A 55-year-old woman has breathlessness on exertion for a week. Her B-type natriuretic peptide is 45. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Order an implantable device
A defibrillator requires established reduced ejection fraction and other criteria. At 45 acute heart failure is ruled out.
Look for a non-cardiac cause
Correct. A level below 100 rules out acute heart failure with a negative predictive value above 90%, so her breathlessness needs another explanation.
Admit for acute heart failure
Acute heart failure is likely only above 900. At 45 it is ruled out, and another cause should be sought.
Start a loop diuretic today
A diuretic treats congestion from heart failure, which a level of 45 rules out acutely. Another cause should be sought.

C.io: Define the following diagnostic and therapeutic groups of HF patients, and the treatment implications/recommendations for each group: a. HF with reduced EF (HFrEF) b. HF with mildly reduced EF (HFmrEF) c. HF with preserved EF (HFpEF)
C.q: A 70-year-old man with reduced ejection fraction (fraction 22%) is breathless even at rest. He does not yet take a renin-angiotensin drug. Which renin-angiotensin option fits his symptom class?
opts: No renin-angiotensin drug once class IV
Class IV does not remove renin-angiotensin therapy; the converting enzyme inhibitor or receptor blocker is recommended through class IV.
A calcium channel blocker such as verapamil
Calcium channel blockers are avoided in heart failure. In functional class IV the renin-angiotensin option is a converting enzyme inhibitor or receptor blocker.
A converting enzyme inhibitor or receptor blocker

Correct. Symptoms at rest are class IV. An angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor or receptor blocker covers class II to IV, while the angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor is recommended for class II to III.
An angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor
The neprilysin combination is recommended for class II to III. At rest he is class IV, which the converting enzyme inhibitor or receptor blocker covers.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
C.q: A 71-year-old man had his diuretic dose increased 10 days ago. He now has lightheadedness on standing, a 28 mmHg systolic fall and a heart rate rise from 70 to 94. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
opts: Reduce the recently increased diuretic
Correct. The offending agent is removed first: iatrogenic hypotension is treated by reducing or removing the medication, with slow position changes meanwhile.
Start midodrine for the pressure
Midodrine is best with neurogenic syncope. Here the cause is a medication, which is reduced rather than counteracted with another drug.
Start fludrocortisone
Fludrocortisone is best with postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome and retains salt and water; it does not address the diuretic.
Add droxidopa as an adjunct
Droxidopa has mild efficacy and is used as an adjunct to midodrine or fludrocortisone, not to offset a diuretic side effect.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
C.q: A 65-year-old woman with long-standing diabetes and numb feet has a 30 mmHg standing pressure fall with a heart rate rise of only 3 beats and no sign of dehydration. What is the most likely mechanism of her syncope?
opts: Inadequate norepinephrine release
Correct. Autonomic dysfunction leaves too little norepinephrine released from sympathetic postganglionic neurons, so vessels fail to constrict and the heart rate rises less than expected.
Reduced volume from fluid loss
Fluid loss is the non-neurogenic mechanism, and it is usually accompanied by dehydration and a brisk heart rate rise.
A fast rhythm reducing output
A fast arrhythmia reducing output is cardiogenic syncope, often with abrupt collapse and palpitations rather than a flat heart rate.
A vagal surge with vasodilation
A vagal surge with sympathetic inhibition is the vasovagal reflex chain, which is transient and triggered rather than postural.

C.io: Differentiate each stage of the American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association (ACC/AHA), natural history classification of heart failure, and associated treatment recommendations of each stage.
C.q: A 59-year-old woman in stage B, pre-heart failure, developed side effects on lisinopril and could not tolerate it. Which is the recommended alternative?
opts: Stopping renin-angiotensin therapy
Intolerance of one agent does not end renin-angiotensin therapy. Stage B switches to an angiotensin receptor blocker such as losartan.
Losartan, an angiotensin receptor blocker
Correct. Stage B lists an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor with an angiotensin receptor blocker if the inhibitor is not tolerated, alongside a beta blocker.
Sacubitril-valsartan combination
The neprilysin combination is recommended for symptomatic reduced ejection fraction in functional class II or III, not stage B. The alternative is a receptor blocker.
Verapamil for blood pressure
Verapamil is a calcium channel blocker, avoided in heart failure. The stage B alternative is an angiotensin receptor blocker such as losartan.

C.io: Compare and contrast risk factors, management, and complications of arteriosclerosis and atherosclerosis.
C.q: A 57-year-old woman without diabetes has low-density lipoprotein of 140 mg/dL and a 10-year atherosclerotic risk of 10%. She is unsure whether to start a statin, and no risk enhancers are present. Which test can help the decision?
opts: Repeat total cholesterol
Her profile is already known; a calcium score adds information that a repeat total cannot.
Fundoscopic examination
Fundoscopy looks for lipemia retinalis in chylomicronemia and has no role in the statin decision.
Skin biopsy for receptor activity
Skin biopsy confirms homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia, which presents in childhood; it does not guide primary prevention.
Coronary artery calcium score

Correct. In adults 40 to 75 without diabetes, with low-density lipoprotein of 70 to 189 and 10-year risk of 7.5% to 19.9%, coronary artery calcium scoring is considered when the statin decision is uncertain.

C.io: Mitral valve prolapse
C.q: What causes mitral valve prolapse?
opts: Myxomatous degeneration of the valve
Correct. Mitral valve prolapse comes from myxomatous degeneration of the mitral valve, which leaves thickened, redundant leaflets that flare into the left atrium during systole.
Papillary muscle rupture after infarction
Papillary muscle rupture after acute myocardial infarction causes acute mitral regurgitation. Prolapse is myxomatous degeneration of the valve.
Rheumatic scarring of the leaflets
Rheumatic scarring thickens and immobilizes the leaflets and causes mitral stenosis. Prolapse comes from myxomatous degeneration.
Calcification of an aging valve
Degenerative calcification is the aortic stenosis process of older patients. Mitral valve prolapse is myxomatous degeneration, usually in young women.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atherosclerosis and lipid disorders: 1. Hypertriglyceridemia 2. Hypercholesterolemia 3. HDL cholesterol 4. LDL and VLDL cholesterol
C.q: A 59-year-old woman started a moderate-intensity statin six weeks ago for primary prevention. She feels well. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Repeat the lipid panel now
Correct. Adherence and percentage response are assessed with a repeat lipid panel 4 to 12 weeks after starting a statin, then every 3 to 12 months as needed; six weeks falls in that window.
Stop the statin, she feels well
Feeling well is expected; the statin prevents events rather than treating symptoms.
Recheck lipids in two years
Two years is far too long to judge adherence and response; the first recheck belongs at 4 to 12 weeks.
Double the intensity without labs
Changes are guided by the measured percentage response, so labs come before any adjustment.

C.io: Mitral regurgitation
C.q: A 64-year-old man, three days after an acute myocardial infarction, has sudden breathlessness, crackles in both lungs and a new holosystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla. Which is the most likely cause?
opts: Myxomatous degeneration
Myxomatous degeneration causes mitral valve prolapse, a chronic cause of mitral regurgitation. The sudden murmur three days after an infarction points to papillary muscle rupture.
Rheumatic heart disease
Rheumatic heart disease is a cause of mitral regurgitation, but it does not arrive suddenly three days after an infarction. Papillary muscle rupture does.
Papillary muscle rupture

Correct. An acute myocardial infarction with papillary muscle rupture is an acute cause of mitral regurgitation, and acute mitral regurgitation presents with left-sided heart failure symptoms such as dyspnea and rales.
Tricuspid annular dilation
Tricuspid annular dilation causes tricuspid regurgitation in pulmonary hypertension, heard at the lower sternal border. An apical murmur after infarction is papillary muscle rupture.

C.topic: Chest pain workup and risk scores
C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following coronary artery disease:
C.q: A 63-year-old man with exertional chest pressure has a nuclear stress test that is abnormal. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Coronary calcium score
A calcium score adds risk stratification, not anatomy, and does not follow an abnormal stress test. The next step is cardiac catheterization.
Discharge with no follow-up
An abnormal nuclear stress test is not a result to walk away from. It is followed by cardiac catheterization to look at the coronary arteries.
Repeat the stress test
Repeating an abnormal nuclear study only delays the answer. An abnormal nuclear stress test goes on to cardiac catheterization.
Cardiac catheterization
Correct. An abnormal nuclear stress test leads to cardiac catheterization, where coronary angiography, the gold standard for diagnosing coronary artery disease, defines the lesions.

C.io: Differentiate between systolic dysfunction and diastolic dysfunction..
C.q: A 58-year-old man with known dilated cardiomyopathy has worsening breathlessness. Blood pressure is 102/64, a third heart sound (an extra sound in early diastole just after the second heart sound) is present, and he has crackles. Which ejection fraction is the echocardiogram expected to show?
opts: About 25%

Correct. Dilated cardiomyopathy is the systolic chain: poor contraction, a reduced ejection fraction of 40% or less, low-normal pressure, a third heart sound and pulmonary edema. A value near 25% fits.
About 60%
A preserved ejection fraction belongs to the diastolic chain of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Dilated cardiomyopathy with these signs gives a reduced value near 25%.
About 75%
A high value is the opposite of a failing squeeze. Dilated cardiomyopathy with a third sound fits a reduced ejection fraction near 25%.
About 45%
45% is mildly reduced, between the two chains. Dilated cardiomyopathy with a third sound and low pressure fits a clearly reduced value near 25%.

C.topic: Post-infarction care and sudden cardiac death
C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following coronary artery disease:
C.q: A 48-year-old man with no known heart disease collapses while jogging and cannot be resuscitated. Autopsy shows extensive coronary artery disease. What is the most likely cause of his sudden cardiac death?
opts: Electrolyte abnormality
Electrolyte abnormalities are among the other causes of sudden cardiac death. The most common cause, and the fit with coronary artery disease, is ventricular fibrillation.
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is one of the other causes of sudden cardiac death, but his autopsy shows coronary disease. The most common cause of sudden cardiac death is ventricular fibrillation.
Complete heart block
Complete heart block follows loss of the atrioventricular node's supply from the right coronary artery. The most common cause of sudden cardiac death is ventricular fibrillation.
Ventricular fibrillation

Correct. The most common cause of sudden cardiac death is ventricular fibrillation, and sudden death is the initial manifestation of coronary artery disease in over 20% of patients, as it was for him.

C.io: Aortic stenosis
C.q: A 64-year-old man has an echocardiogram for palpitations that incidentally shows mild aortic stenosis. He has no chest pain, breathlessness or fainting. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: No follow-up is needed
Aortic stenosis progresses; 10 to 20% reach significant stenosis within 10 to 15 years. Evidence of it on echocardiogram calls for a cardiology consult to set follow-up.
Start a nitrate for prevention
Nitrates drop preload and are avoided in aortic stenosis, and medical treatment does not change its course. The step is a cardiology consult to plan follow-up.
Cardiology consultation

Correct. All patients with evidence of aortic stenosis on echocardiogram should have a cardiology consult to evaluate them and set the frequency of follow-up, even when the finding is mild and incidental.
Transcatheter valve replacement
Replacement is for severe aortic stenosis with symptomatic systolic dysfunction or a bicuspid valve. Mild asymptomatic disease is referred to cardiology for evaluation and follow-up.

C.io: Compare and contrast anticoagulation therapy for prosthetic heart valves.
C.q: A 66-year-old man has just recovered from replacement of his aortic valve with a mechanical valve. Which long-term antithrombotic therapy is recommended?
opts: Heparin as permanent outpatient therapy
Heparin is used to bridge when surgery interrupts warfarin until the ratio is therapeutic. The long-term therapy for a mechanical valve is a vitamin K antagonist.
No therapy after the recovery period
Stopping after the postoperative period applies to biological valves. A mechanical valve needs lifelong anticoagulation with a vitamin K antagonist.
Warfarin, a vitamin K antagonist

Correct. In patients with mechanical heart valves, vitamin K antagonist therapy is recommended for long-term management over no vitamin K antagonist and over antiplatelet agents. Warfarin is the most commonly used vitamin K antagonist.
Aspirin alone as antiplatelet therapy
Vitamin K antagonist therapy is recommended over antiplatelet agents for a mechanical valve. Aspirin alone does not meet the need for lifelong anticoagulation.

C.io: Acute coronary syndrome
C.q: A standard troponin I result is 0.12 ng/mL; how is it read?
opts: Too low to report
Only very small standard troponin I values (below 0.03 ng/mL) are reported as a range. A result of 0.12 ng/mL is reportable and abnormal.
Abnormal
Correct. Standard troponin I above 0.04 ng/mL is abnormal, and 0.12 ng/mL is three times that 99th percentile. The value is then repeated to watch the trend.
Normal for a woman
Sex-specific values apply to high-sensitivity troponin I in ng/L. Standard troponin I above 0.04 ng/mL is abnormal in anyone.
Not abnormal
Not abnormal applies at or below 0.04 ng/mL of standard troponin I. At 0.12 ng/mL the result is abnormal.

C.q: A 50-year-old man starting home monitoring asks how to do it. What should he be told?
opts: One reading each morning for three days
That collects far less data than the standard schedule and is more vulnerable to a single odd value.
Two readings morning and evening for seven days

Correct, and the accompanying instruction matters as much: do not overreact to the highest single reading, because acting on outliers generates anxiety and unnecessary changes in therapy. They are taken at least a minute apart and the average is reported.
Readings only when he feels unwell
Most patients with mild to moderate hypertension have no reliable blood pressure-related symptoms, so symptom-triggered readings would miss the point.
Continuous monitoring over twenty-four hours at home
That describes ambulatory monitoring rather than the home schedule with a validated upper-arm device.

C.io: Compare and contrast precipitating factors, clinical manifestations, diagnosis (including role of B-type natriuretic peptide, BNP), and treatment of acute decompensated heart failure.
C.q: An 80-year-old man in the intensive care unit with acute heart failure has cool extremities and hypotension, and inotropic support is being considered. Which agents are used for this?
opts: Losartan or irbesartan
These are angiotensin receptor blockers for chronic therapy. Inotropic support in intensive care uses dobutamine or milrinone.
Spironolactone or eplerenone
These are mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists for chronic reduced ejection fraction. Inotropic support uses dobutamine or milrinone.
Dobutamine or milrinone
Correct. Inotropic therapy for intensive care use includes the sympathomimetics dobutamine, norepinephrine and epinephrine and the phosphodiesterase inhibitor milrinone.
Diltiazem or verapamil
These are calcium channel blockers, which are avoided in heart failure. Inotropic support uses dobutamine or milrinone.

C.io: Tricuspid stenosis
C.q: Which valve replacement is preferred for severe tricuspid stenosis?
opts: Transcatheter aortic
A transcatheter aortic valve replaces the aortic valve in aortic stenosis. Tricuspid stenosis replacement is preferably bioprosthetic.
Human donor
A donor valve is not the listed option. For severe tricuspid stenosis a bioprosthetic replacement is preferred.
Bioprosthetic

Correct. When severe symptomatic tricuspid stenosis needs replacement, a bioprosthetic valve is preferred. Balloon valvotomy and repair are reserved for hepatic congestion or severe systemic venous congestion.
Mechanical
Mechanical valves need lifelong anticoagulation; for tricuspid stenosis the preferred replacement is bioprosthetic.

C.io: Differentiate each stage of the American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association (ACC/AHA), natural history classification of heart failure, and associated treatment recommendations of each stage.
C.q: For a patient at risk for heart failure who has diabetes, which drug class is recommended first?
opts: Beta blocker as the first agent
A beta blocker is not recommended in stage A. It enters at stage B. The first drug for an at-risk patient with diabetes is a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor.
Loop diuretic such as furosemide
Diuretics treat congestion, which a stage A patient does not have. The recommended drug for an at-risk patient with diabetes is a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor.
Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist
These belong to symptomatic heart failure, strongly for reduced ejection fraction. In stage A with diabetes the drug is a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor.
Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor

Correct. In stage A, at risk for heart failure, the one strongly recommended drug is a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor in patients with diabetes. A beta blocker enters only at stage B, once structural disease exists.

C.io: Identify medical care strategies for hypotension in the lecture topic list for the following populations. a. infant b. child c. adolescent d. adult e. elderly
C.q: An 81-year-old woman has a pressure of 104/64 at a routine visit and feels well. She worries because it is lower than her usual readings. What should she be told about this reading?
opts: It proves autonomic nerve failure
Autonomic failure is shown by a postural fall with a minimal heart rate rise, not by one low resting reading.
Any reading this low needs pressors
Pressors are for the emergency department and intensive care; an asymptomatic outpatient reading does not call for them.
Pressure norms are fixed for all ages
Blood pressure norms are affected by age, which is exactly why a reading needs context rather than a single fixed cutoff.
One reading is a snapshot in time
Correct. Each reading is only a snapshot in time and is judged against age, comorbidities and the possibility of relative hypotension, together with symptoms.

C.io: Tricuspid regurgitation
C.q: A 29-year-old man who injects drugs has fevers for two weeks. There is a holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border near the epigastrium that grows louder with inspiration (Carvallo sign), and his neck veins pulsate. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Tricuspid stenosis
Tricuspid stenosis is at the same location and also increases with inspiration, but it is a mid-diastolic rumble with an opening snap, not a holosystolic murmur.
Pulmonic stenosis
Pulmonic stenosis is a harsh mid-systolic ejection murmur at the left upper sternal border. A holosystolic murmur near the epigastrium is tricuspid regurgitation.
Mitral regurgitation
Mitral regurgitation is holosystolic too, but it is at the apex radiating to the axilla and does not increase with inspiration. The Carvallo sign separates the two.
Tricuspid regurgitation

Correct. A holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border near the epigastrium that increases with inspiration is tricuspid regurgitation; in an injection drug user the primary cause is infective endocarditis.

C.q: A 61-year-old man's blood pressure is 148/88 in the right arm and 132/80 in the left at his first visit. He has no chest pain and his pulses are symmetric and normal. Which arm should be used at follow-up visits?
opts: Image immediately for aortic dissection
Asymmetric pressures raise concern for dissection when they are NEW and accompanied by abrupt severe pain. Neither is present here.
Compare arm and leg pressures to exclude coarctation
Coarctation is suggested by weak or delayed femoral pulses with upper limb hypertension, not by a difference between the two arms.
Use the right arm for all subsequent measurements

Correct. Both arms are measured at the initial visit precisely to find a difference, and the higher consistent arm becomes the one used for follow-up. Averaging the two would systematically understate his pressure.
Average the two readings and record 140/84
The higher consistent arm is used rather than an average, since the lower arm underestimates the central pressure.

C.io: Acute coronary syndrome
C.q: Which antithrombotic class has fallen out of favor in coronary care?
opts: Fibrinolytic agents
Fibrinolytics are still given when the nearest intervention unit is 2 or more hours away, and tenecteplase is the most common today. Glycoprotein 2b/3a inhibitors are the class out of favor.
Cyclooxygenase inhibitors

Aspirin, the cyclooxygenase inhibitor, is still recommended after infarction and forms the other half of dual antiplatelet therapy. Glycoprotein 2b/3a inhibitors are the class that has fallen out of favor.
Glycoprotein 2b/3a inhibitors
Correct. Glycoprotein 2b/3a inhibitors (eptifibatide, abciximab, tirofiban) have fallen out of favor. Aspirin with a P2Y12 receptor antagonist is the antiplatelet pairing in use.
P2Y12 receptor antagonists
P2Y12 receptor antagonists such as clopidogrel remain central: they are half of dual antiplatelet therapy after a stent. The class that has fallen out of favor is the glycoprotein 2b/3a inhibitors.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
C.q: A 72-year-old woman has supine hypertension (high blood pressure while lying flat). Lying down she is 176/96; after 3 minutes standing she is 152/90, and she feels mildly lightheaded. Do these readings meet the orthostatic criterion?
opts: Yes; the fall exceeds 20 mmHg
More than 20 mmHg is the systolic threshold for a normal baseline. Supine hypertension raises the systolic threshold to more than 30 mmHg.
No; readings need 10 minutes
Ten minutes is the window for the heart rate criteria of the tachycardia syndrome; orthostatic pressure criteria use 3 minutes.
Yes; any fall with symptoms counts
The criteria are numeric thresholds within 3 minutes of standing; symptoms alone do not meet them.
No; a fall over 30 mmHg is needed
Correct. With an elevated baseline or supine hypertension the systolic fall must exceed 30 mmHg; hers is 24 and the diastolic fall is only 6.

C.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education, and prognosis
C.q: A 46-year-old woman consistently reads 150/92 in clinic but her seven-day home average is 118/74 with a validated upper-arm device and correct technique. Which pattern does this represent?
opts: Resistant hypertension
Resistance means pressure above goal despite three complementary drugs at maximally tolerated doses, which is not the situation here.
White coat hypertension
Correct: raised office readings with normal out-of-office readings. Recognizing it avoids treating a patient whose true pressure is normal.
Stage 2 hypertension
Her out-of-office readings are normal, so the office values do not establish a stage.
Masked hypertension
Masked hypertension is the reverse pattern, with normal office readings and raised out-of-office readings, and it carries clinically important cardiovascular risk.

C.io: Unstable
C.q: A 60-year-old woman has chest pressure that began at rest. Her electrocardiogram shows T-wave inversion in two consecutive leads. Which result would make this a non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction?
opts: Inverted T waves persisting
Inverted T waves occur in both unstable angina and non-ST-elevation infarction. The electrocardiogram cannot separate them; an elevated troponin I does.
Troponin I above 0.04 ng/mL
Correct. Elevated cardiac markers (troponin or high-sensitivity troponin) are what separate a non-ST-elevation infarction from unstable angina. A standard troponin I above 0.04 ng/mL is abnormal.
Pain that began at rest
Pain at rest defines unstable angina as well as infarction. What makes it a non-ST-elevation infarction is an elevated troponin I.
Relief with nitroglycerin
Nitroglycerin usually, but not always, helps unstable angina and may help an infarction too. Relief does not separate them; an elevated troponin I does.
