C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, prevention, and prognosis for heart failure.
C.q: A 58-year-old man has leg edema and jugular venous distension (distended neck veins) with a raised B-type natriuretic peptide. Right-sided heart failure is suspected. Which test establishes the definitive diagnosis?
opts: Repeat natriuretic peptide
The peptide supports heart failure but cannot say which ventricle has failed. The echocardiogram gives the definitive diagnosis.
Right heart catheterization
Catheterization measures hemodynamic severity once right-sided failure is suspected or confirmed. The definitive diagnosis comes from the echocardiogram.
Twelve-lead electrocardiogram
The electrocardiogram may show right heart strain but does not make the diagnosis. The echocardiogram does.
Echocardiogram
Correct. Clinical heart failure with distended neck veins raises suspicion of right-sided failure, and the echocardiogram gives the definitive diagnosis by ejection fraction.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, prevention, and prognosis for heart failure.
C.q: A 65-year-old man with new heart failure also describes pressure-like chest pain for the past day. His electrocardiogram shows new T-wave inversions. Which additional laboratory test is indicated?
opts: Thyroid hormone level
Thyroid testing looks for a high-output cause. Chest pain with ischemic changes calls for troponin.
Repeat natriuretic peptide
The natriuretic peptide supports heart failure but does not address infarction. Troponin does.
Hepatic function panel
Liver tests do not address ischemia. Chest pain with new inversions calls for troponin.
Cardiac troponin
Correct. Troponin is ordered when there is concern for an acute infarction or for heart failure secondary to ischemic cardiomyopathy, and chest pain with new inversions raises exactly that concern.

C.io: Pulmonic regurgitation
C.q: A 40-year-old woman with no cardiac symptoms is found to have pulmonic regurgitation. Which is the most common way this lesion comes to attention?
opts: Syncope during strenuous exercise
Exertional syncope is a cardinal symptom of aortic stenosis. Pulmonic regurgitation is usually an incidental echo or examination finding.
Chest pain with a new infarction
Chest pain with an infarction is how acute mitral regurgitation from papillary muscle rupture presents. Pulmonic regurgitation is usually found incidentally.
An incidental echo or exam finding
Correct. Pulmonic regurgitation is usually an incidental finding on an echocardiogram or on physical examination; the murmur is soft and hard to hear.
Sudden shock and pulmonary edema
Shock with pulmonary edema is the picture of acute severe aortic regurgitation. Pulmonic regurgitation is usually discovered incidentally.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, prevention, and prognosis for heart failure.
C.q: A 69-year-old woman with reduced ejection fraction (fraction 27%) has blood pressure above goal on her heart failure regimen. Verapamil is proposed. What is the most appropriate response?
opts: Add it once she reaches class IV
Advancing class does not make calcium channel blockers appropriate. They are avoided in heart failure at every class.
Avoid it and use recommended classes
Correct. Verapamil is a calcium channel blocker, and calcium channel blockers are avoided in heart failure. Pressure control comes from optimizing the recommended classes as tolerated.
Use it in place of her beta blocker
Replacing a core beta blocker with a calcium channel blocker is backwards; the calcium channel blocker is avoided in heart failure.
Start it as first-line pressure control
Calcium channel blockers are not first-line in heart failure; they are avoided. The recommended classes are optimized instead.

C.io: ST segment elevation
C.q: A 57-year-old woman has chest pain with ST elevation in leads I, aVL, V5 and V6. Which artery is the most likely culprit?
opts: Right coronary artery
The right coronary artery is the culprit for the inferior leads II, III and aVF. Leads I, aVL, V5 and V6 are lateral, pointing to the circumflex.
Right marginal branch
The right marginal branch arises from the right coronary artery along the right ventricle. Lateral ST elevation in I, aVL, V5 and V6 points to the circumflex.
Posterior interventricular
The posterior interventricular branch supplies the posteromedial papillary muscle and the inferior wall. Lateral leads point to the left circumflex artery.
Left circumflex artery
Correct. Leads I, aVL, V5 and V6 are the lateral leads, and lateral ST elevation points to the left circumflex artery (or a diagonal branch of the left anterior descending artery).

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atherosclerosis and lipid disorders: 1. Hypertriglyceridemia 2. Hypercholesterolemia 3. HDL cholesterol 4. LDL and VLDL cholesterol
C.q: A 45-year-old man has a fasting triglyceride of 780 mg/dL and low-density lipoprotein of 110 mg/dL. Diabetes, kidney disease, alcoholism and hypothyroidism have been excluded. Which management plan is most appropriate?
opts: Very low-fat diet plus a fibrate
Correct. Above 500 mg/dL the plan is a very low-fat diet (under 15% of calories from fat), weight management, physical activity and a fibrate, niacin or both.
Ezetimibe with a high-carbohydrate diet
Ezetimibe lowers triglyceride only 5% to 10%, and excess carbohydrate raises hepatic very-low-density triglyceride secretion.
Bile acid sequestrant with no diet change
Sequestrants lower low-density lipoprotein as adjuncts; they do not address triglyceride above 500.
Observation with a recheck in a year
Triglyceride above 500 carries a risk of acute pancreatitis, so it is treated now rather than watched.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atherosclerosis and lipid disorders: 1. Hypertriglyceridemia 2. Hypercholesterolemia 3. HDL cholesterol 4. LDL and VLDL cholesterol
C.q: A 50-year-old woman has a waist circumference of 38 inches, triglyceride of 190 mg/dL, high-density lipoprotein of 45 mg/dL, blood pressure of 134/88 and fasting glucose of 104 mg/dL. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Metabolic syndrome
Correct. Any three of five criteria establish it; she meets four: waist above 35 inches, triglyceride above 150, high-density lipoprotein below 50 in a woman and blood pressure above 130/85.
Familial dysbetalipoproteinemia
Dysbetalipoproteinemia raises triglyceride and total cholesterol together to 250 to 500 with palmar xanthomas.
Severe hypertriglyceridemia
The severe form requires triglyceride above 500 mg/dL; hers is 190, which is only borderline high.
Mixed dyslipidemia
Mixed dyslipidemia needs low-density lipoprotein above 130 or non-high-density above 160 with triglyceride above 150; her findings are the metabolic cluster.

C.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education, and prognosis
C.q: A 49-year-old man who drinks heavily is admitted for an unrelated procedure. On the second day his blood pressure rises sharply. What explains this?
opts: Alcohol withdrawal can produce acute severe hypertension
Correct, and the relationship runs both ways: excess alcohol raises blood pressure chronically, and withdrawal from it can raise it acutely.
Only chronic excess raises pressure; withdrawal has no effect
Withdrawal is specifically capable of producing acute severe hypertension, which is what is happening here.
Alcohol lowers pressure, so stopping returns him to baseline
Excess alcohol raises rather than lowers blood pressure, so this reverses the relationship.
Moderate alcohol should be resumed for cardiovascular benefit
Starting or resuming alcohol for cardiovascular benefit is specifically not recommended; intake is limited to low-risk thresholds.

C.io: Angina pectoris
C.q: A 52-year-old woman has recurrent anginal chest pain during periods of work stress and anxiety. Her electrocardiogram shows ST changes during symptoms, and coronary angiography shows normal coronary arteries. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Vasospastic angina

Vasospastic angina strikes at rest between midnight and early morning, mostly in smokers under 50, with transient ST elevation. Her stress-related angina in a woman with normal arteries fits microvascular angina.
Microvascular angina

Correct. Microvascular angina (formerly cardiac syndrome X) is angina with ST changes, possibly with elevated biomarkers, but normal coronary arteries on the angiogram; it is more frequent in women and often associated with stress or anxiety.
Unstable angina
Unstable angina is a change in stable angina from atherosclerotic plaque and is an acute coronary syndrome. Normal coronary arteries in a stressed woman point to microvascular angina.
Stable angina
Stable angina comes from atherosclerotic narrowing that coronary angiography, the gold standard for coronary artery disease, would show. Her coronary arteries are normal.

C.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis
C.q: What is the normal relationship between leg and arm systolic pressure?
opts: Arm systolic is normally higher than leg
The normal relationship runs the other way, which is what makes a reversal meaningful in suspected coarctation.
Leg systolic is normally higher than arm
Correct, so a leg pressure that is not higher is the abnormal finding. Leg pressures are measured when the pulse examination suggests coarctation.
The relationship varies unpredictably and cannot be used
The relationship is consistent enough to be diagnostically useful when coarctation is suspected.
They are normally identical
Leg systolic normally exceeds arm systolic rather than matching it, which is what makes a leg pressure equal to or below the arm a meaningful finding.

C.io: Develop a differential diagnosis for a patient presenting with hypotension based on history, physical examination, and diagnostic findings.
C.q: A 73-year-old man has a faint while urinating at night, with nausea and sweating beforehand and quick recovery. Which test is used to exclude a cardiac dysrhythmia?
opts: A tilt-table test
Tilt-table testing is for postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome and does not show the cardiac rhythm.
A blood glucose level
A blood glucose excludes hypoglycemia, a non-hypotensive cause, rather than a dysrhythmia.
Orthostatic vital signs
Orthostatic readings look for a postural pressure fall; the rhythm is assessed with an electrocardiogram.
An electrocardiogram
Correct. A normal electrocardiogram lowers suspicion of a dysrhythmia, just as a normal glucose excludes hypoglycemia and blood tests address infection.

C.io: Define the following diagnostic and therapeutic groups of HF patients, and the treatment implications/recommendations for each group: a. HF with reduced EF (HFrEF) b. HF with mildly reduced EF (HFmrEF) c. HF with preserved EF (HFpEF)
C.q: Which ejection fraction defines heart failure with preserved ejection fraction?
opts: 65% or more
That sets the bar too high. Preserved ejection fraction is 50% or more, matching the normal range.
41% or more
Values of 41 to 49% are mildly reduced ejection fraction, a separate group. Preserved ejection fraction starts at 50%.
35% or more
Values from 35 to 40% are reduced ejection fraction. Preserved ejection fraction starts at 50%.
50% or more
Correct. Preserved ejection fraction is 50% or more, the same line as a normal ejection fraction. Below that come mildly reduced at 41 to 49% and reduced at 40% or less.

C.q: Which drug combinations are preferred as initial therapy?
opts: An angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor with an angiotensin receptor blocker
This combination is specifically prohibited: dual renin-angiotensin blockade raises hyperkalemia and kidney injury risk without additional benefit.
A beta blocker with a non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker
This pairing risks severe bradycardia and heart block because both slow nodal conduction.
Two thiazide-type diuretics together
Combining agents of the same class adds adverse effects without the complementary mechanism that the preferred pairings provide.
A renin-angiotensin blocker with a calcium blocker or diuretic

Correct, because the classes act by complementary mechanisms. A single-pill combination is preferred where two agents are started, since it improves adherence. That means an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker paired with a dihydropyridine or a thiazide-type diuretic.

C.q: In a patient aged 0 to 19 years, what does a diagnosis of familial hypercholesterolemia call for?
opts: A statin
Correct. In the 0-to-19 age group, lifestyle prevents or reduces risk, and a diagnosis of familial hypercholesterolemia leads to a statin.
Apheresis in every case
Apheresis is the treatment of choice for the homozygous form specifically, not for every young patient with the diagnosis.
A fibrate
Triglyceride is normal in familial hypercholesterolemia; in the 0-to-19 group the diagnosis leads to a statin.
Lifestyle alone until age 40
Waiting until 40 ignores an inherited receptor defect; a familial hypercholesterolemia diagnosis in youth leads to a statin.

C.q: An 8-year-old boy has firm yellow nodules over the backs of his hands, elbows and heels. His total cholesterol is 780 mg/dL with a normal triglyceride, and both parents have markedly elevated cholesterol. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia
The heterozygous form runs low-density lipoprotein of 200 to 400 mg/dL and is usually found incidentally on screening, not with childhood xanthomas and cholesterol near 800.
Familial chylomicronemia syndrome
Chylomicronemia raises triglyceride above 1000 mg/dL and causes eruptive papules and pancreatitis; this child has a normal triglyceride.
Homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia

Correct. Presentation in childhood with cutaneous xanthomas on the hands, elbows and heels, total cholesterol of about 400 to above 1000 mg/dL, normal triglyceride and two affected parents fits two mutant alleles.
Familial dysbetalipoproteinemia
Dysbetalipoproteinemia raises triglyceride and total cholesterol together to 250 to 500 mg/dL with palmar xanthomas, not isolated cholesterol near 800.

C.q: Which pattern defines dyslipidemia?
opts: High cholesterol or triglyceride, or low high-density lipoprotein
Correct. Dyslipidemia is a disorder of lipoprotein metabolism with elevated total, low-density or non-high-density cholesterol or triglyceride, and/or decreased high-density lipoprotein.
Triglyceride elevation only after a fatty meal
A post-meal rise reflects normal chylomicron transport; dyslipidemia is a disorder of lipoprotein metabolism, not a meal effect.
Low low-density lipoprotein with high high-density lipoprotein
That is the favorable pattern; high-density lipoprotein of 60 mg/dL or more even counts as a negative risk factor.
Any cholesterol value outside a fixed normal range
There are no 'normal' levels for cholesterol, and mean values vary across the globe, so dyslipidemia is not defined by a normal range.

Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
C.q: A 75-year-old man with neurogenic orthostatic hypotension from multiple system atrophy has supine hypertension (high blood pressure while lying flat). He remains symptomatic on standing despite slow position changes. Which treatment should be avoided?
opts: Slow position changes
Slow positional changes are first-line for every orthostatic patient and are continued whatever medication is chosen.
Midodrine
Correct. Midodrine is best with neurogenic syncope but is avoided with supine hypertension, severe heart disease and chronic kidney disease.
Fludrocortisone
Fludrocortisone is avoided in heart failure because it retains salt and water; supine hypertension is not its listed contraindication.
Droxidopa
Droxidopa is the better choice with supine hypertension, which makes it the drug to consider here rather than the one to avoid.

C.q: A 38-year-old woman who smokes a pack of cigarettes a day asks whether smoking really matters for her heart at her age. Which counseling point is accurate?
opts: It matters only with diabetes
Smoking is an independent modifiable risk factor; it does not need diabetes to count. It is a strong predictor especially in women younger than 45.
It matters only after menopause
Smoking is not a postmenopausal risk only. It is a strong predictor of coronary disease especially in women younger than 45, which is exactly her group.
It is a strong predictor at her age
Correct. Smoking is a modifiable coronary risk factor and a strong predictor, especially in women younger than 45. Her age makes the counseling more urgent, not less.
It raises risk only in men
Smoking raises risk in both sexes and is a strong predictor especially in women younger than 45, so it matters for her now.

C.q: A 63-year-old man on lisinopril remains above goal. A colleague suggests adding losartan. What is the problem?
opts: Dual blockade raises hyperkalemia and kidney injury risk

Correct, and the instruction is absolute rather than cautionary: one is used INSTEAD of the other. The two look complementary if the mechanism is read loosely, which is why the rule is stated so plainly. It adds no benefit in exchange.
The combination is acceptable if potassium is monitored
The instruction is never to combine them rather than to combine them with monitoring.
The two cancel each other out pharmacologically
They act at different points on the same pathway rather than canceling; the problem is additive harm.
Angioedema occurs in most patients on the combination
Angioedema is a recognized risk of angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibition specifically; the reason to avoid the combination is renal and potassium harm.

C.q: A 52-year-old man reads 124/78 in clinic, but his home average over seven days is 142/90. Why does this matter?
opts: It indicates his home device is miscalibrated
A validated upper-arm device used to the standard schedule is the reference, not the office reading.
It means he has white coat hypertension
White coat hypertension is the opposite pattern, with high office and normal home readings.
It carries real risk despite normal office readings
Correct. This is masked hypertension, and it is the reason out-of-office measurement is not merely a way of avoiding overtreatment: it also finds the patients whose risk the clinic reading conceals.
It is a benign pattern requiring no follow-up
It carries clinically important cardiovascular risk, which is precisely why identifying it matters.

C.q: A 16-year-old girl has palpitations and dizziness on standing. Within 10 minutes of standing her heart rate rises from 70 to 114, and her pressure does not fall. Does this meet the heart rate criterion for her age?
opts: Yes; the rise exceeds 40 per minute
Correct. In adolescents the threshold is an increase of 40 beats per minute; her rise of 44 within 10 minutes meets it.
Yes; any rise over 20 per minute
A rise of 20 is too low for any age group; the adult threshold is more than 30 and the adolescent threshold 40.
No; adolescents need a rise of 50
The adolescent threshold is 40 beats per minute, and her rise of 44 clearly exceeds it.
No; the rise must occur in 3 minutes
The window for this syndrome is 10 minutes; 3 minutes is the window for orthostatic pressure criteria.

C.io: Aortic regurgitation
C.q: A 63-year-old woman with acute severe aortic regurgitation from endocarditis is waiting for valve surgery that is delayed by several hours. Which is the most appropriate temporary stabilization in the intensive care unit?
opts: Intravenous diuretics and nitroprusside

Correct. If surgery for acute severe aortic regurgitation is delayed, temporary stabilization may be attempted in the intensive care unit with intravenous diuretics and a vasodilator such as nitroprusside.
Oral hydralazine and discharge home
Oral afterload reduction is chronic outpatient therapy. Acute severe regurgitation awaiting surgery is stabilized in intensive care with intravenous diuretics and nitroprusside.
A fluid bolus to raise her preload
Adding volume worsens the pulmonary edema of acute regurgitation. Temporary stabilization uses intravenous diuretics and a vasodilator such as nitroprusside.
Percutaneous balloon valvuloplasty
Balloon valvuloplasty relieves stenosis in children and young adults; it does not stabilize a leaking valve. The bridge to surgery is intravenous diuretics and nitroprusside.

C.q: A 74-year-old woman presents with acute right hemiparesis and aphasia of two hours' duration. Her blood pressure is 196/104. How should her blood pressure be managed?
opts: Reduce the pressure to below 130/80 immediately
Applying a chronic prevention target acutely is exactly what the caution warns against.
Follow the acute stroke protocol, not chronic targets
Correct. Acute stroke is specifically excepted from the general emergency reduction approach, because driving the pressure to a chronic target can extend the ischemic injury.
Reduce the mean arterial pressure by a quarter in an hour
That is the general hypertensive emergency approach, and acute stroke follows a distinct protocol instead.
Leave the blood pressure entirely untreated
A distinct protocol applies rather than no management at all, so the pressure is managed by different rules.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
C.q: What triggers situational reflex syncope?
opts: Standing after autonomic nerve damage
A postural drop from autonomic damage is neurogenic orthostatic syncope, a sustained drop rather than a triggered reflex.
Certain bodily functions or actions
Correct. Situational syncope is triggered by certain bodily functions or physical actions, such as urination at night, coughing or sneezing.
A rapid ventricular rhythm
A rapid ventricular rhythm causes arrhythmic cardiogenic syncope, often abrupt and with palpitations, rather than reflex syncope.
Emotional stress, fear or pain
Emotional stress, fear, pain, heat exposure and prolonged standing are the triggers of vasovagal syncope, the other reflex type.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
C.q: How does the heart rate behave in neurogenic orthostatic hypotension?
opts: It rises only minimally
Correct. Failed autonomic signaling means the heart rate rises less than expected even as pressure falls, which is the tell that separates it from volume loss.
It rises significantly
A significant rise shows an intact baroreceptor-mediated sympathetic response, which favors the non-neurogenic form instead.
It falls sharply first
A sudden slowing belongs to the vasovagal reflex, where vagal outflow surges, rather than to autonomic failure on standing.
It exceeds 120 per minute
A rate above 120 per minute within 10 minutes of standing is a criterion for postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome.

C.q: A 50-year-old woman on a statin has reached her low-density lipoprotein goal, but her triglyceride remains 260 mg/dL after lifestyle changes. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Stop the statin and watch
The statin achieved the primary target and stays; the residual triglyceride is treated in addition.
Begin apheresis sessions
Apheresis is the treatment of choice for homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia, not for residual triglyceride.
Add a fibrate or niacin
Correct. The primary aim is the low-density goal, and if triglyceride stays above 200 mg/dL once it is reached, additional triglyceride-lowering therapy (a fibrate or niacin) is indicated.
Continue with no change
Triglyceride above 200 after the low-density goal is reached is the trigger for more treatment.

C.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, prevention, and prognosis for heart failure.
C.q: A 44-year-old woman has weight loss, tremor, heat intolerance and palpitations for two months, and now ankle edema and breathlessness. Heart rate is 124 and B-type natriuretic peptide is elevated. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Systolic failure from ischemic disease
Nothing suggests infarction or ischemia, and the thyroid picture explains increased demand. This is high-output failure from hyperthyroidism.
High-output failure from hyperthyroidism

Correct. Hyperthyroidism raises peripheral demand, and the heart answers with a faster rate and stronger contraction until the heart failure syndrome appears: fatigue, dyspnea, edema and palpitations.
Right-sided failure from mitral stenosis
Mitral stenosis gives a diastolic rumble with an opening snap, not a hyperthyroid picture. This is high-output failure from hyperthyroidism.
Diastolic failure from hypertension
She has no long hypertension or fourth sound. The weight loss, tremor and heat intolerance point to high-output failure from hyperthyroidism.

C.q: A 70-year-old man with heart failure and congestion is started on furosemide. Which counseling point is most appropriate?
opts: It will raise his potassium to high levels
Loop diuretics waste potassium rather than raising it; it is the mineralocorticoid antagonists that spare it. Potassium and renal function will be checked.
No blood tests are needed on this drug
Monitoring is needed. Furosemide wastes potassium, so potassium and renal function are followed on the metabolic panel.
Potassium and kidney labs will be checked
Correct. Furosemide is a potassium-wasting loop diuretic, so potassium and renal function are followed on the complete metabolic panel.
His liver enzymes will be checked weekly
Liver tests are not the monitoring a loop diuretic needs. Potassium and renal function are followed on the metabolic panel.

C.q: A 61-year-old woman has confirmed resistant hypertension: adherent, correctly measured, above goal on three complementary agents. What is the first step in management?
opts: Refer to a hypertension specialist
Referral is for truly difficult cases after the described sequence rather than as the first step.
Stop all agents and restart from the beginning
The approach is to optimize and titrate what is in place rather than to begin again.
Add spironolactone immediately
Spironolactone is the fourth agent, added after the diuretic is optimized and the foundational three are titrated.
Optimize the diuretic, with chlorthalidone preferred
Correct, and it comes before adding anything. An inadequate or inappropriate diuretic is a common reason the other two agents appear to be failing. The diuretic class is matched to renal function.

C.topic: ST-elevation infarction and right ventricular infarct
C.io: ST segment elevation
C.q: A 63-year-old man has ST elevation in leads II, III and aVF and in the right-sided lead V4R, consistent with right ventricular infarction. His blood pressure is 104/66 mmHg. Which medication should be avoided?
opts: A heparin drip
A heparin drip is started once catheterization is confirmed in an ST-elevation infarction. In right ventricular infarction the drug to avoid is nitroglycerin.
Nitroglycerin

Correct. In a right ventricular infarct, do not give nitroglycerin: it lowers preload, the failing right ventricle loses its Frank-Starling support, output falls further and the patient can go into shock.
Chewable aspirin
Chewable aspirin is given in every ST-elevation infarction, including one involving the right ventricle. The drug to avoid here is nitroglycerin, which drops preload.
Clopidogrel
Clopidogrel, a P2Y12 receptor antagonist, is given once catheterization is confirmed. Right ventricular involvement rules out nitroglycerin, not antiplatelet therapy.

C.io: Compare and contrast precipitating factors, clinical manifestations, diagnosis (including role of B-type natriuretic peptide, BNP), and treatment of acute decompensated heart failure.
C.q: A 67-year-old woman with heart failure has cool, clammy extremities, a narrow pulse pressure and sleepiness, along with orthopnea (breathlessness lying flat) and leg edema. Which bedside hemodynamic profile fits?
opts: Cold and wet
Correct. Low-perfusion signs (cool extremities, narrow pulse pressure, obtundation) plus congestion signs (orthopnea, edema) place her in the cold and wet profile, hypoperfusion with congestion.
Warm and wet
Warm and wet is congestion with adequate perfusion. Her cool extremities, narrow pulse pressure and sleepiness mean perfusion is low, so she is cold and wet.
Cold and dry
Cold and dry is low perfusion without congestion. Her orthopnea and edema mean she is congested, so she is cold and wet.
Warm and dry
Warm and dry is the normal profile. She has both low perfusion and congestion, so she is cold and wet.

Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
D.q: A 74-year-old man reports fainting twice after standing. Before any test is ordered, which part of his evaluation is most important for identifying the source?
opts: A chest radiograph
A chest radiograph is not part of the orthostatic evaluation; the history is what identifies the likely source.
A tilt-table test
Tilt-table testing is for postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome and cannot replace the history in orthostatic syncope.
An echocardiogram
Echocardiography evaluates structural cardiogenic syncope; the history comes first and decides whether it is needed.
A detailed history
Correct. History is the most important portion of accurately diagnosing the source of orthostatic syncope, or of referring to the right specialty for confirmation.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, prevention, and prognosis for heart failure.
D.q: A 72-year-old woman with heart failure asks why she must take several medicines when she already feels better. Which explanation matches the goals of treatment?
opts: They are only needed while she has symptoms
Symptom relief is one goal among three. Increasing survival and limiting progression continue after she feels better.
They are meant to cure her cardiomyopathy
Cure is not among the treatment goals. The goals are fewer symptoms, longer survival and slower progression.
They are meant to make her ejection fraction normal
A normal ejection fraction is not a goal of treatment. The goals are fewer symptoms, longer survival and slower progression.
They also extend life and slow progression
Correct. The goals are to decrease symptoms, increase survival and limit disease progression. Feeling better meets only the first of the three, so the regimen continues.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, prevention, and prognosis for heart failure.
D.q: A 46-year-old woman with high-output heart failure from untreated hyperthyroidism has leg edema and breathlessness. Which treatment approach is most appropriate?
opts: Treat the thyroid disease and add a diuretic
Correct. High-output failure is treated by correcting the underlying cause of increased demand, here hyperthyroidism, with a diuretic for congestion.
Start dobutamine to support contractility
Dobutamine raises output further and is an inotrope for intensive care use only. The approach is to treat the cause and add a diuretic.
Refer for heart transplant evaluation
Transplant does not address a problem of excess demand. The approach is to treat the thyroid disease and add a diuretic.
Start verapamil to slow the heart rate
Verapamil is a calcium channel blocker, avoided in heart failure. The approach is to treat the cause and add a diuretic.

D.io: Mitral valve prolapse
D.q: A 31-year-old woman with known mitral valve prolapse is followed over several years. Which complication can the prolapse progress to?
opts: Mitral regurgitation
Correct. Mitral valve prolapse may develop the signs and symptoms of mitral regurgitation; prolapse is also listed among the chronic causes of mitral regurgitation.
Tricuspid stenosis
Tricuspid stenosis is mainly rheumatic worldwide and congenital in the United States. Mitral valve prolapse may progress to mitral regurgitation.
Aortic stenosis
Aortic stenosis is degenerative in older adults or from a bicuspid valve. Mitral valve prolapse progresses to mitral regurgitation.
Mitral stenosis
Mitral stenosis is a narrowing that comes mostly from rheumatic heart disease. Prolapse lets the leaflets flare backward, so it progresses to regurgitation.

D.io: Compare and contrast anticoagulation therapy for prosthetic heart valves.
D.q: A 49-year-old man is discharged after receiving a mechanical aortic valve. Which medication must he be told he will take for life?
opts: Heparin
Heparin is only a bridge when warfarin has to stop for surgery. The medication for life after a mechanical valve is warfarin.
Warfarin
Correct. A mechanical valve of titanium and carbon needs lifelong anticoagulation, and warfarin, the most commonly used vitamin K antagonist, is recommended for long-term management.
Nitroprusside
Nitroprusside is an intravenous vasodilator used briefly in intensive care for acute aortic regurgitation. A mechanical valve needs lifelong warfarin.
Aspirin
Aspirin is an antiplatelet agent, and vitamin K antagonist therapy is recommended over antiplatelet agents for a mechanical valve. Warfarin is the lifelong drug.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
D.q: A 22-year-old woman faints while having blood drawn. Just before, she felt warm, nauseated and sweaty, and she recovered fully within a minute of lying down. Her examination and standing readings afterward are normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Cardiogenic arrhythmic syncope
Arrhythmic syncope tends to strike abruptly without a warm, nauseated prodrome, often after palpitations.
Neurogenic orthostatic hypotension
Neurogenic orthostatic hypotension produces a reproducible fall on standing with a minimal heart rate rise; her standing readings are normal.
Vasovagal reflex syncope
Correct. Fear and pain are vasovagal triggers, a prodrome of warmth, nausea and sweating precedes it, and it is most common in young women; recovery is rapid and complete.
Situational reflex syncope
Situational syncope is triggered by a bodily function or physical action such as urination, not by fear or pain.

D.q: A 47-year-old man has blood pressure of 162/98 on three agents. His potassium is 3.1 mmol/L without diuretic use. Which screening test is appropriate?
opts: Plasma free metanephrines
Metanephrines screen for pheochromocytoma, suggested by episodic headache, sweating and palpitations rather than by hypokalemia.
A morning aldosterone to renin ratio
Correct. Resistant hypertension with unexplained hypokalemia is a classic trigger to screen, and the ratio is positive above roughly 20:1 provided the aldosterone concentration itself is adequate.
Renal duplex ultrasound
Renal duplex investigates renovascular disease, suggested by an abdominal bruit and asymmetric kidneys.
A low-dose dexamethasone suppression test
That screens for Cushing syndrome, suggested by proximal muscle weakness, easy bruising, thin skin and broad purple striae.

D.io: Acute myocardial infraction
D.q: A 72-year-old woman with no current symptoms has a routine electrocardiogram showing pathologic Q waves in leads II, III and aVF. What do these Q waves indicate?
opts: A completed prior infarct
Correct. Pathologic Q waves appear hours to a day after an infarction and persist for months: they mean the infarct has already happened. They mark completed damage rather than ischemia in progress.
Coronary vasospasm
Vasospasm causes transient ST changes during an episode of rest pain that resolve. Pathologic Q waves are a lasting mark of a completed infarct.
Subendocardial ischemia
Subendocardial ischemia shows ST depression over the ischemic region. Pathologic Q waves are the persistent sign of an infarct that has already occurred.
Hyperacute ischemia now
Hyperacute T waves with ST elevation appear in the first minutes to hours of an ST-elevation infarction. Persistent Q waves without symptoms mark an old, completed infarct.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
D.q: Which drug is best suited to postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome?
opts: Midodrine
Midodrine is best with neurogenic syncope and is avoided with supine hypertension, severe heart disease and chronic kidney disease.
Fludrocortisone
Correct. Fludrocortisone is best with the tachycardia syndrome; because it causes salt and water retention it is avoided in heart failure.
Phenylephrine
Phenylephrine is among the pressors used only in the emergency department and intensive care, not for an outpatient syndrome.
Droxidopa
Droxidopa has mild efficacy, is better with supine hypertension, and is usually an adjunct to midodrine or fludrocortisone.

D.io: Aortic stenosis
D.q: A 78-year-old man has chest pressure and lightheadedness when climbing stairs. He has a harsh systolic crescendo-decrescendo murmur at the second right intercostal space at the sternal border that radiates to both carotids. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Pulmonic stenosis
Pulmonic stenosis is also harsh and systolic, but it sits at the left second to fourth intercostal space and grows louder with inspiration. It does not radiate to the carotids.
Aortic stenosis

Correct. Harsh means stenosis and systolic narrows it to the aortic or pulmonic valve; the second right intercostal space with radiation to the carotids places it at the aortic valve. Exertional angina and near-syncope are cardinal symptoms.
Aortic regurgitation
Aortic regurgitation is a high-pitched blowing diastolic murmur at the third intercostal space on the left, radiating to the apex. This murmur is harsh and systolic, which is stenosis.
Mitral regurgitation
Mitral regurgitation is a holosystolic blowing murmur at the apex that radiates to the axilla. Blowing means regurgitation, and this murmur is harsh and at the right upper sternal border.

D.io: Tricuspid regurgitation
D.q: A 71-year-old woman with long-standing pulmonary hypertension and a dilated right ventricle develops a holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border that increases with inspiration. Which process most likely produced her valve leak?
opts: Rheumatic leaflet narrowing
Rheumatic disease narrows valves, most commonly the mitral, causing stenosis. Her leak is from annular dilation due to right ventricular dilation.
Dilation of the tricuspid annulus
Correct. The most common cause of tricuspid regurgitation is dilation of the tricuspid annulus from right ventricular dilation in the setting of pulmonary hypertension.
A prior valvuloplasty
A prior valvuloplasty for outflow obstruction is the most common cause of pulmonic regurgitation. Her tricuspid leak comes from annular dilation.
Endocarditis of the leaflets
Infective endocarditis is the primary cause of tricuspid regurgitation in injection drug users. With pulmonary hypertension and a dilated ventricle, annular dilation is the cause.

D.io: Differentiate between systolic dysfunction and diastolic dysfunction..
D.q: Most systolic heart failure traces back to which causes?
opts: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy from hypertension
Hypertension and hypertrophy lead the diastolic chain. Systolic failure traces to ischemic or dilated cardiomyopathy.
High-output states such as anemia
Anemia causes high-output failure, a separate type. Systolic failure traces to ischemic or dilated cardiomyopathy.
Ischemic or dilated cardiomyopathy

Correct. Systolic failure runs to ischemic or dilated cardiomyopathy in the great majority of patients, then a reduced ejection fraction, normal or low blood pressure, a third heart sound and pulmonary edema.
Mitral stenosis with pulmonary hypertension
Those are causes of right-sided failure. Systolic left-sided failure traces to ischemic or dilated cardiomyopathy.

D.io: Identify medical care strategies for heart failure in the lecture topic list for the following populations. 1. infant 2. child 3. adolescent 4. adult 5. elderly
D.q: An 81-year-old woman has progressive breathlessness and ankle edema over three months. Her N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide is 720. What does this level suggest for her age?
opts: The level is normal for her age
The age-adjusted threshold over 75 is 450, and 720 exceeds it. Heart failure is likely.
Heart failure is ruled out
No rule-out applies at 720. Older than 75, a level above 450 makes heart failure likely.
Heart failure is likely
Correct. Older than 75, an N-terminal fragment above 450 makes heart failure likely. In a younger patient the threshold would be 125.
Only a younger cut-off applies
The age-specific threshold exists precisely for patients older than 75: above 450 heart failure is likely.

D.io: Aortic regurgitation
D.q: A 60-year-old man with aortic insufficiency has an echocardiogram showing a regurgitant fraction of 62%. Which severity does this indicate?
opts: Ungradeable by echocardiogram
Regurgitant fraction is exactly how echocardiography grades aortic regurgitation; catheterization is definitive but not necessary. A fraction of 62% is severe.
Moderate regurgitation
Moderate aortic regurgitation is a regurgitant fraction of 30 to 49%. At 62%, more than half the output is returning, which is severe.
Mild regurgitation
Mild aortic regurgitation is a regurgitant fraction below 30%. A fraction of 62% is well into the severe range of 50% or more.
Severe regurgitation
Correct. Aortic regurgitation is severe when 50% or more of the blood that passed the valve comes back. A fraction of 30 to 49% is moderate and below 30% is mild.

D.io: Pulmonic regurgitation
D.q: When should pulmonic regurgitation be referred?
opts: Never, since it is always benign
Significant pulmonic regurgitation overloads the right ventricle and causes right heart failure. It is referred when seen on echo or with those signs.
Only when the cause is iatrogenic
The cause does not decide referral. Pulmonic regurgitation is referred when seen on an echocardiogram or with right heart failure.
On echo or with right heart failure
Correct. Pulmonic regurgitation is referred when it is seen on an echocardiogram or when there are symptoms and signs of right heart failure.
Only after a first episode of syncope
Syncope is not the trigger. Pulmonic regurgitation is referred when seen on an echocardiogram or with right heart failure symptoms or signs.

D.io: Acute coronary syndrome
D.q: A 59-year-old man had 30 minutes of chest pressure at rest. His electrocardiogram shows nonspecific T-wave changes, and his first troponin I is not abnormal. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Discharge him home now
A single troponin I that is not abnormal does not end the workup after rest pain. Troponin is used to rule an infarction out, and that takes a repeat level.
Repeat the troponin I
Correct. Troponin is drawn serially: when one is drawn, a second follows, because the change over time is what matters. A rising troponin I would turn this presentation into an infarction.
Give a thrombolytic agent
Thrombolytics are for an ST-elevation infarction when percutaneous intervention is two or more hours away. Nonspecific T-wave changes do not qualify; repeat the troponin I.
Order a calcium score
A coronary calcium score stratifies future risk and is not used to diagnose an acute coronary syndrome. The next step after rest pain is a repeat troponin I.

D.q: A 54-year-old arrives late for a routine visit, is taken straight to the room and has her blood pressure measured immediately while she describes her morning. The cuff is placed over her sleeve and her legs are crossed. The reading is 152/94. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Repeat it after five minutes of quiet rest

Correct. Every departure here inflates the reading: no rest period, talking during the measurement, a sleeved arm and crossed legs. A diagnosis rests on readings taken to standard, and acting on this one would start treatment on an artifact. Correct technique matters as much as the rest period.
Order plasma metanephrines to exclude pheochromocytoma
Metanephrines are ordered when the history suggests episodic headache, sweating and palpitations, not because one office reading was high.
Diagnose stage 2 hypertension and start two agents
Two complementary agents are reasonable when pressure is substantially above goal, but not on a single reading taken outside standard conditions.
Reassure her that a single elevated reading is meaningless
It is not meaningless; it needs repeating under proper conditions. At least two readings are obtained, with any deviation from standard technique documented.

D.q: A patient's creatinine rises markedly after an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor is started. What does that suggest?
opts: Bilateral renal artery stenosis

Correct. Blocking the renin-angiotensin system removes the efferent arteriolar constriction that was maintaining filtration across a stenosis, so the finding points at the anatomy rather than at drug toxicity. A hemodynamically significant unilateral stenosis can do the same.
Obstructive sleep apnea
Sleep apnea is suggested by snoring, witnessed apneas and nocturnal or resistant hypertension rather than by this laboratory change.
Primary aldosteronism
Aldosteronism is suggested by resistant blood pressure with unexplained hypokalemia rather than by a creatinine rise after starting a renin-angiotensin blocker.
An expected effect requiring no further thought
A marked acute rise is specifically flagged as raising concern rather than being dismissed as an anticipated change.

D.q: A 64-year-old man has had both a heart attack and an ischemic stroke. On a maximal statin plus ezetimibe his low-density lipoprotein is 88 mg/dL. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Add a bile acid sequestrant only
Sequestrants are adjuncts, but the next step after statin plus ezetimibe in very high-risk disease is the injectable class.
No change, as he is below 100
Below 100 is not the target in very high-risk disease; the threshold for adding nonstatin therapy is 70.
Add evolocumab or alirocumab

Correct. In very high-risk disease, if low-density lipoprotein stays 70 or more on a maximally tolerated statin and ezetimibe, adding a proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 inhibitor is reasonable.
Replace the statin with a fibrate
Fibrates lower triglyceride; replacing the statin would remove his most effective low-density therapy.

D.io: Define each class of the New York Heart Association (NYHA) symptomatic and functional classification of heart failure.
D.q: A 71-year-old man with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction is comfortable at rest but becomes breathless after only a few steps across a room. Which New York Heart Association class describes him?
opts: Class I
Class I is the absence of any heart failure symptoms. Breathlessness with only slight exertion is class III.
Class II
Class II is symptoms with ordinary exertion. Breathlessness after only slight effort, like a few steps across a room, is class III.
Class IV
Class IV is symptoms at rest, and he is comfortable at rest. Slight exertion provoking symptoms is class III.
Class III
Correct. Symptoms with only slight exertion, such as a few steps across a room, and none at rest are class III. Class II is symptoms with ordinary exertion and class IV is symptoms at rest.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, prevention, and prognosis for heart failure.
D.q: A 64-year-old woman with non-ischemic dilated cardiomyopathy has an ejection fraction of 30% after six months of optimized guideline-directed therapy. She is breathless with exertion but not at rest and is otherwise healthy. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Inotropes in the intensive care unit
She is stable and class II; inotropes are for critical illness. She meets the criteria for an implantable defibrillator.
A calcium channel blocker for rate
Calcium channel blockers are avoided in heart failure. She meets the criteria for an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator.
Implantable cardioverter-defibrillator
Correct. She meets every criterion: non-ischemic cardiomyopathy with ejection fraction 35% or less, class II, optimal guideline-directed therapy and life expectancy of at least one year.
Heart transplant listing right away
Transplant is for failure beyond control; she is class II. She meets the criteria for an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator.

D.topic: Post-infarction care and sudden cardiac death
D.io: Acute myocardial infraction
D.q: A 63-year-old woman recovering from a myocardial infarction cannot take a beta blocker. Her echocardiogram shows preserved left ventricular function. Which agent can reduce her mortality?
opts: Nitroglycerin
Nitroglycerin is the cornerstone of angina relief but carries no survival benefit claim. With preserved left ventricular function, diltiazem or verapamil reduces mortality after infarction.
Diltiazem
Correct. Calcium channel blockers do not improve prognosis overall after infarction, but diltiazem and verapamil reduce mortality in patients with preserved left ventricular function, which she has.
Warfarin
Warfarin is recommended after a large anterior wall infarction to prevent clot. With preserved function and an intolerance to beta blockers, diltiazem is the agent that lowers mortality.
Amlodipine

Amlodipine is a first-line calcium channel blocker for vasospastic angina. After infarction, only diltiazem and verapamil are credited with lowering mortality, and only with preserved left ventricular function.

D.q: A 57-year-old woman presents with an average blood pressure of 168/104 and no comorbidities. How should treatment begin?
opts: Lifestyle measures alone for six months
Lifestyle applies to every category, but it does not replace medication at this level.
One first-line agent, titrated upward as needed
A single agent is reasonable in stage 1; at this level two complementary agents are considered.
Two complementary first-line agents

Correct. Pressure substantially above goal is the reason to start with two rather than one, and a single pill is preferred because adherence is itself a major determinant of control. A single-pill combination is preferred.
Four agents from the outset
Two complementary first-line agents are considered when pressure is substantially above goal, not four.

D.io: Mitral stenosis
D.q: Left atrial enlargement in mitral stenosis predisposes to which rhythm?
opts: Complete heart block
Heart block is not the rhythm the stretched left atrium produces. Mitral stenosis predisposes to atrial fibrillation and thromboembolism.
Sinus bradycardia
A slow sinus rhythm is not the danger here. The enlarged left atrium of mitral stenosis predisposes to atrial fibrillation.
Ventricular tachycardia
Ventricular tachycardia arises from the ventricles. The dilated left atrium of mitral stenosis predisposes to atrial fibrillation.
Atrial fibrillation
Correct. Rising left atrial size and pressure predispose to atrial fibrillation, which is a risk factor for thromboembolism and is common in severe mitral stenosis.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
D.q: A 24-year-old woman with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome has palpitations and lightheadedness on standing that ease when she lies down. Within 8 minutes of standing her heart rate rises from 72 to 108 while her pressure stays steady. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome

Correct. A rise of more than 30 beats per minute within 10 minutes of standing, improving when lying down, in a young woman with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome fits the syndrome, sometimes expanded as positional.
Neurogenic orthostatic hypotension
Neurogenic orthostatic hypotension combines a pressure fall with a minimal heart rate rise, the opposite of her pattern.
Non-neurogenic orthostatic hypotension
Non-neurogenic orthostatic hypotension requires a pressure fall that meets criteria; her pressure stays steady.
Vasovagal reflex syncope
Vasovagal syncope follows triggers such as fear or heat with bradycardia, not a sustained tachycardia on standing.

D.q: A 45-year-old man is newly diagnosed with hypertension. Which baseline studies are obtained?
opts: Creatinine alone, with nothing further
The panel is considerably broader, covering renal assessment, electrolytes, metabolic studies, thyroid screening and urinalysis.
A chest radiograph and echocardiogram in every patient
Neither is routine: chest radiography is specifically not indicated for uncomplicated hypertension, and echocardiography is reserved for defined indications.
Plasma free metanephrines in every patient
Metanephrines are ordered when the history suggests pheochromocytoma rather than as a universal baseline study.
Renal function, electrolytes, glucose, lipids and urinalysis

Correct, with a urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio alongside the creatinine. The panel does three jobs at once: screens for secondary causes, measures organ damage, and establishes a baseline before drugs that alter potassium and renal function are started. Thyroid-stimulating hormone and a full blood count complete it.

D.io: Compare and contrast precipitating factors, clinical manifestations, diagnosis (including role of B-type natriuretic peptide, BNP), and treatment of acute decompensated heart failure.
D.q: Which description fits acute heart failure?
opts: Failure limited to the right ventricle
Right-sided failure describes which ventricle is involved, not the time course. Acute heart failure is defined by sudden onset, new or as an exacerbation.
Sudden onset, either new or an exacerbation
Correct. Acute means sudden, and it covers both acute new-onset heart failure and an exacerbation of established disease, which in a chronic patient is called acute on chronic heart failure.
Structural disease with no symptoms at all
Asymptomatic structural heart disease is pre-heart failure, stage B. Acute heart failure is symptomatic and sudden in onset.
Symptoms present for more than a year
Duration over a year defines chronic heart failure. Acute heart failure is defined by sudden onset rather than by how long it has lasted.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atherosclerosis and lipid disorders: 1. Hypertriglyceridemia 2. Hypercholesterolemia 3. HDL cholesterol 4. LDL and VLDL cholesterol
D.q: A 50-year-old man has low-density lipoprotein of 178 mg/dL. He reports fatigue, weight gain and cold intolerance over the past year. Before a statin is started, which test should be ordered?
opts: Fasting triglyceride only
Triglyceride is part of his profile, but his symptoms point to hypothyroidism, which raises low-density lipoprotein.
Skin biopsy for receptor activity
Skin biopsy confirms homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia in childhood; his picture suggests a secondary cause.
Thyroid function tests
Correct. Decreased thyroid hormone down-regulates hepatic low-density lipoprotein receptors and raises low-density lipoprotein, so elevated levels call for screening for low thyroid before a statin.
Coronary artery calcium score
Calcium scoring helps an uncertain intermediate-risk statin decision; a treatable secondary cause must be excluded first.

D.io: Acute coronary syndrome
D.q: After plaque rupture, what does exposed tissue factor set off?
opts: Calcification of the wall
Calcification is a slow change measured by a calcium score, not the response to rupture. Tissue factor triggers the clotting cascade and fibrin deposition.
Smooth muscle relaxation
Relaxation of smooth muscle does not follow tissue factor. Tissue factor sets off the clotting cascade, ending in fibrin deposition over the ruptured plaque.
The clotting cascade
Correct. Plaque rupture activates platelets, and tissue factor triggers the clotting cascade with fibrin deposition: the thrombus that turns stable disease into an acute coronary syndrome.
Platelet inhibition
Rupture does the opposite: platelets are activated, and tissue factor triggers the clotting cascade that lays down fibrin.

D.io: Acute coronary syndrome
D.q: Where does the pain of acute coronary syndrome most commonly refer?
opts: Right lower quadrant
The right lower quadrant is not a coronary referral site. Acute coronary syndrome refers mostly to the jaw, tooth or arm, sometimes the epigastrium.
Right scapular region
Right scapular pain is the gallbladder pattern. Acute coronary syndrome pain most commonly refers to the jaw, tooth or arm.
Straight to the back
Pain going straight through to the back is the pancreatic pattern. Acute coronary syndrome most commonly refers to the jaw, tooth or arm.
Jaw, tooth or arm
Correct. Acute coronary syndrome pain refers most commonly to the jaw, tooth or arm, but it can go to the back, the scapular region, or the epigastrium and left upper quadrant.

Hypertriglyceridemia 2. Hypercholesterolemia 3. HDL cholesterol 4. LDL and VLDL cholesterol
D.q: Which is a function of apolipoproteins?
opts: Storage of triglyceride in fat cells
Triglyceride sits in the hydrophobic core of the particle; the apolipoproteins are the proteins on its surface with structural, enzyme and receptor roles.
Ligands for cell-surface receptors
Correct. Apolipoproteins provide the structural foundation of lipoproteins, activate enzymes important in lipoprotein metabolism and act as ligands for cell-surface receptors.
Forming the particle's hydrophobic core
The core is hydrophobic lipid (triglyceride and cholesteryl esters); apolipoproteins sit with the hydrophilic shell as structural proteins.
Excretion of cholesterol into the bile
Delivering cholesterol to the liver for biliary excretion is the job of high-density lipoprotein as a whole, not one of the three apolipoprotein functions.

D.q: A 50-year-old man says he can tell when his blood pressure is high because he gets a headache. How should this be addressed?
opts: Absence of headache confirms his pressure is controlled
Most patients with mild to moderate hypertension have no reliable symptoms at all.
Headache is a reliable indicator and can guide his dosing
Headache is common but nonspecific, and specifically described as an unreliable guide to the pressure.
Most patients have no reliable blood pressure-related symptoms
Correct. Headache is common but nonspecific and cannot be relied on to indicate the pressure, which is why the diagnosis and its control rest on measurement rather than on how he feels.
Any headache requires emergency evaluation
It is the ABRUPT SEVERE headache that warrants immediate evaluation, not any headache.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
D.q: A 73-year-old man has vomited for 2 days and fainted on standing. Supine he is 136/78 with a heart rate of 66; after 3 minutes standing he is 104/64 with a heart rate of 94. What does this heart rate response indicate?
opts: A reflex surge in vagal tone
A vagal surge slows the heart, as in vasovagal syncope, rather than producing a brisk rise on standing.
A primary ventricular arrhythmia
A ventricular arrhythmia is suspected from abrupt collapse and palpitations; a proportional rise on standing is a reflex, not an arrhythmia.
Failure of the autonomic system
Autonomic failure blunts the heart rate rise; a rise of 28 beats shows the reflex is working.
An intact autonomic response
Correct. A heart rate rise from 66 to 94 as pressure falls shows an intact baroreceptor-mediated sympathetic response, which favors non-neurogenic orthostatic hypotension.

D.io: Pulmonic stenosis
D.q: A 12-year-old boy has a harsh mid-systolic ejection murmur at the left upper sternal border that increases with inspiration. Which is the most appropriate test to evaluate the valve?
opts: Chest radiograph
A chest radiograph cannot show valve motion or flow across the valve. Pulmonic stenosis is diagnosed by echocardiogram, with an increased jet on Doppler.
Echocardiogram
Correct. Pulmonic stenosis is diagnosed by echocardiogram, which shows abnormal valve motion and an increased jet velocity across the valve on Doppler.
Electrocardiogram only
An electrocardiogram may show right axis deviation and right ventricular hypertrophy, but it cannot show the valve. An echocardiogram is needed.
Cardiac catheterization
Catheterization is not the test used to diagnose pulmonic stenosis. An echocardiogram shows abnormal valve motion and the increased Doppler jet.

D.io: Compare and contrast risk factors, management, and complications of arteriosclerosis and atherosclerosis.
D.q: What does the Pooled Cohort Equation estimate?
opts: 10-year risk of atherosclerotic disease
Correct. It estimates the 10-year primary risk of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease in patients aged 40 to 79 without pre-existing cardiovascular disease, and it identifies statin candidates.
Risk of pancreatitis from triglycerides
Pancreatitis risk follows triglyceride above 500 mg/dL; the equation estimates atherosclerotic cardiovascular risk.
30-day risk after a heart attack
The equation is for primary prevention in people without pre-existing cardiovascular disease, over a 10-year horizon.
Lifetime risk of familial hypercholesterolemia
Familial hypercholesterolemia is suspected from very high low-density lipoprotein and family history; no risk equation diagnoses it.

D.io: Non-ST segment elevation
D.q: A 64-year-old woman with an hour of chest pressure at rest has ST depression in two consecutive leads and a standard troponin I of 0.3 ng/mL. Which diagnosis fits?
opts: A non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction

Correct. ST depression greater than 1 mm and/or T-wave inversion in two or more consecutive leads with an elevated troponin is a non-ST-elevation infarction. A standard troponin I above 0.04 ng/mL is abnormal, and 0.3 ng/mL is well above it.
Stable angina
Stable angina is exertional pain relieved by rest, with no troponin rise. Rest pain with ST depression and an abnormal troponin I is a non-ST-elevation infarction.
An ST-elevation myocardial infarction
An ST-elevation infarction needs ST elevation in two or more leads. She has ST depression with an abnormal standard troponin I (0.3 ng/mL), a non-ST-elevation infarction.
Unstable angina
Unstable angina has normal troponin levels. A standard troponin I of 0.3 ng/mL is above the 0.04 ng/mL cut-off, and the elevated troponin is what separates infarction from unstable angina.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, prevention, and prognosis for heart failure.
D.q: An 84-year-old woman with right-sided heart failure has progressive symptoms despite treatment of its cause and is not a transplant candidate. Which approach is most appropriate?
opts: Palliative care focused on symptoms

Correct. Right-sided failure is treated like left-sided failure, with symptom management, treatment of the cause, heart transplant or palliative care. When transplant is not an option, palliative care is the route.
Inotropes started for home use
Inotropes are for intensive care use only. Without a transplant option, palliative care focused on symptoms is the route.
Discharge without follow-up care
Withdrawing care is not the plan. Without a transplant option, palliative care focused on symptoms is the route.
Calcium channel blocker for comfort
Calcium channel blockers are avoided in heart failure. Without a transplant option, palliative care focused on symptoms is the route.

D.topic: ST-elevation infarction and right ventricular infarct
D.io: ST segment elevation
D.q: A 66-year-old man is admitted with an inferior ST-elevation myocardial infarction that extends into the right ventricle, with ST elevation in the right-sided lead V4R. His daughter asks why he is not being given nitroglycerin for his chest pain. What should she be told?
opts: It would lower his preload

Correct. In a right ventricular infarct, nitroglycerin is not given: decreasing the preload reduces the Frank-Starling effect on the right ventricle, which can fail into right-sided heart failure, dropping output and precipitating shock.
It would slow his heart rate
Slowing the heart rate is the concern with a beta blocker, which is withheld for bradycardia. Nitroglycerin is withheld because it lowers the preload his failing right ventricle needs.
It would cause bleeding
Bleeding, including intracerebral hemorrhage, is the risk of thrombolytics, not nitroglycerin. Nitroglycerin is withheld because it lowers the preload his right ventricle depends on.
It would cause coronary spasm
Nitroglycerin relieves coronary spasm rather than causing it, and response to it is part of diagnosing vasospastic angina. Here it is withheld because lowering preload can drop his output into shock.

D.io: Differentiate each stage of the American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association (ACC/AHA), natural history classification of heart failure, and associated treatment recommendations of each stage.
D.q: A 52-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes and hypertension has no cardiac symptoms. Her echocardiogram is normal. Which drug class is recommended first to lower her risk of heart failure?
opts: Loop diuretic such as bumetanide
A loop diuretic treats congestion, which she does not have. Stage A with diabetes calls for a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor.
Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor

Correct. Risk factors with a normal heart and no symptoms are stage A, at risk for heart failure, and the one strong drug recommendation there is a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor in patients with diabetes, not a beta blocker.
Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist
The antagonist belongs to symptomatic heart failure, strongly in reduced ejection fraction. Stage A with diabetes calls for a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor.
Beta blocker as the first agent
A beta blocker is a stage B therapy, added once structural disease exists. In stage A with diabetes the first drug is a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor.

D.io: Angina pectoris
D.q: A 49-year-old woman has anginal chest pain with ST changes, and her physician suspects microvascular angina. Which test is required before that diagnosis can be made?
opts: Coronary calcium score
A calcium score is risk stratification for future disease, not a test that excludes coronary artery disease. Microvascular angina needs angiography showing normal arteries.
Transthoracic echocardiogram
An echocardiogram shows wall motion, such as hypokinesia or akinesia, but not the coronary lumen. Excluding coronary artery disease for microvascular angina requires angiography.
Exercise treadmill test
An exercise treadmill test can show ischemic changes but cannot show whether the coronary arteries are normal. Microvascular angina requires angiography to rule out coronary artery disease.
Coronary angiography
Correct. Microvascular angina is a diagnosis of exclusion, and it requires angiography to rule out coronary artery disease; the arteries must be shown to be normal before the label applies.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
D.q: A 79-year-old man with Parkinson disease faints when he gets up at night. His readings show a postural fall with a minimal heart rate rise. Which counseling point is most appropriate?
opts: Sit first, then stand up slowly
Correct. Slow positional changes are listed treatment for orthostatic syncope, and understanding why helps him follow the advice.
Cut fluids to avoid night trips
Reducing fluid lowers volume and worsens postural falls; it is not listed advice for orthostatic syncope.
Leap up to trigger his reflexes
Abrupt standing is what provokes the fall; with autonomic failure the reflex cannot compensate, so slow change is the advice.
Stop all activity for a month
Inactivity is not a listed treatment; the advice targets how he changes position, alongside treating the cause.

D.io: Tricuspid stenosis
D.q: A 53-year-old woman with severe symptomatic tricuspid stenosis is scheduled for valve replacement. Which valve type is preferred?
opts: Annuloplasty ring
Annuloplasty treats tricuspid regurgitation from annular dilation. When a stenotic tricuspid valve is replaced, bioprosthetic is preferred.
Bioprosthetic valve

Correct. For severe symptomatic tricuspid stenosis, bioprosthetic valve replacement is preferred; balloon valvotomy and repair are reserved for hepatic congestion or severe systemic venous congestion.
Mechanical valve
A mechanical valve needs lifelong anticoagulation. In tricuspid stenosis bioprosthetic replacement is the preferred valve.
Balloon valvotomy
Balloon valvotomy is reserved for tricuspid stenosis with hepatic congestion that may lead to cirrhosis or severe venous congestion. The preferred replacement is bioprosthetic.

D.q: A 38-year-old man has an average home blood pressure of 126/78. He has no diabetes, no kidney disease and no cardiovascular history. What should he be advised?
opts: Start a thiazide-type diuretic now
Medication is not indicated at this reading, and lifestyle measures apply first and throughout.
No intervention is needed until he reaches stage 1
Lifestyle treatment is recommended for every category, including readings below the threshold for medication.
Recheck in five years with no advice in the interim
That defers an intervention recommended at every blood pressure category, including this one.
Lifestyle treatment

Correct. An elevated reading that does not yet warrant medication still warrants an intervention, and lifestyle measures continue alongside drugs later rather than being replaced by them. It is recommended at every blood pressure category.

D.io: Compare and contrast precipitating factors, clinical manifestations, diagnosis (including role of B-type natriuretic peptide, BNP), and treatment of acute decompensated heart failure.
D.q: A 70-year-old man admitted with acute heart failure has diuresed well. On the day of planned discharge his B-type natriuretic peptide is 360. What does this predischarge level suggest?
opts: Lower risk of 30-day readmission
Correct. A predischarge level below 430 carries a lower risk of readmission within 30 days, which supports discharge planning.
Acute heart failure is still likely
Acute failure becomes likely above 900. A predischarge level of 360 is below 430 and linked to lower readmission.
Higher risk of 30-day readmission
Risk rises with higher levels. Below 430 predischarge, the readmission risk is lower.
The level carries no prognostic value
Predischarge levels do carry prognostic meaning: below 430 is linked to lower 30-day readmission.

D.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following atherosclerosis and lipid disorders: 1. Hypertriglyceridemia 2. Hypercholesterolemia 3. HDL cholesterol 4. LDL and VLDL cholesterol
D.q: A 24-year-old man has severe epigastric pain radiating to his back. Clusters of small yellowish-white papules (eruptive xanthomas) cover his buttocks and the backs of his arms, and fundoscopy shows opalescent retinal vessels (lipemia retinalis). His fasting triglyceride is 2100 mg/dL. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Familial chylomicronemia syndrome

Correct. Fasting triglyceride above 500 and usually above 1000 mg/dL, acute pancreatitis, eruptive xanthomas and lipemia retinalis (sometimes with hepatosplenomegaly) define this syndrome, which can present in childhood or adulthood.
Heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia
The heterozygous cholesterol disorder has low-density lipoprotein of 200 to 400 with normal triglyceride and tendon xanthomas, not pancreatitis.
Familial dysbetalipoproteinemia
Dysbetalipoproteinemia raises triglyceride and total cholesterol together to 250 to 500 mg/dL with palmar xanthomas, far below 2100.
Metabolic syndrome
Metabolic syndrome needs three of five criteria such as triglyceride above 150; it does not produce triglyceride above 2000 with lipemia retinalis.

D.q: A 52-year-old man with low high-density lipoprotein has improved his lifestyle, and his clinician is weighing a drug chosen specifically to raise high-density lipoprotein. Which drug raises it most?
opts: Pravastatin
Statins such as pravastatin raise high-density lipoprotein 5% to 22%, less than niacin.
Ezetimibe
Ezetimibe raises high-density lipoprotein only about 8% and is used mainly as a low-density adjunct.
Colesevelam
Colesevelam is a bile acid sequestrant that lowers low-density lipoprotein 15% to 30% as an adjunct and is not used to raise high-density lipoprotein.
Niacin
Correct. Niacin raises high-density lipoprotein 15% to 35%, better than other medications, compared with fibrates 10% to 30%, statins 5% to 22% and ezetimibe 8%.

D.q: A 55-year-old South Asian man without diabetes has low-density lipoprotein of 150 mg/dL and a calculated 10-year atherosclerotic risk of 12%. His father had a heart attack at 50. After discussion he favors treatment. What is the most appropriate therapy?
opts: High-intensity statin with ezetimibe
Combination therapy is for very high-risk disease or severe hypercholesterolemia that stays elevated; this is intermediate-risk primary prevention.
Moderate-intensity statin

Correct. At intermediate risk with risk enhancers (South Asian ancestry, premature family history) and a discussion that favors therapy, start a moderate-intensity statin to lower low-density lipoprotein by 30% or more.
Lifestyle alone without any drug
Lifestyle continues, but risk enhancers at intermediate risk favor starting a statin.
A fibrate for his cholesterol
Fibrates are the triglyceride drugs; low-density lipoprotein is lowered most by statins.
