D.q: Which categories of disease are listed behind neurogenic orthostatic hypotension?
opts: Infarction, heart failure and valve disease
These are structural cardiogenic causes of syncope, evaluated with echocardiography and cardiology consultation rather than orthostatic vitals.
Diabetic, genetic and autoimmune disorders
Correct. Each can damage the autonomic nervous system, and long-standing diabetes with peripheral neuropathy is the classic route to diabetic autonomic neuropathy.
Dehydration, blood loss and poor intake
These describe who develops non-neurogenic orthostatic hypotension, where the problem is volume and the autonomic response remains intact.
Coughing, sneezing and urination
These bodily functions are triggers of situational reflex syncope, which is a reflex event rather than autonomic failure.

D.q: A 64-year-old hypertensive man also has a raised low-density lipoprotein. What principle should guide his management?
opts: Treat the lipids first and defer blood pressure control
Neither is deferred; total cardiovascular risk is addressed, since both drive the same vascular injury.
Treat total cardiovascular risk, not pressure alone

Correct. Hypertension accelerates atherosclerosis through shear stress, intimal injury, lipid oxidation and smooth muscle proliferation, so antiplatelet and lipid-lowering therapy are considered where indicated.
Treat the blood pressure and address lipids only if it fails
The two are managed together, because the vascular injury they produce is a single process.
Lipid therapy is unnecessary once blood pressure reaches goal
Reaching the pressure goal does not remove the contribution of lipids to the same process.

D.q: A 27-year-old woman reports several brief faints over 6 months with a warm, nauseated prodrome, but she cannot recall what was happening before most of them. Her examination is normal. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Order a tilt-table test
Tilt-table testing is the listed test for postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome, and a negative result tells little.
Arrange an echocardiogram
Echocardiography evaluates structural cardiogenic syncope, which her prodrome and normal examination do not suggest.
Start fludrocortisone now
Fludrocortisone is best with the tachycardia syndrome; reflex syncope is managed by identifying and avoiding triggers.
Keep a log of each episode
Correct. A log of pattern and frequency supports a history-based diagnosis of reflex syncope and helps identify the triggers to avoid.

Blood pressure does not make dobutamine a home drug. Inotropes are for intensive care use only.
Yes, in place of his other medicines
Inotropes do not replace guideline-directed therapy and are for intensive care use only.
Inotropes are for intensive care only

Yes, as long-term home maintenance

D.q: A 54-year-old woman with pulmonary arterial hypertension has edema and distended neck veins. Her electrocardiogram shows right axis deviation, right bundle branch block and T-wave inversions in V1 to V3. What does this pattern indicate?
opts: A normal variant tracing
This combination is not a normal variant; axis deviation, bundle branch block and inversions form the right heart strain pattern.
Acute lateral infarction
Infarction shows ischemic changes in a coronary territory. Her pattern is right heart strain.
Right heart strain
Correct. Right axis deviation, right bundle branch block and T-wave inversions in V1 to V3 are the right heart strain pattern, fitting right-sided failure from pulmonary arterial hypertension.
Left ventricular hypertrophy
Hypertrophy shows tall R waves in V5 and V6 with deep S waves in V1 and V2. Her pattern is right heart strain.

D.q: Why is overly rapid blood pressure reduction harmful in a hypertensive emergency?
opts: It precipitates hyperkalemia
Potassium disturbance relates to renin-angiotensin blockade and mineralocorticoid antagonists rather than to the rate of pressure reduction.
It has no harm; rapid reduction is preferred
Rapid reduction is specifically described as capable of causing ischemic stroke, myocardial injury or renal failure.
Autoregulation has adapted to the higher pressure

Correct. The organs have reset the range over which they protect their own perfusion, so returning the pressure to normal too quickly leaves them underperfused at a value that would be safe in anyone else. Reducing too fast can cause ischemic stroke, myocardial injury or renal failure.
It causes rebound hypertension within hours
Rebound on abrupt withdrawal is a limitation of central alpha-2 agonists rather than the reason for controlled reduction here.

D.q: A 16-year-old boy with homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia has progressive atherosclerosis despite maximal drug therapy and apheresis. Which referral may help by supplying the receptors he lacks?
opts: Liver transplantation
Correct. Liver transplantation may prove helpful in the homozygous disorder by providing low-density lipoprotein receptors that his own liver lacks or cannot use.
Kidney transplantation
The kidney does not clear low-density lipoprotein through receptors; the liver is the organ that supplies them.
Bariatric surgery
Weight loss improves triglyceride and high-density lipoprotein, but cannot fix an inherited receptor defect.
Carotid ultrasound only
Imaging would describe the disease, not treat it; transplantation addresses the missing receptors.

D.q: A 57-year-old man had an ejection fraction of 25% two years ago. On guideline-directed therapy his repeat echocardiogram now shows 46%. How is his heart failure now classified?
opts: Improved ejection fraction
Correct. A fraction that was 40% or less and has recovered above 40% is improved ejection fraction. The number alone would read mildly reduced, but his history is what defines the group.
Mildly reduced ejection fraction
46% alone would be mildly reduced, but his earlier 25% changes the label. Recovery from the reduced range above 40% is improved ejection fraction.
Preserved ejection fraction
Preserved ejection fraction is 50% or more, which he has not reached. Recovery above 40% from a reduced value is improved ejection fraction.
Resolved heart failure
Heart failure is not relabeled as resolved when the fraction recovers. Recovery above 40% from 25% is improved ejection fraction.

D.q: A 66-year-old man with chest pain has a nuclear stress test showing a perfusion defect that does not reverse at rest. What does this fixed defect indicate?
opts: Reversible ischemia
Ischemia produces a reversible defect that fills in at rest. A defect that stays at rest is non-reversible and indicates infarction.
Coronary vasospasm
Vasospasm is diagnosed by provoking spasm at angiography, not by a fixed nuclear defect. A non-reversible defect indicates infarction.
Prior infarction
Correct. On a nuclear stress test, a reversible perfusion defect indicates ischemia, while a non-reversible (fixed) defect indicates infarction.
A normal study
A normal study shows no perfusion defect at all. A defect that does not reverse at rest indicates infarction.

D.q: A 32-year-old man has a white-gray ring around the edge of each cornea (corneal arcus). His low-density lipoprotein is 250 mg/dL with a normal triglyceride, and his father died of a heart attack at 52. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Familial dysbetalipoproteinemia
Dysbetalipoproteinemia raises triglyceride and total cholesterol together with palmar xanthomas; his triglyceride is normal.
Familial chylomicronemia syndrome
Chylomicronemia raises triglyceride above 1000 with eruptive papules and lipemia retinalis; his triglyceride is normal.
Homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia
The homozygous form presents in childhood with xanthomas and total cholesterol of about 400 to above 1000; an adult with low-density lipoprotein of 250 fits one mutant allele.
Heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia

Correct. Corneal arcus before 40 usually indicates a genetic condition, and low-density lipoprotein of 200 to 400 with normal triglyceride and premature family coronary disease fits the heterozygous form, in which arcus is common.

D.q: A 62-year-old woman is newly diagnosed with heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (fraction 28%). She is breathless with ordinary exertion but comfortable at rest, and takes no renin-angiotensin drug. Which agent fits her symptom class?
opts: Dobutamine
Dobutamine is an inotrope for intensive care use only. Her class II reduced ejection fraction fits sacubitril-valsartan.
Metolazone alone
Metolazone is a thiazide-like diuretic used as needed for congestion, not renin-angiotensin therapy. Her class fits sacubitril-valsartan.
Diltiazem
Diltiazem is a calcium channel blocker, which is avoided in heart failure. Her class II reduced ejection fraction fits sacubitril-valsartan.
Sacubitril-valsartan
Correct. Symptoms with exertion are New York Heart Association class II, and the angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor is recommended for class II to III in reduced ejection fraction.

D.q: A 72-year-old man's electrocardiogram shows runs of nonsustained ventricular tachycardia after an abrupt faint preceded by palpitations. Which referral is most appropriate?
opts: Physical therapy referral
Physical therapy has no listed role in cardiogenic syncope, whose work-up pairs cardiac testing with cardiology.
Neurology consultation
Neurologic input suits autonomic failure or suspected seizure; an arrhythmic faint is referred to cardiology.
Cardiology consultation
Correct. Every type of cardiogenic syncope, arrhythmic, structural and vascular, lists cardiology consultation alongside its tests.
Endocrinology referral
Endocrine disease such as diabetes causes neurogenic orthostatic hypotension, not a ventricular arrhythmia.

D.q: A 22-year-old man is found to have a blood pressure of 158/92 in both arms. His femoral pulses are weak and delayed relative to the radial pulses, and his leg systolic pressure is lower than his arm pressure. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Primary hypertension
Onset this early, with an abnormal pulse examination, points away from primary hypertension and toward a structural cause.
Renovascular disease from fibromuscular dysplasia
Fibromuscular dysplasia causes early-onset hypertension in young patients, but through renal artery narrowing, which produces an abdominal bruit rather than radial-femoral delay.
Primary aldosteronism
Aldosteronism is screened for in early or resistant hypertension, but it does not alter the femoral pulses or the arm-to-leg pressure relationship.
Coarctation of the aorta

Correct. Leg systolic normally EXCEEDS arm systolic, so a reversal is the abnormal finding, and radial-femoral delay places a structural obstruction between the two territories. Early onset hypertension is itself a clue to a secondary cause.

E.q: A 67-year-old woman with 20 years of type 2 diabetes has fainted twice shortly after getting out of bed. Her mucous membranes are moist, and vibration and light-touch sensation are reduced in both feet. Supine she is 140/80 with a heart rate of 70; after 3 minutes standing she is 110/66 with a heart rate of 74. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Vasovagal reflex syncope
Vasovagal syncope follows triggers such as fear, pain or heat with a transient reflex, not a reproducible postural fall on standing.
Cardiogenic arrhythmic syncope
An arrhythmia typically causes abrupt collapse without warning and often palpitations; her faints follow standing, with a regular exam.
Non-neurogenic orthostatic hypotension
The non-neurogenic form shows a significant heart rate rise from an intact autonomic reflex and usually volume depletion; she has neither.
Neurogenic orthostatic hypotension
Correct. The systolic fall of 30 mmHg meets the criterion, the heart rate barely rises, and long-standing diabetes with neuropathy points to diabetic autonomic neuropathy.

E.q: A 62-year-old woman with exertional chest tightness develops T-wave inversion during an exercise stress test. Which test is the gold standard for confirming coronary artery disease?
opts: Transthoracic echocardiogram
An echocardiogram shows regional wall motion abnormalities such as hypokinesia or akinesia. It does not image the coronary lumen; coronary angiography is the gold standard.
Nuclear stress test
A nuclear stress test shows reversible perfusion defects (ischemia) and fixed ones (infarction), and an abnormal result leads to catheterization. It is not the gold standard; angiography is.
Coronary calcium score
A cardiac computed tomography calcium score is used for risk stratification, not to diagnose an acute syndrome or confirm disease. Coronary angiography is the gold standard.
Coronary angiography

Correct. Coronary angiography, with dye injected at catheterization and pictures taken of the coronary arteries, is the gold standard for diagnosing coronary artery disease after a positive stress test.

E.q: A 69-year-old woman has sudden severe breathlessness, crackles and edema. Her B-type natriuretic peptide is 1,150. How should this level be read?
opts: The result is indeterminate
The indeterminate range is 100 to 400. A level of 1,150 makes acute heart failure likely.
Acute heart failure is likely
Correct. Above 900 acute heart failure is likely. Above 400 heart failure is likely in general, 100 to 400 is indeterminate, and below 100 rules acute failure out.
Acute heart failure is ruled out
Rule-out applies only below 100. A level of 1,150 is far above that and makes acute heart failure likely.
Only chronic heart failure fits
Levels above 900 point to acute heart failure, and her sudden onset fits. The result makes acute failure likely.

E.q: A 59-year-old man with dilated cardiomyopathy has an ejection fraction of 25%, breathlessness with exertion and no symptoms at rest. He takes furosemide and sacubitril-valsartan. Which drug class should be added as core therapy?
opts: Calcium channel blocker such as diltiazem
Calcium channel blockers are avoided in heart failure. The missing core classes include the sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor.
Hydralazine with isosorbide dinitrate
That pairing is for African American patients in functional class III or IV, added after the core classes. He still lacks the sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor.
Milrinone as an outpatient infusion
Milrinone is an inotrope reserved for the intensive care unit. The missing core classes include the sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor.
Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor

Correct. Reduced ejection fraction carries strong recommendations for a beta blocker, renin-angiotensin blockade, a mineralocorticoid antagonist and a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor; he has only the renin-angiotensin piece so far.

E.q: Which outcome is associated with consuming fatty fish or fish-oil supplements?
opts: Higher high-density lipoprotein than niacin
Niacin raises high-density lipoprotein better than other medications; fish oil's benefit is lower coronary risk and coronary death.
More low-density lowering than statins
Statins are the most effective low-density drugs; fish oil is not a low-density lowering drug.
Cure of familial hypercholesterolemia
No drug cures the receptor defect; the homozygous form needs apheresis and multiple drugs.
Lower risk of coronary death

Correct. Fatty fish or fish-oil supplements are associated with lower risk of coronary heart disease and coronary death, may lower thrombotic stroke risk, and at least 2 servings of fish a week are advised.

E.q: A 78-year-old woman with chronic heart failure has increasing lethargy, episodes of near-syncope and cool extremities, without new edema. Which feature of the heart failure syndrome do these findings reflect?
opts: Worsening pulmonary congestion
Congestion shows as orthopnea, crackles and edema, which she lacks. Lethargy, near-syncope and cool extremities reflect inadequate perfusion.
Inadequate tissue perfusion
Correct. Weakness, fatigue, lethargy, malaise, syncope or near-syncope and obtundation are signs of inadequate tissue perfusion, the low-output side of the syndrome, distinct from congestion.
Systemic volume overload
Systemic overload shows as edema and distended neck veins, which she lacks. Her findings reflect inadequate perfusion.
Portal venous overload
Portal overload gives nausea, poor appetite and an enlarged liver. Her findings reflect inadequate perfusion.

E.q: A 66-year-old woman with long-standing diabetes fainted after walking to the bathroom. Supine she is 146/84 with a heart rate of 70; after 3 minutes standing she is 118/70 with a heart rate of 72. What does her heart rate response indicate?
opts: The autonomic response is intact
An intact response produces a significant heart rate rise as pressure falls, as seen with volume loss; hers rose by only 2 beats.
An arrhythmia is present
An arrhythmia is suggested by abrupt collapse with palpitations and is shown on an electrocardiogram, not by a flat heart rate response.
The autonomic response has failed
Correct. A pressure fall with only a minimal heart rate rise means the sympathetic reflex is not compensating, which favors neurogenic orthostatic hypotension.
Volume depletion is the cause
Volume depletion is usually accompanied by a significant compensatory heart rate rise, which she does not show.

E.q: A 43-year-old woman's previously well-controlled blood pressure has risen over two months. She denies missing doses. What should the medication review specifically cover beyond her prescriptions?
opts: Only agents started within the past week
The review is not bounded that tightly; a substance taken for months can be responsible.
Only her antihypertensive agents
Reviewing the antihypertensives addresses adherence, but the question is what else may be raising the pressure.
Only intravenous medications given in hospital
The categories named are over-the-counter, recreational, licorice and herbal supplements.
Over-the-counter drugs, licorice and supplements

Correct, and patients frequently do not volunteer any of these because they do not regard them as medication. A sudden loss of previously stable control is itself a clue to a secondary cause. Recreational substances belong in the same review.

E.q: A 32-year-old man arrives for his first adult screening visit, having eaten lunch an hour ago. Which lipid test can be done today without fasting?
opts: Total and high-density cholesterol
Correct. Total and high-density cholesterol need no fasting; their ratio is the most efficient and cost-effective way to predict coronary risk.
Triglyceride and total cholesterol
Triglyceride requires a 9- to 12-hour fast, so it cannot be done validly after lunch.
Calculated low-density lipoprotein
A calculated low-density value relies on fasting triglyceride and needs a 9- to 12-hour fast.
Triglyceride with high-density cholesterol
Triglyceride is the fasting-dependent value, so this pair cannot be drawn after a meal.

E.io: Aortic stenosis
E.q: A 74-year-old man with untreated severe aortic stenosis now has breathlessness on exertion, orthopnea (breathlessness lying flat) and ankle swelling. Without valve replacement, which average survival is expected from this symptom?
opts: About 10 years
A decade is far too long; once aortic stenosis becomes symptomatic, prognosis is severely worsened. With heart failure symptoms the average survival is about 2 years.
About 3 years
About 3 years belongs to exertional syncope. Heart failure or exertional dyspnea is the most common cardinal symptom and has the shortest survival, about 2 years.
About 5 years
About 5 years is the average survival once angina appears. Heart failure symptoms such as exertional dyspnea and orthopnea carry the worst prognosis, about 2 years.
About 2 years
Correct. Of the cardinal symptoms, heart failure or exertional dyspnea is the most common and carries the worst prognosis, about 2 years. Angina carries about 5 years and syncope about 3 years.

E.q: A 56-year-old man with a triglyceride of 380 mg/dL is already on a moderate-intensity statin and at his low-density goal. Which drug is the most effective choice to add for his triglyceride?
opts: Alirocumab
Alirocumab is an injectable for refractory or very-high-risk low-density lipoprotein, not a triglyceride drug.
Ezetimibe
Ezetimibe lowers triglyceride only 5% to 10%, much less than the 20% to 50% of a fibrate.
Colestipol
Colestipol is a bile acid sequestrant used as an adjunct for more low-density lowering, not for triglyceride.
Fenofibrate
Correct. Fibrates such as fenofibrate are the most effective for lowering triglyceride, by 20% to 50%, and they also raise high-density lipoprotein 10% to 30%.

E.q: A 55-year-old man with hypertensive retinopathy achieves good blood pressure control. What can be expected of his retinal findings?
opts: The changes have no relationship to blood pressure
Retinal changes are a direct consequence of the pressure, and they predict long-term stroke risk.
The changes will progress regardless of control
Progression is not inevitable, and regression of the retinopathy with good control is described.
Control can lead to regression of the retinopathy
Correct, so the finding is both a prognostic marker and something that can improve with treatment. Retinopathy predicts long-term stroke risk independently of the pressure level.
The changes are permanent once established
Control of hypertension can produce regression of retinopathy, so the finding is not a fixed one.

E.q: A 71-year-old man with ischemic cardiomyopathy has an ejection fraction of 25%, is class II on optimal guideline-directed therapy, and has metastatic cancer with an expected survival of a few months. Which is most appropriate regarding an implantable defibrillator?
opts: Implant it once he is class IV
Class IV falls outside the class II to III criterion, and his life expectancy still fails. The device is not indicated.
Implant it before discharge
His fraction and class qualify, but the life expectancy criterion of at least one year does not. The device is not indicated.
Implant it after a cardiac arrest
The criteria do not wait for an arrest, and his life expectancy of months fails them. The device is not indicated.
It is not indicated for him

Correct. The device is indicated only with a life expectancy of at least one year, together with ejection fraction 35% or less, class II or III and optimal therapy. His expected survival of months fails that criterion.

E.q: A 58-year-old man is found to have a raised creatinine. What is required before chronic kidney disease can be diagnosed?
opts: Structural renal disease demonstrated on imaging
Imaging may support a cause, but the definition turns on a persisting abnormality rather than a structural finding.
A kidney abnormality persisting three months
Correct. A single raised value may reflect a reversible insult, so duration is part of the definition rather than an optional confirmation.
A single raised creatinine measurement
One measurement does not establish chronicity, which is what the three-month requirement tests.
Albuminuria alone, regardless of duration
Albuminuria is one marker of kidney damage, but the three-month persistence requirement still applies.

E.q: For reflex hypotension, what is the treatment principle?
opts: Treat the autonomic disease
Treating an underlying condition is the approach for orthostasis, such as autonomic failure or volume loss, rather than for reflex causes.
Reduce or remove the medication
Reducing or removing a medication is the approach for iatrogenic hypotension, where a drug is the offending agent.
Start a vasopressor infusion
Vasopressor infusions are for the emergency department and intensive care only, not the management of reflex hypotension.
Reduce or remove the trigger
Correct. The principle is to remove the offending agent or trigger: reflex causes are managed by reducing or removing the trigger.

E.io: Mitral regurgitation
E.q: A 67-year-old woman has severe mitral regurgitation with symptoms of left ventricular systolic dysfunction. Her ejection fraction is 52% and the left ventricular end-systolic dimension is 45 mm. Which is the most appropriate treatment?
opts: Percutaneous balloon valvotomy
Balloon valvotomy opens a stenotic mitral valve; it would not stop a leak. Severe symptomatic mitral regurgitation is treated with a clip or valve replacement.
A loop diuretic and yearly echo
Medical management alone is not enough once severe regurgitation has an ejection fraction below 60% and an end-systolic dimension above 40 mm. She meets the surgical indications.
A mitral valve clip or replacement

Correct. Surgery is indicated for severe mitral regurgitation with symptomatic left ventricular systolic dysfunction, an ejection fraction below 60% or an end-systolic dimension above 40 mm. Options include a mitral valve clip or transcatheter mitral valve replacement.
Aortic valve replacement
Aortic valve replacement treats aortic stenosis or regurgitation. Her lesion is mitral, so the intervention is a mitral valve clip or replacement.

E.q: A 40-year-old man is newly found to have heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia with low-density lipoprotein of 250 mg/dL. He has read about a new injectable and wants it instead of any pill. Which option is inappropriate as initial therapy?
opts: Addressing smoking and blood pressure
Aggressive reduction of vascular risk factors such as smoking, hypertension and diabetes is recommended, so this is appropriate.
A high-intensity statin
A high-intensity statin is the common first regimen in heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia and is entirely appropriate.
A low saturated-fat, low-cholesterol diet
A diet low in saturated fat and cholesterol is part of his treatment, alongside the statin, so it is appropriate.
Evolocumab before trying a statin
Correct. The steps must be followed: high-intensity statins first, then ezetimibe and nicotinic acid, and the injectable only for patients refractory to drug therapy.

E.io: Compare and contrast precipitating factors, clinical manifestations, diagnosis (including role of B-type natriuretic peptide, BNP), and treatment of acute decompensated heart failure.
E.q: A 75-year-old man with heart failure diagnosed three years ago has had four days of worsening orthopnea (breathlessness lying flat) and leg swelling. How is this episode classified?
opts: Acute on chronic heart failure

Correct. Heart failure present for more than a year is chronic, and a sudden worsening on top of it is acute on chronic heart failure, the last step of the sequence from pre-heart failure through exacerbation.
Acute new-onset heart failure
New-onset failure is a first symptomatic episode. He has had heart failure for three years, so this is acute on chronic heart failure.
High-output heart failure
Nothing suggests anemia, hyperthyroidism or a fistula. This is a sudden worsening of chronic disease, acute on chronic heart failure.
Pre-heart failure, stage B
Pre-heart failure is asymptomatic structural disease. He is symptomatic with known chronic disease: acute on chronic heart failure.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, prevention, and prognosis for heart failure.
E.q: Which statement captures the etiology of all heart failure?
opts: Every case has a cardiomyopathy etiology
Correct. All heart failure, as a syndrome, has a cardiomyopathy behind it, whether ischemic or non-ischemic. That is why the causes are sorted as ischemic cardiomyopathy versus everything else.
Every case begins with valve disease
Valve disease, most often aortic stenosis, is only one cause. All heart failure shares an underlying cardiomyopathy.
Every case begins with coronary disease
Coronary disease drives ischemic cardiomyopathy, but non-ischemic causes such as hypertension, valve disease and toxins also cause heart failure.
Every case begins with hypertension
Hypertension is common but not universal. What all heart failure shares is an underlying cardiomyopathy, ischemic or non-ischemic.

E.q: Which baseline studies are obtained in a newly diagnosed hypertensive patient?
opts: Renal function, electrolytes, glucose, lipids and urinalysis

Correct. The panel does three jobs at once: it looks for secondary causes, measures organ damage, and establishes a baseline before drugs that alter potassium and renal function are started. The panel also carries a urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio, thyroid-stimulating hormone and a full blood count.
Plasma free metanephrines in every patient
Metanephrines are ordered when pheochromocytoma is suspected from the history rather than as a universal baseline study.
Serum creatinine alone, with nothing further
The baseline panel is considerably broader, covering renal assessment, electrolytes, metabolic studies, thyroid screening and urinalysis.
A chest radiograph and echocardiogram in every patient
Chest radiography is specifically not indicated routinely for uncomplicated hypertension.

E.io: Tricuspid stenosis
E.q: A 49-year-old woman with severe tricuspid stenosis develops worsening hepatic congestion, and her team fears progression to cirrhosis. Which intervention is reserved for this situation?
opts: Afterload reduction therapy only
Afterload reduction treats chronic aortic regurgitation. Tricuspid stenosis threatening cirrhosis calls for balloon valvotomy or valve repair.
Balloon valvotomy or valve repair
Correct. Balloon valvotomy and valve repair are reserved for tricuspid stenosis with hepatic congestion that may lead to cirrhosis, or with severe systemic venous congestion.
Mitral valve clip placement
A mitral valve clip treats severe mitral regurgitation. Hepatic congestion from tricuspid stenosis is the indication for balloon valvotomy or repair.
Transcatheter aortic valve replacement
Transcatheter aortic valve replacement treats severe aortic stenosis. In tricuspid stenosis with threatening hepatic congestion, balloon valvotomy or repair is reserved.

E.q: A 66-year-old woman with prior heart attacks collapsed without any prodrome while climbing stairs and woke within 20 seconds. Which referral should accompany her cardiac testing?
opts: Dietitian referral
A dietitian has no listed role in cardiogenic syncope, whose work-up pairs cardiac tests with cardiology consultation.
Cardiology consultation
Correct. Arrhythmic, structural and vascular cardiogenic syncope each pair their tests with cardiology consultation.
Physical therapy referral
Physical therapy is not part of the listed cardiogenic work-up, which pairs cardiac tests with cardiology.
Neurology consultation
Neurology suits autonomic failure or seizure; an abrupt collapse with cardiac history points to cardiology.

E.io: Differentiate each stage of the American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association (ACC/AHA), natural history classification of heart failure, and associated treatment recommendations of each stage.
E.q: A 63-year-old man had a myocardial infarction a year ago. He has no symptoms of heart failure and no diabetes, and his echocardiogram shows systolic dysfunction. Which regimen is recommended?
opts: Dapagliflozin alone, since he has no symptoms
The sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor in stages A and B is for patients with diabetes, which he does not have. Stage B relies on a converting enzyme inhibitor and a beta blocker.
Hydralazine with isosorbide dinitrate
That pairing is for symptomatic reduced ejection fraction in African American patients in functional class III or IV. Stage B relies on a converting enzyme inhibitor and a beta blocker.
A converting enzyme inhibitor and a beta blocker

Correct. Asymptomatic structural disease is stage B, pre-heart failure, where an angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitor and a beta blocker are strong recommendations; a receptor blocker replaces the inhibitor if it is not tolerated.
A loop diuretic started at once
Diuretics are used as needed for congestion, which he does not have. Stage B relies on a converting enzyme inhibitor and a beta blocker.

E.q: A 69-year-old man with poorly controlled hypertension asks which strokes he is at risk of. What should he be told?
opts: Both ischemic and hemorrhagic stroke
Correct. Hypertension raises the risk of both mechanisms, and chronic small-vessel injury separately contributes to white matter change, lacunar infarcts and cognitive decline.
Ischemic stroke only
Intracerebral hemorrhage is also described, which is part of why sustained systolic burden matters so much.
Subarachnoid hemorrhage specifically
The described events are ischemic stroke and intracerebral hemorrhage rather than subarachnoid bleeding.
Intracerebral hemorrhage only
Ischemic stroke is described alongside hemorrhage and chronic small-vessel injury.

E.q: A 51-year-old woman with newly diagnosed hypertension has proximal muscle weakness, easy bruising, thin skin and broad purple abdominal striae with central adiposity. What is the most likely underlying cause?
opts: Primary aldosteronism
Aldosteronism presents with resistant hypertension and unexplained hypokalemia rather than striae and proximal weakness.
Cushing syndrome
Correct. The cluster of proximal weakness, bruising, thin skin, broad purple striae and central adiposity points to glucocorticoid excess as the secondary cause of her hypertension.
Pheochromocytoma
Pheochromocytoma produces episodic headache, sweating, palpitations and pallor rather than the skin and muscle changes described.
Obstructive sleep apnea
Sleep apnea is suggested by loud snoring, witnessed apneas and daytime sleepiness.

E.io: Unstable
E.q: A 63-year-old man has had chest pressure at rest for two days. His electrocardiogram shows inverted T waves, and two standard troponin I levels are 0.01 ng/mL. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: ST-elevation infarction
An ST-elevation myocardial infarction shows ST elevation above 1 mm in two or more leads with elevated troponin I. His tracing shows only inverted T waves and his troponin I is not abnormal.
Unstable angina
Correct. Pain at rest with nonspecific electrocardiogram changes, usually inverted T waves, and a normal troponin I is unstable angina. A standard troponin I at or below 0.04 ng/mL is not abnormal.
Stable angina
Stable angina is brought on by exertion and relieved by rest and nitroglycerin. Pain that now occurs at rest has become unstable angina, an acute coronary syndrome.
Infarction without ST elevation
A non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction needs an elevated troponin I, meaning standard troponin I above 0.04 ng/mL. His two values of 0.01 ng/mL are not abnormal, so this is unstable angina.

E.io: Aortic regurgitation
E.q: A 47-year-old man has a Corrigan pulse (a very rapid upstroke followed by rapid collapse) and a de Musset sign (head bobbing with each heartbeat). Which valve lesion is most likely?
opts: Tricuspid stenosis
Tricuspid stenosis causes neck vein distension and low-output symptoms, not a collapsing arterial pulse. These peripheral signs belong to aortic regurgitation.
Mitral regurgitation
Mitral regurgitation is a holosystolic apical murmur radiating to the axilla. The collapsing pulse and head bobbing are signs of aortic regurgitation.
Aortic regurgitation

Correct. The Corrigan pulse, also called a water hammer or collapsing pulse, and the de Musset sign are findings of chronic aortic regurgitation, along with a diastolic blowing murmur and a displaced point of maximal impulse.
Aortic stenosis
Aortic stenosis gives a delayed, weakened carotid pulse, the opposite of a rapid upstroke with collapse. The Corrigan pulse and head bobbing point to aortic regurgitation.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of the following hypotensive disorders: a. Orthostatic hypotension b. Vasovagal hypotension
E.q: A 76-year-old woman with neurogenic orthostatic hypotension from diabetes asks what she can do herself to stop fainting when she gets out of bed. Which counseling point is most appropriate?
opts: Stand quickly to train her reflexes
Abrupt standing provokes the fall in pressure; the advice is the opposite, slow position changes.
Stay in bed until symptoms stop
Bed rest does not treat the cause; slow position changes and treating the underlying condition are the measures.
Drink less water in the evening
Reducing fluid lowers volume and makes a postural fall worse; it is not listed advice for orthostatic syncope.
Change position slowly when rising
Correct. Slow positional changes are listed treatment for orthostatic syncope, with a pause sitting before standing, alongside treatment of the underlying cause.

E.q: Which setting is typical of micturition syncope?
opts: Voiding while standing at night
Correct. Nocturnal urination after abruptly standing from bed, voiding in the standing position, triggers an exaggerated autonomic reflex with vagal activity and reduced vascular tone.
Shock at hearing bad news
Emotional stress and fear are triggers of vasovagal syncope, the common faint, rather than the situational micturition type.
Exertion while climbing stairs
Syncope during exertion raises concern for a cardiogenic cause, which needs electrocardiography, echocardiography and cardiology input.
Diarrhea for several days
Several days of diarrhea cause volume depletion and non-neurogenic orthostatic hypotension, with a significant heart rate rise on standing.

E.io: Differentiate between systolic dysfunction and diastolic dysfunction..
E.q: A 71-year-old woman with 20 years of poorly controlled hypertension has ankle swelling that has recently spread to crackles at both lung bases. Blood pressure is 176/98. A fourth heart sound (a sound in late diastole just before the first heart sound) is heard. Echocardiogram shows thick left ventricular walls with an ejection fraction of 62%. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Systolic failure from ischemic cardiomyopathy
Ischemic cardiomyopathy leads the systolic chain with a reduced ejection fraction and low-normal pressure. Her hypertension, fourth sound and preserved fraction are diastolic.
Systolic failure from dilated cardiomyopathy
Dilated cardiomyopathy gives a weak squeeze, a reduced ejection fraction, a normal or low pressure and a third sound. Her findings are the diastolic chain.
High-output failure from thyroid excess
Hyperthyroid high-output failure brings tachycardia and palpitations from increased demand. Her long hypertension and fourth sound point to diastolic failure.
Diastolic failure from hypertrophic disease

Correct. The diastolic chain is complete: hypertension driving hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, a fourth heart sound from atrial contraction against a stiff ventricle, peripheral then pulmonary edema, and a preserved ejection fraction.

E.io: Differentiate each stage of the American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association (ACC/AHA), natural history classification of heart failure, and associated treatment recommendations of each stage.
E.q: Why is a beta blocker the wrong first choice for an at-risk patient with diabetes and a normal heart?
opts: The first drug is a sodium-glucose inhibitor
Correct. In stage A the only strongly recommended drug is a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor in patients with diabetes. The beta blocker is a stage B therapy once structural disease exists.
Beta blockers are banned in all heart failure
Beta blockers are core therapy in reduced ejection fraction and a stage B recommendation. They are simply not the first choice in stage A.
Diabetes makes any drug unnecessary
Diabetes is exactly what triggers treatment in stage A: a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor.
A loop diuretic must be started first
A stage A patient has no congestion to treat. The first drug is a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor.

E.q: A 17-year-old girl began isotretinoin for severe acne three months ago. Her triglyceride has risen from 120 to 410 mg/dL, with normal thyroid and kidney function. Which is the most likely cause of the rise?
opts: Hypercholesterolemia
Hypercholesterolemia is a raised low-density lipoprotein state, not a cause of a new triglyceride rise.
Anabolic steroids
Anabolic steroids decrease high-density lipoprotein; they are not the triglyceride-raising acne therapy.
Familial chylomicronemia
Chylomicronemia usually raises triglyceride above 1000 with pancreatitis; a rise that tracks a new drug points to the drug.
Isotretinoin
Correct. Isotretinoin, used for acne, can elevate triglyceride, as can estrogen, glucocorticoids, beta blockers and bexarotene.

E.io: Pulmonic stenosis
E.q: A 27-year-old woman has echocardiogram-confirmed pulmonic stenosis that is mild. She has no symptoms and asks about her outlook. Which is the most appropriate counseling?
opts: She will need lifelong warfarin
Lifelong warfarin is for a mechanical heart valve. Mild pulmonic stenosis needs no treatment and carries an excellent 20-year survival.
Balloon valvuloplasty is needed now
Pulmonic balloon valvuloplasty is for severe pulmonic stenosis with symptoms. Mild disease needs no treatment and has 94% survival at 20 years.
No treatment; survival is excellent
Correct. Mild to moderate pulmonic stenosis needs no treatment, and survival is 94% at 20 years. Intervention is reserved for severe disease with symptoms.
Survival is about two years
About two years is the untreated survival once aortic stenosis causes heart failure. Mild pulmonic stenosis has 94% survival at 20 years.

E.io: Compare and contrast anticoagulation therapy for prosthetic heart valves.
E.q: Which drug is the most commonly used vitamin K antagonist for a mechanical valve?
opts: Warfarin

Correct. Warfarin is the most commonly used vitamin K antagonist, the long-term anticoagulant for mechanical heart valves; if surgery requires heparin instead, warfarin is bridged until the ratio is therapeutic.
Heparin
Heparin is not a vitamin K antagonist; it is the bridging agent used around surgery. The most common vitamin K antagonist is warfarin.
Aspirin
Aspirin is an antiplatelet agent, and antiplatelets are ranked below vitamin K antagonists for mechanical valves. The vitamin K antagonist is warfarin.
Clopidogrel
Clopidogrel is an antiplatelet agent, not a vitamin K antagonist. The most commonly used vitamin K antagonist is warfarin.

E.topic: ST-elevation infarction and right ventricular infarct
E.io: ST segment elevation
E.q: A 68-year-old woman with right ventricular infarction (ST elevation in V4R) is given sublingual nitroglycerin in triage, and her blood pressure falls to 70/40 mmHg. What explains the fall?
opts: Ventricular aneurysm
A ventricular aneurysm develops later as a complication of infarction. An abrupt fall after nitroglycerin in right ventricular infarction is from lost preload.
Lost preload

Correct. Nitroglycerin reduces preload, which removes the Frank-Starling effect the injured right ventricle depends on. Output drops further, the right ventricle fails and the patient goes into shock.
Myocardial rupture
Myocardial rupture is a mechanical complication of infarction, not the immediate effect of a nitrate. Here nitroglycerin removed the preload the right ventricle needs.
Thrombolytic bleeding
Thrombolytics carry a risk of intracerebral hemorrhage, but she received nitroglycerin, not a thrombolytic. The fall comes from lost preload to the right ventricle.

E.io: Distinguish between acute and chronic hypotension
E.q: A 34-year-old man is brought in after taking a large quantity of a relative's blood pressure pills. His pressure dropped suddenly over the past hour and he is dizzy. How is his hypotension best classified?
opts: Acute hypotension from a toxic cause
Correct. Medication-mediated overdose is a toxic cause of acute hypotension, which is of sudden onset, usually symptomatic and tied to a specific trigger.
Chronic hypotension from a cardiac cause
Chronic hypotension comes from cardiogenic causes such as cardiomyopathy and waxes and wanes over time.
Long-lasting acute infectious hypotension
Infection causes long-lasting acute hypotension, and nothing here suggests bacteremia or sepsis.
Neurogenic orthostatic hypotension
Neurogenic orthostatic hypotension is a postural fall from autonomic failure, not a sudden drop after an overdose.

E.q: A 68-year-old smoker with peripheral arterial disease has blood pressure of 168/94 despite three agents. An abdominal bruit is audible, ultrasound shows a right kidney 2 cm smaller than the left, and he has had two episodes of sudden pulmonary edema. What is the most likely underlying cause?
opts: Obstructive sleep apnea
Sleep apnea contributes to resistant hypertension, but through nocturnal sympathetic activation, without bruits or asymmetric kidneys.
Primary aldosteronism
Aldosteronism also presents with resistant hypertension, but with unexplained hypokalemia rather than asymmetric kidneys and an abdominal bruit.
Renovascular disease

Correct. The cluster is characteristic: resistant pressure, an abdominal bruit, asymmetric kidneys and recurrent flash pulmonary edema. In an older patient with established vascular disease the mechanism is atherosclerotic stenosis, often bilateral and progressive.
Chronic kidney disease from diabetes
Diabetic kidney disease reduces both kidneys' function together rather than producing a 2 cm size discrepancy with a bruit.

E.q: A 12-year-old boy with confirmed homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia has total cholesterol of 610 mg/dL on a high-intensity statin with ezetimibe. What is the treatment of choice for his disorder?
opts: Very low-fat diet alone for a year
A very low-fat diet is advised for triglyceride above 500 mg/dL; diet alone cannot correct a receptor defect.
Low-density lipoprotein apheresis

Correct. Apheresis is the treatment of choice, like dialysis: the elective removal of low-density particles from the circulation. Most patients also need several drugs, starting with high-intensity statins.
Add a fibrate for his triglyceride
Triglyceride is normal in familial hypercholesterolemia, so a fibrate targets the wrong lipid.
Switch to a moderate-intensity statin
Lowering statin intensity moves in the wrong direction; high-intensity statins are the usual regimen alongside apheresis.

E.io: Compare and contrast precipitating factors, clinical manifestations, diagnosis (including role of B-type natriuretic peptide, BNP), and treatment of acute decompensated heart failure.
E.q: A 60-year-old woman wore a defibrillator vest for three months after an infarction, with optimized guideline-directed therapy and cardiac rehabilitation. Her repeat echocardiogram shows an ejection fraction of 28%. She is class II and expected to live many years. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Heart transplant evaluation now
Transplant is reserved for failure that cannot be controlled. She is class II and meets the criteria for an implantable defibrillator.
Implantable cardioverter-defibrillator

Correct. The pathway ends with an implantable device when the repeat echocardiogram shows no improvement. She also meets the criteria: ejection fraction 35% or less, class II or III, optimal therapy and life expectancy of at least one year.
Stop therapy and recheck in a year
Stopping therapy would undo the optimization. With no improvement, the next step is an implantable defibrillator.
Continue the vest indefinitely
The vest bridges the recovery period. With no improvement on the repeat echocardiogram, the next step is an implantable defibrillator.

E.q: A 46-year-old woman with microvascular angina asks which factor tends to go along with her episodes. Her coronary arteries were normal on angiography. What should she be told?
opts: Cocaine or amphetamine use
Cocaine and amphetamine are drugs that precipitate vasospastic angina, not the association described for microvascular angina, which is stress or anxiety.
Triptan migraine therapy
Triptans can precipitate vasospastic angina and are avoided in it. The factor described for microvascular angina is stress or anxiety.
Stress or anxiety

Correct. Microvascular angina is more frequent in women and is often associated with stress or anxiety. Proposed mechanisms include endothelial dysfunction, insulin resistance and estrogen deficiency.
The hours after midnight
Episodes between midnight and early morning describe vasospastic angina. Microvascular angina is often associated with stress or anxiety and is more frequent in women.

E.io: Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing (including ordering and interpretation), management (acute and chronic, including applicable rehabilitative and palliative care), appropriate referrals, patient education, prevention, and prognosis for heart failure.
E.q: A 61-year-old woman has had left-sided heart failure with reduced ejection fraction for five years. Over two months she has developed leg edema, jugular venous distension (distended neck veins), an enlarged liver, nausea and poor appetite. Which is the most likely explanation for her new findings?
opts: Primary liver disease with ascites
The enlarged liver here is congestion from right ventricular failure, which also explains her distended neck veins and edema.
Right-sided failure from her left-sided failure

Correct. Chronic left-sided failure is the most common cause of right-sided failure. Systemic overload gives edema and distended neck veins; portal overload gives nausea, poor appetite and hepatomegaly.
Worsening systolic failure of the left only
Left-sided worsening would add orthopnea and crackles. Edema, neck veins and portal congestion mean the right ventricle has now failed.
High-output failure from increased demand
High-output failure comes from anemia, hyperthyroidism or an arteriovenous fistula. Her picture is right-sided failure following chronic left-sided disease.

E.io: Mitral stenosis
E.q: A 39-year-old woman who emigrated from a country where rheumatic fever is common has breathlessness on exertion and orthopnea (breathlessness lying flat). A diastolic rumble is heard at the apex. Which is the most appropriate initial test?
opts: Electrocardiogram only
An electrocardiogram may show left atrial abnormality or atrial fibrillation, but it does not show the valve. Suggestive symptoms call for an echocardiogram.
No test until symptoms worsen
She already has suggestive symptoms, and dyspnea on exertion or orthopnea is the trigger for an echocardiogram. Waiting would miss a treatable stenosis.
Transthoracic echocardiogram
Correct. Any patient with symptoms suggestive of mitral stenosis, such as dyspnea on exertion or orthopnea, should get an echocardiogram. It shows a large left atrium and the stenotic mitral valve.
Cardiac catheterization
Cardiac catheterization is not necessary for mitral stenosis and is usually done for an ischemic evaluation. The test that answers her symptoms is a transthoracic echocardiogram.

E.io: Tricuspid regurgitation
E.q: What is the most common cause of tricuspid regurgitation?
opts: Endocarditis from intravenous drug use
Endocarditis in intravenous drug users is the primary cause of tricuspid regurgitation, but not the most common. That is annular dilation with pulmonary hypertension.
Rheumatic scarring of the leaflets
Rheumatic scarring leads to stenosis of the mitral valve and, worldwide, the tricuspid valve. Tricuspid regurgitation most often follows annular dilation.
Pulmonary hypertension dilating the annulus

Correct. Tricuspid regurgitation is most commonly due to dilation of the tricuspid annulus from right ventricular dilation in the setting of pulmonary hypertension. Primary disease is infective endocarditis in drug users.
Carcinoid disease of the valve
Carcinoid disease is listed for pulmonic and tricuspid stenosis and pulmonic regurgitation. Tricuspid regurgitation most often follows annular dilation.

E.io: ST segment elevation
E.q: Lead V4 belongs to which territory?
opts: Septal
The septal leads are V1 and V2. V4 sits with V3 in the anterior group; both anterior and septal changes point to the left anterior descending artery.
Inferior
The inferior leads are the limb leads II, III and aVF. V4 is a precordial lead in the anterior group, with V3.
Anterior
Correct. V1 and V2 are septal and V3 and V4 anterior, while V5 and V6 join I and aVL as lateral. Read from V3 to V1 the groups spell A-S-S, and from V4 to V6 A-L-L.
Lateral
The lateral leads are I, aVL, V5 and V6. V4 sits with V3 in the anterior group, both pointing to the left anterior descending artery.

E.io: Hypertension: classification, subtypes, effects on target organs, etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis
E.q: How do hyperthyroidism and hypothyroidism differ in their effect on blood pressure?
opts: Hyperthyroidism raises systolic; hypothyroidism raises diastolic

Correct, and the heart rate separates them further: tachycardia accompanies the systolic pattern and bradycardia the diastolic one, so the pulse points to which is operating. Hyperthyroidism does it by raising cardiac output, hypothyroidism by raising vascular resistance.
Hyperthyroidism raises vascular resistance and hypothyroidism raises output
The mechanisms are the other way round: raised output belongs to hyperthyroidism and raised resistance to hypothyroidism.
Neither affects blood pressure
Both are described as contributors, which is why thyroid-stimulating hormone is among the baseline screening tests.
Both raise systolic pressure with tachycardia
Only hyperthyroidism produces that pattern. Hypothyroidism raises vascular resistance with diastolic elevation and bradycardia.

E.q: A 70-year-old man fainted at home and has recovered. His electrocardiogram and glucose are normal. Which tests look for an infectious or metabolic contributor?
opts: An echocardiogram and stress test
These evaluate structural and arrhythmic cardiac causes rather than infection or metabolic disturbance.
A tilt-table test and a log
A tilt-table test belongs to the tachycardia syndrome and a log to reflex syncope; neither screens for infection.
A blood count and metabolic panel
Correct. Unremarkable blood counts and a metabolic panel lower suspicion of an infectious or metabolic source, as glucose and the electrocardiogram address hypoglycemia and dysrhythmia.
Orthostatic vitals only
Orthostatic readings test for a postural fall and cannot detect an infectious or metabolic source.

E.io: Unstable
E.q: A 61-year-old man has new chest pain at rest, T-wave inversion on his electrocardiogram and a standard troponin I of 0.01 ng/mL. What does this troponin I result indicate?
opts: It is not abnormal

Correct. A standard troponin I is abnormal above 0.04 ng/mL, so 0.01 ng/mL is not abnormal. Rest pain with nonspecific T-wave changes and a normal troponin is unstable angina, and the troponin I is still repeated.
It confirms an infarction
Infarction requires an elevated troponin. A standard troponin I of 0.01 ng/mL is below the 0.04 ng/mL cut-off, which is what keeps this picture at unstable angina.
It needs no repeat draw
One troponin I value never stands alone: when you get one, you get two, because a rising second value changes the diagnosis. His 0.01 ng/mL standard troponin I is repeated.
It is abnormal for a man
Sex-specific cut-offs belong to the high-sensitivity troponin I (20 ng/L in men). A standard troponin I is abnormal above 0.04 ng/mL for anyone, and 0.01 ng/mL is not.

E.q: A 44-year-old man with a sedentary job has a triglyceride of 280 mg/dL, low-density lipoprotein of 165 mg/dL and non-high-density cholesterol of 205 mg/dL. He has no xanthomas. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Familial chylomicronemia syndrome
Chylomicronemia has fasting triglyceride usually above 1000 with pancreatitis and eruptive xanthomas.
Homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia
The homozygous form presents in childhood with total cholesterol of about 400 to above 1000 and normal triglyceride.
Mixed dyslipidemia
Correct. Triglyceride above 150 with low-density lipoprotein above 130 or non-high-density above 160 defines mixed dyslipidemia, the most common type in clinical practice.
Severe hypertriglyceridemia
The severe form needs triglyceride above 500 mg/dL, usually without raised low-density lipoprotein.

E.io: Angina pectoris
E.q: A 68-year-old woman with long-standing diabetes and peripheral neuropathy has had two days of shortness of breath, nausea and fatigue, with no chest pain. Which is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Reassure her and send her home
The absence of chest pain does not exclude ischemia in diabetes or neuropathy; these patients have silent ischemia. She needs a stat electrocardiogram first.
Obtain a stat electrocardiogram

Correct. Chest discomfort may be absent in silent ischemia, which occurs with diabetes, peripheral neuropathy and a transplanted heart. Dyspnea, nausea and fatigue can be the presentation, and every chest pain workup starts with a stat electrocardiogram.
Order an outpatient stress test
A stress test belongs to the stable workup. Possible acute ischemia presenting silently needs a stat electrocardiogram now, not a delayed outpatient study.
Treat as viral gastroenteritis
Nausea and fatigue in a patient with diabetes and neuropathy may be silent ischemia. Labeling it gastroenteritis skips the stat electrocardiogram she needs.

E.io: Differentiate each stage of the American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association (ACC/AHA), natural history classification of heart failure, and associated treatment recommendations of each stage.
E.q: A 50-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes and a normal echocardiogram asks whether she should take metoprolol, as her father did, to prevent heart failure. Which reply is most accurate?
opts: Dapagliflozin comes first, not a beta blocker

Correct. As an at-risk patient with diabetes and a normal heart she is stage A, where the first recommended drug is a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor such as dapagliflozin or empagliflozin. A beta blocker enters at stage B.
A loop diuretic is the preventive drug
Loop diuretics relieve congestion and do not prevent heart failure. In stage A with diabetes the first drug is a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor.
Metoprolol is the first drug for prevention
A beta blocker is not the first drug in stage A. For an at-risk patient with diabetes the recommended first drug is a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor.
No drug helps until symptoms appear
Stage A with diabetes carries a strong drug recommendation before any symptoms: a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor.

E.q: A 70-year-old man with hypertension and atrial fibrillation is on metoprolol. A colleague suggests adding verapamil for rate control and blood pressure. What is the concern?
opts: Dependent ankle edema
Ankle edema is the commonest effect of the DIHYDROPYRIDINE calcium channel blockers rather than a hazard of this pairing.
Hyperkalemia and acute kidney injury
Hyperkalemia and kidney injury follow dual renin-angiotensin blockade rather than this combination.
Severe bradycardia and heart block
Correct. Both agents slow the sinus and atrioventricular nodes, so combining them stacks the same effect. Both are also avoided where the ejection fraction is already reduced.
Rebound hypertension on withdrawal
Rebound on abrupt withdrawal is a limitation of the central alpha-2 agonists such as clonidine.

E.q: A 57-year-old man with confirmed resistant hypertension has had his diuretic optimized and his other two agents titrated to maximally tolerated doses. His filtration rate and potassium are normal. Which fourth agent has the most evidence?
opts: Hydralazine
Hydralazine is a later addition and requires combination therapy because of reflex tachycardia and fluid retention.
Spironolactone
Correct, provided the filtration rate and potassium allow. It is added after the foundational three are optimized rather than instead of doing so.
A beta blocker
Beta blockade appears among the later escalation options chosen by physiology and comorbidity rather than as the evidence-supported fourth agent.
A second dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker
Adding a second agent of the same class is not among the described steps and duplicates a mechanism.

E.q: A 60-year-old woman without diabetes has a 10-year atherosclerotic risk of 11% and an uncertain statin decision. She has never smoked and has no family history of premature disease. Her coronary artery calcium score is zero. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Start a high-intensity statin
High intensity is for clinical disease, very high low-density lipoprotein or high 10-year risk, not a zero calcium score.
Order a skin biopsy
Skin biopsy confirms homozygous familial hypercholesterolemia and plays no part in this decision.
Add ezetimibe now
Ezetimibe is an add-on to a maximal statin in very high-risk disease, not a primary-prevention starter.
Withhold or delay the statin
Correct. A calcium score of zero lowers risk, so statin therapy may be withheld or delayed, except in cigarette smokers, diabetes or a strong family history of premature disease.

E.topic: Post-infarction care and sudden cardiac death
E.io: Acute myocardial infraction
E.q: A 59-year-old man is ready for discharge after an ST-elevation myocardial infarction. His heart rate is 78/min with no bradycardia. Which drug class improves survival rates across the board after infarction?
opts: Glycoprotein 2b/3a inhibitor
Glycoprotein 2b/3a inhibitors have fallen out of favor and are not a survival therapy after discharge. The class that improves survival rates across the board is the beta blocker.
Beta blocker
Correct. Beta blockers improve survival rates across the board after myocardial infarction, so they belong in post-infarction management unless bradycardia or another contraindication is present.
Sublingual nitroglycerin
Sublingual nitroglycerin relieves anginal pain as needed but carries no survival claim. The post-infarction class that improves survival across the board is the beta blocker.
Calcium channel blocker

Calcium channel blockers do not improve prognosis overall after infarction; only diltiazem and verapamil reduce mortality, and only with preserved left ventricular function. Beta blockers improve survival across the board.

E.q: Which is a coronary heart disease risk equivalent?
opts: Low dietary fiber
Fiber intake is a lifestyle measure, not a condition that carries the same risk as established coronary heart disease.
Borderline triglyceride of 170
Borderline triglyceride of 150 to 199 is a lab category, not a coronary heart disease risk equivalent.
Isolated high-density lipoprotein of 65
A high-density lipoprotein of 60 or more is protective and counts as a negative risk factor, the opposite of a risk equivalent.
Diabetes mellitus
Correct. Coronary risk equivalents include diabetes mellitus, peripheral arterial disease, abdominal aortic aneurysm, symptomatic carotid disease and a Framingham risk above 20%.

E.io: Mitral valve prolapse
E.q: A 24-year-old woman has a mid-systolic click at the apex. An echocardiogram is ordered. Which finding confirms the suspected valve problem?
opts: A calcified, narrowed aortic valve
Thickened, calcified aortic leaflets with reduced opening are the echo finding of aortic stenosis. Prolapse shows thickened, redundant mitral leaflets.
Thick, redundant mitral leaflets

Correct. Mitral valve prolapse is diagnosed by echocardiogram showing thickened, redundant mitral leaflets greater than 5 mm, flaring into the left atrium during systole, from myxomatous degeneration.
A dilated tricuspid annulus
A dilated tricuspid annulus causes tricuspid regurgitation in pulmonary hypertension. The echo finding of prolapse is thickened, redundant mitral leaflets.
A dilated aortic root
A dilated aortic root is a cause of aortic regurgitation found on echo. Prolapse is confirmed by thickened, redundant mitral leaflets over 5 mm.

E.io: Define the following diagnostic and therapeutic groups of HF patients, and the treatment implications/recommendations for each group: a. HF with reduced EF (HFrEF) b. HF with mildly reduced EF (HFmrEF) c. HF with preserved EF (HFpEF)
E.q: A 61-year-old man with reduced ejection fraction asks why his clinician raises one medicine at a time rather than starting everything at full strength. Which explanation is accurate?
opts: Only one drug can be taken at once
Reduced ejection fraction uses several classes together. They are increased step by step as blood pressure and tolerance allow.
Medicines stop once symptoms go
Therapy aims to improve survival and slow progression as well as symptoms, so it continues. It is optimized as tolerated.
Therapy is optimized as tolerated
Correct. Guideline-directed therapy is prioritized for his comorbidities and optimized as hemodynamically stable, so each class is increased as blood pressure and tolerance allow.
Full doses are unsafe in any patient
The point is not a universal ban on full doses. Therapy is optimized as hemodynamically stable, increasing each class as tolerated.

E.io: Acute myocardial infraction
E.q: Which test shows a regional wall motion abnormality?
opts: Echocardiogram
Correct. Regional wall motion abnormalities (hypokinesia, akinesia, dyskinesia) are seen on an echocardiogram, which images the moving walls of the ventricle segment by segment.
Troponin I level
Troponin I shows myocardial injury in the blood, not how a wall moves. Hypokinesia, akinesia and dyskinesia are seen on an echocardiogram.
Calcium score
A computed tomography calcium score stratifies long-term risk and does not show movement. Regional wall motion is assessed on an echocardiogram.
Chest radiograph
A chest radiograph is part of every chest pain workup, but it shows the lungs and silhouette, not wall movement. Wall motion is seen on an echocardiogram.

E.q: A 60-year-old man is newly diagnosed with heart failure and will start a loop diuretic. Which laboratory panel should be checked before starting?
opts: Complete metabolic panel
Correct. The metabolic panel gives potassium and renal function (blood urea nitrogen, creatinine and filtration rate), both of which a potassium-wasting loop diuretic affects.
Coagulation panel
Clotting tests are not the pre-diuretic check. Potassium and renal function come from the complete metabolic panel.
Hepatic function panel
Liver tests are not what the diuretic calls for. Potassium and renal function come from the complete metabolic panel.
Thyroid function panel
Thyroid testing is not the pre-diuretic check. Potassium and renal function come from the complete metabolic panel.

E.q: A 21-year-old woman has just been diagnosed with postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome after her heart rate rose by 38 within 10 minutes of standing. Which is the most appropriate first treatment?
opts: Increase water and salt intake
Correct. Increasing water and salt intake is the first listed treatment, with fludrocortisone as the drug best suited to the syndrome.
Start midodrine
Midodrine is best with neurogenic syncope, a postural pressure fall from autonomic failure, not this syndrome.
Begin vasopressin
Vasopressin is a pressor reserved for the emergency department and intensive care, not an outpatient syndrome.
Restrict salt and fluid
Restriction runs opposite to the treatment, which increases water and salt intake.
